To inform system designers, it's essential to develop a system utilization model that accounts for aerial UAVs and ground sensors working together. To achieve this goal, this paper utilizes a queueing network model incorporating certain factors. It accurately models the interaction between UAVs and ground sensors through their use of wireless backhaul links when designing a system. Performance metrics such as waiting times, reception rates, and complex data analysis such as probability distributions and those which are difficult to calculate, such as VaR and PD-Fit, are also evaluated. A Two-Ray model is utilized to inform a receive signal power analysis. To validate the model's accuracy, simulation results showing certain characteristics are presented.

The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) is a comprehensive experiment designed to investigate the properties of neutrinos with a high-energy density detector. Equipped with a substantial amount of proton density, the DUNE detector has remarkable potential to detect rare signals, such as the proton decay, which is a significant indication of new physical phenomena beyond standard theories. This study provides an in-depth examination of the proton decay detection capabilities of DUNE, employing various theoretical models for neutrinos and hadron physics, and utilizing the most recent predictions for proton decay lifetimes to determine the performance of the DUNE detector. Based on the analysis, the DUNE experiment is expected to achieve breakthroughs in detecting rare signals with distinct characteristics, such as duration and energy patterns, and will set definitive limits on the proton decay rates for multiple neutrino theory hypotheses.

The Shapley framework has revolutionized our understanding of feature importance within machine learning, allowing comprehensive evaluations of pre-trained models via post-training analyses. By empirically examining features in isolated instances, feature importance measures how contributions to outcomes arise from individual features or groups. The paper introduces a broad Shapley framework, encompassing existing methods and new approaches like a contextual addition to understand feature importance. The framework also highlights inconsistencies and limitations in existing metrics, as well as a new divergence measure for feature importance. The research demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed addition in producing features with low information gain according to SHAP, as well as its ability to offer unique insights into datasets like IMDB, demonstrating its potential in explaining and generating text.

This paper presents a conceptual framework for Understanding Voctions, specifically the mechanisms driving Voctional online community development, which act as drivers of abstract concept exploration within the knowledge base. By studying the principles of natural language and philosophical inquiry into implicit meaning, we have derived a method to identify and classify the Voctional principles guiding each creator's content creation, known as Voctional postulates. Through an in-depth analysis of 321 Google Keep notes from 150 creators, we have developed a system to both measure the frequency of Voctional postulates and map their relationships, ultimately revealing the evolutionary stages of Voctional online community development through logical combinations of these postulates. By introducing the concept of 'vacillating Voctional states', our study provides a predictive framework for the progress of Voctional online community development, pointing out challenges for their theoretical and practical implications.

Off-policy reinforcement learning using policy gradient methods can be an efficient approach for tackling partially-observed environments. Yet, policy gradient estimation is often hampered by variance, especially when using unweighted, off-policy trial data to estimate gradients. To overcome this limitation, we've developed a variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) framework incorporating a Strang-Cordex scheme with an adapted weighted moving average. VRER introduces a novel weighted replay buffer and uses a mean square error loss that adjusts for biased gradient estimation. We provide theoretical evidence that the VRER framework reduces the variance of policy gradient estimation relative to conventional methods. Furthermore, we've implemented a VRER-based improvement to the state-of-the-art PPO (2) (proximal policy optimization version 2) algorithm and tested its performance against P(2) on a range of benchmark environments. The results show that the proposed VRER-based P(2) outperformed the original P(2) in all trials, ultimately achieving higher scores in every evaluation trial.

Utilizing superbosonization, an innovative technique, we demonstrate the equivalence between a generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula. This discovery opens up the possibility of employing superbosonization to transform the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation back into a Gaussian action, which can then be easily evaluated. We successfully apply this approach to the model of the superconducting superfluid, resulting in a new Gaussian action that allows for a straightforward calculation of the superconducting superfluid model's partition function.

The Detail Context Block, a proposed module for spatiotemporal learning, employs an efficient attention mechanism that effectively incorporates spatial and temporal context while minimizing computational requirements, maintaining a complexity of O(n) despite using these larger contexts. By augmenting each target point with neighboring details, the DCB significantly enhances model accuracy both in single-target and multi-target prediction tasks, notably in tasks like gesture recognition in RGB images and resonance position prediction in audio signals. Evaluations demonstrate that the Detail Context Block outperforms state-of-the-art methods with a notable margin in both training and test phases, yielding an accuracy gain of 4-10% across various datasets.

Imperative language fault tolerance through effect tracking has become more widespread in recent times, incorporating features like error handling, resource management, and more, which can create conflicts in execution and consequently faults. Typically, ensuring the safe execution of such tracked effects across multiple pathways in a program necessitates a thorough check of the code, often resulting in a significant performance trade-off. This research proposes a type system capable of checking for valid coexistence of tracked effects in object-oriented languages with such mechanisms, offering more flexibility and efficiency compared to conventional checks. The proposed approach focuses on these languages because they pose the greatest challenge in implementing checked exception handling. The theoretical foundation of this type system is rooted in a verifiable checking framework called 'eeft', which allows for the safe mixing of tracked effects in methods and classes, followed by a practical implementation of this theory into the Spoofy programming language. The goal of this type system is to aid developers in writing 'eeft'-compliant code, reducing the number of faults that may arise during program execution by marking areas with potential errors and preventing unwanted effect flows. The type system's overall aim is to implement a checked mechanism for tracked effects that strikes a balance between being conservative and accurate, based on the underlying concept that a type system is best suited for checked exception handling in object-oriented languages.

A concept of chiral e-color is introduced, serving as a suitable quantum number for heavy neutral leptons to induce lepton number violation in tree-level particle interactions. Heavy neutral leptons, possessing one unit of e-color, may be part of a fermion non-SUSY extension of the electroweak sector, which remains compatible with existing data. This sector includes six particles: four singlet fermions and two dark leptons, with properties similar to neutrinos and serving as dark states. Under a $Z_2$ symmetry, e-color is the sole non-trivial charge, while it matches the corresponding $U(1)_{L_\psi}$ charge, introduced by Grossman and Zaidi, at the quantum level. This sector's discovery is likely to occur at the LHC during the latter stages of its current run due to its expected low production cross-section. In the second part of this paper, the model receives an extension through $U(1)_{N_5}$. In response, dark leptons, gaining e-color charge, may be produced in various processes at the LHC, including those facilitated by photons and hadrons. With sufficient luminosity, this sector's discovery is likely to take place at the LHC in upcoming experiments, while also being within existing data constraints.

This study presents an innovative joint decoding approach for pre-transformed polar codes under both systematic and non-systematic formats. The proposed method enables efficient use of cyclic redundancy check (CRC) aid decoding by incorporating CRC check in the decoder, effectively eliminating incorrect decisions in the decoder. Unlike existing joint decoding techniques, the proposed approach enables the use of CRC aid without increasing the receiver complexity. Building upon this foundation, a new joint decoding approach is introduced for systematic polar codes with CRC, involving the parallel use of error correction capabilities in the upper and lower halves of the code. Experimental results show that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing joint decoding approaches for both systematic and non-systematic codes, with performance comparable to CRC-aided capacity under infinite SNR and SNR values above 5, in scenarios with limited SNR values down to 3.

The lack of uniformity in the noise characteristics among stars across diverse spatial and temporal distributions, as resulting from the application of non-linear coaddition techniques, poses a challenge for the uniformity of the photometric calibration system. Unlike their linear counterparts, algorithms such as median and clipped-mean fail to maintain a consistent profile for the point spread function due to their non-linear nature. As a result, calibrations based on these methods produce inconsistent results among stars of different colors. To overcome this limitation, we have introduced a novel algorithm aimed at eliminating spatial and temporal noise while maintaining a consistent profile for the point spread function and the noise properties. This algorithm, derived from the Bayesian noise modeling framework, demonstrates the ability to produce results analogous to those obtained from homogeneous, independent data sets. Furthermore, our work highlights the significance of incorporating prior knowledge of the PSF in the noise modeling process to produce accurate results.

A theoretical study has been conducted to examine the development of sharp cracks within a soft elastic material lacking memory and the associated fracture characteristics. By leveraging a variational model describing linearly incompatible compressible solids developed by Kohn and Vogelius in 1984, the research provides an analysis of both plain and notch-fractured specimens. We discover that a type of instability at the tip of an notch leads to an accurate prediction of the notch-initiation stress, which further aligns with the predictions generated by a prominent fracture theory established by Kachanov in 1958. Moreover, the research demonstrates that this type of instability at the notch tip exhibits similarities with the linear-elastic Paris-law associated with progressive cracks in other types of materials. It is worth noting that the model developed in this study has recently been applied in the manufacturing of soft-exponential metamaterials by E. Azari, J. Eslinger, and S. Guz zhang in 2021.

We introduce the concept of chordal Schramm--Loewner evolution, an extension of the Schramm--Loewner evolution with the ability to cross, and prove its equivalent status as an imaginary surface. Additionally, we establish a relationship between this evolution and conformal welding, specifically that it can be derived from the combination of two pre-images of beta/gamma dual trees, and further that these pre-images themselves constitute a beta/gamma dual tree in a specific sense. As an outcome of this connection, we develop a new method for constructing loop-erased and self-referential SLEs.

This study establishes the existence of local and global solutions for the Navier-Stokes equations in a specific fractional power-continuous domain using the maximum initial value theorem and the concept of fractional derivatives. By repeatedly applying the maximum initial value theorem, it shows that the Navier-Stokes equations' solution with initial data in a specified fractional space has derivatives whose maximum value does not exceed a constant times the maximum initial data value, provided that the initial data is not too large and the time frame of interest is not too short. The work enables the derivation of upper bounds for the solution's maximum norm in terms of relevant physical parameters and fractional norms of the initial data, valid for an infinite duration of time. The results are then validated with the assistance of a specific example.

Our new CVQC protocol, specifically the PoS version, offers the fastest verification time among existing quantum computing verifiers, specifically 5 time units. This is because our CVQC protocol verifies a computation in just one time unit, making it significantly faster. To achieve this, we utilize a novel quantum verification approach that can check every qubit of a quantum computation at once, instead of verifying each one individually as traditional methods do. This faster verification time allows CVQC to complete verification nearly twice as quickly as the fastest prior verifiers, specifically the QAPC and PCQDT protocols. Notably, our CVQC protocol also boasts faster average verification times in challenging scenarios, as well as lower complexity and a more modest overhead compared to prior methods.

Integrating blockchain technology into supply chain management has generated significant interest as a way to enhance transparency, trust, and validity. To build efficient blockchain systems, novel consensus mechanisms that minimize computational and storage usage are being created. Unlike traditional consensus algorithms, which focus on a single type of node (computers or IoT devices), many proposed mechanisms support diverse network configurations (homogeneous or heterogeneous). However, in a multi-agent system consisting of IoT devices and computers working together, which is ideal for supply chain management applications, the LC4IoT consensus is the first to utilize linear cryptography for IoT applications. This new consensus algorithm aims to speed up the block creation process, reduce computational and storage usage on IoT devices, and improve transparency and trustfulness by incorporating multiple block generators. We have carried out extensive simulations to validate the LC4IoT consensus and the results show that it outperforms existing algorithms in terms of block propagation speed, reduces computational and storage usage on IoT devices by more than 90%, and enhances transparency and trustfulness.

For the analysis of cells, shapes, and functions, cells are the most basic units 
of biological systems that need to be studied. Developing accurate cell segmentation 
requires tracking cells across consecutive images of the same location over time. 
Improving cell tracking techniques can significantly benefit from synthetic data generated 
using deep generative models, particularly in scenarios with limited labeled data available. 
However, existing deep learning-based methods for cell tracking, although highly performing, 
are prone to errors when dealing with rare cell trajectories or when local features confuse 
the tracking process in crowded environments. In contrast, approach, which combines several 
models, effectively synthesizes a vast amount of annotated data, thus boosting the efficiency 
of cell tracking. Our research on combined demonstrates the potential for significant enhancements 
in the detection and localization of cells, as well as overall accuracy, when using data created 
with the help of deep learning. Our research on combined demonstrates the potential for significant 
improvements in the detection and localization of cells, as well as overall accuracy, when using 
data enriched with the help of deep learning. Our method effectively utilizes data created with the 
help of deep learning to produce new information and thus boost the performance of cell 
tracking in various challenging scenarios. Our method effectively utilizes data created with the 
help of deep learning to produce new information and thus boost the performance of cell 
tracking in various challenging scenarios. Our research on combined demonstrates the potential 
for significant improvements in the detection and localization of cells

This research offers a novel vision-based approach to guide individuals, particularly those who are print-disabled, in navigating internal links within complex scientific documents like journals and papers. To aid users in accessing in-depth information quickly, modern interactive systems utilize links or shortcuts. However, for users who cannot access a computer, we focus on enhancing navigation via optical scanners or reading devices equipped with cameras, which can capture in-depth images of documents and provide real-time access to the relevant sections. Given the often faint difference between background content and text or the presence of complex layouts, accurate object detection proves challenging. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an alternative method grounded in image processing. Our proposed method incorporates specific key features - a reference icon and the section title - to facilitate navigation. After extensive testing on various documents across multiple disciplines, our approach demonstrates remarkable success in identifying reference icons and accurately locating the section titles on a wide variety of documents across multiple disciplines. To further compare performance, we also evaluated how accurate our approach is in finding the section titles when compared to actual manual annotations.

Extreme classification, where the possible outcomes are few and distinct, is encountered in news categorization and emotion recognition. Deep neural networks have shown superior performance in these areas but have struggled with the scarcity of labeled data. Contrary to traditional approaches, recent methods, including BERT and PLSM, have achieved exceptional success by ignoring the scarcity of data and instead relying on pre-trained models. Unfortunately, these methods remain costly in computational resources. Our research proposes XPoKE, a high-performance extreme learning method, which uses pre-trained models like XLNet and applies a novel, efficient technique to overcome the scarcity of data. Our experiments demonstrate XPoKE achieves the best results on benchmark datasets, outperforming XLNet and PLSM in accuracy and computational efficiency, with a notable reduction in training time to just minutes from hours or days.

The identification of binary star systems as hosts to exoplanets is a typical case when starting to investigate the planetary system. However, distinguishing whether spectral line broadening is primarily due to the rapid gravitational pull of a planet or the stellar contamination that occurs during orbital motion requires more specific analysis. To address this challenge, we employed high-resolution spectroscopic techniques to monitor the radial velocity variations of two known exoplanets transit-observed in binary star systems: KPD 3526, which may harbor a Jupiter-like planet and an additional J-uparc system with the potential for a smaller planet, as well as LTT 1448, which is associated with a possible Neptune-like planet in a binary system consisting of two low-mass stars. Our spectroscopic investigation revealed radial velocity patterns that are consistent with gravitational pull caused by two distinct objects: a massive object similar to a Jupiter-type planet and a second object whose properties are still undetermined. In the case of KPD 3526, we propose that the secondary object could be a low-mass star or a normal sub-stellar component due to radial velocity patterns that are consistent with the findings of Mart\'i-nez et al. Additionally, we found no conclusive evidence of the Neptune-like uparc in LTT 1448; nonetheless, our data suggest the presence of a sub-stellar object with a mass not exceeding 30 Jupiter masses. To further investigate the uparc in KPD 3526 and rule out the possibility of a

We classify topologically non-trivial complete metrics with constant curvature on the sphere possessing a specified number of conical singularities at non-polar points, and we demonstrate that such metrics are uniquely determined by their curvature and singularities. Conversely, we verify that it's possible to choose the spherical triholomorphism in a way that leads to non-trivial connectedness. Furthermore, using federal properties, we expand these findings to cover the case of complete metrics with constant curvature on the sphere possessing any number of conical singularities at non-polar points.

The physics behind a creature's movement through fluidic environments can be
explained by using an advanced mathematical model. A well-studied centipede model,
comprising straight body segments connected by joints, has been analyzed in a fluid
environment in the past. However, the new research focuses on 'flexible' centipedes
with only one degree of freedom. By employing computational methods to solve the
Navier-Stokes equations, the researchers found that the drag caused by the movement
of fluid waves can significantly impact a creature's swimming speed. Interestingly,
increasing the fluidic drag can enhance swimming performance, a finding that contradicts
the influence of inertia. Therefore, the findings suggest that fluidic drag has a more
critical role in enhancing movement efficiency than inertia. The research also indicates
that flexible bodies can use their elasticity to overcome the barriers to movement and
improve their overall efficiency. Finally, the study demonstrates that at high swimming
speeds, the movement of fluidic waves can lead to a'snaking' motion that allows for
more efficient gliding at high speeds.

A proposed hybrid methodology, referred to as adaptive simulation, enables the bridge between deep ocean to coastal zone modeling during tsunami events. This approach involves running complex tsunami models with high resolution in spatial and temporal scales in the open ocean, where hydrodynamic features are dominant, whereas coarser-resolution models, incorporating additional water quality processes, take over in the more complex coastal zone. The boundary conditions between these models are updated regularly based on detailed results, allowing for improved accuracy and efficient computation. The method is demonstrated in the Mozambique Channel and coastal zone of Mozambique, specifically during the most impactful tsunami of the 20th century, the one attributed to the rupture of the Mozambique-Swaziland Fault. The update frequency of the boundary conditions plays a crucial role in the results accuracy in the coastal zone models.

Detecting massive galaxies beyond redshift 3 through spectroscopy is essential for completing the cosmic census during the reionization era. By combining data from various sources, a potential massive galaxy candidate was found, AzGI1, based on observations conducted with VIMOS and SPIRou on the Coma cluster at redshifts around 3.2. These observations were supported by photometric data from several sources. Further spectroscopic observations conducted with SPIRou confirmed the massive galaxy hypothesis by identifying a broad Lyman-alpha absorption feature and overall agreement with the predicted redshifts. By identifying a clear emission line, AzGI1's redshift was precisely determined as 3.43, making it the largest known giant halo at redshift 3, and estimating its stellar mass as 1.46 x 10^11 solar masses. This discovery was further validated by comparing the Lyman-alpha absorption against the predicted redshifts from the candidate's photometric data. As a result, AzGI1, a massive galaxy at redshift 3.43, was identified as the largest known giant halo, and its Lyman-beta flux was used to estimate the predicted Lyman-alpha flux in the candidate's spectral profile. Additionally, AzGI1's metallicity was estimated as around 0.02 and 0.06, and its expected Lyman-alpha flux was calculated to be around two times the detection limit of the current SPIRou equipment.

Recently, four-dimensional Einstein spaces have been studied in a novel framework of four-dimensional gravity. This led to discovering rotating black holes and boson star solutions within it. In this research, we expand upon such findings and explore their five-dimensional analogs, yielding novel applications within the framework. Specifically, we have derived rotating black holes and boson stars in five-dimensional spacetime. Notably, our solutions contain rotating AdS$^5$ black holes and pure boson star spacetimes, as well as novel combinations of these types. Moreover, our solution set encompasses all known rotating solutions within the framework, including DMOS and CH solutions. In addition to these discoveries, we have utilized the Poincaré patch approach and studied the thermodynamic properties and phase structures of these five-dimensional solutions.

We investigate two rows of vertically aligned wafer disks of varying weights, tightly packed in a container. The top disk and every sixth disk from the top are subjected to force, applied perpendicularly to the disks' common plane. We find that the heaviest disks contribute most to the force applied to the disks in the confined space. When the applied force is increased, the disks begin to jam in a step-like manner, where the distance between these phases remains consistent. We demonstrate that the phase where the top disk is moved first repeats indefinitely. We propose a mathematical model, based on a simple material deformation theory, to estimate the force required to move a disk when the disks are compressed before adding more disks on top. We compare this model's predictions to simulations and find a consistent pattern of power-law relationships between the weights of the disks and the force required to move the disks for a given number of layers. However, the model shows discrepancies with the observed behavior when the number of layers is variable.

Recent studies indicate that general theories of precipitation phenomena may not apply universally as distinct types of El Ni\~no and La Ni\~na exhibit varying spatial and temporal precipitation patterns. This realization has raised important questions about the validity and implications of this phenomenon. Investigating this problem involves examining the characteristics of stationary waves in three different climate models, which suggests that a significant factor influencing this disorder could be unexpected interactions between certain atmospheric factors. This factor can lead to the creation of contrasting modes for reflecting heat from the ground back into the atmosphere, resulting in reduced uniformity in precipitation patterns. This theory is supported by examining the characteristics of stationary waves in models and observing their impact on regional precipitation patterns.

Researchers were previously unable to determine experimentally whether nonaffine arrangements, a characteristic feature of materials' elastic response and a key element in modeling their fracture, actually occur in solids at a nondestructive level.  A study employed in situ x-ray diffraction to directly investigate the affine and nonaffine components of materials' deformable solids.  By utilizing two-dimensional X-ray diffraction images to map and distinguish between affine and nonaffine parts of a material's deformation, the experiment successfully detected the occurrence of nonaffinity in a nondestructive area of a polymer material.  This new finding provides essential insights for developing models that take into consideration the energy-related consequences of nonaffine arrangements and could potentially benefit the creation of advanced technologies in fields like soft robotics and drug delivery.

By exploring the properties of L\'evy distributions, we have expanded the base two-tier model into a comprehensive multi-tier framework. The three-parameter L\'evy distribution accurately models the probability distribution of jump size, enabling the use of existing single-population models even in the presence of random processes. The resulting multi-tier model retains an analytically soluble form and retains all properties found in the base two-tier model. The existence of three distinct types of random processes is demonstrated, along with the corresponding forms of the model. The use of our work as a foundation for developing multi-tier models involving multiple random processes is also proposed.

This study investigates the expression and expression manipulation capabilities of fuzzy logic MTL using $\kappa$-fuzzy logic operators and linguistic terms within the framework of standard and generalized predicate logic with countably infinite modalities. Our research is based on a previously introduced ordering on the set of natural numbers, which extends classical fuzzy logic operators in a language with modalities. By applying expression manipulation techniques to a normalized and compact form of fuzzy MTL expressions, we establish a decidable equivalence check between these expressions and certain generalized first-order formulas, effectively reducing the complexity of the equivalence problem from 2-EXPTIME to co-NP. Additionally, we also provide a complete description of the expression manipulation techniques and a calculational method to further simplify and normalize the expressions. Moreover, we demonstrate that these techniques are effective for both standard and generalized predicate logic with modalities and a range of related languages, including MTL, graded MTL, and $\kappa$-fuzzy MTL with language-based operators. By doing so, we address two main research questions: (1) Is the membership and subset relationship problem for $\kappa$-fuzzy MTL classes with modalities solvable within certain bounds?   (2) Can a generalized first-order representation be found for a normalized form of these expressions, effectively reducing the equivalence problem complexity, which is known to be 2-EXPTIME.

Performing taxonomy expansion - the process of populating an existing taxonomy with newly discovered taxonomic relationships - is extremely challenging due to the vast number of possible combinations of concept and relationship. To date, most solutions have employed a set of predefined relationships, significantly reducing the scope. Nonetheless, such an approach restricts the potential for comprehensive expansion. To overcome this limitation, we have devised the HyperExpan algorithm, enabling taxonomy expansion with an unlimited set of relationships. Notably, this approach utilizes the inherent semantic connections within the taxonomy and outside contexts provided by structured knowledge databases like Wikidata. The elevated efficacy of HyperExpan was demonstrated through experimental comparisons with existing state-of-the-art techniques on two datasets: the Ontology of Semi.synthetic Worlds and the Drug Ontology.

This study examines the performance of density functional approximations in modeling electric properties of molecular pairs. The results indicate a significant disparity between their ability to predict electric properties and other properties like geometric structures, binding affinities, and molecular properties. In general, approximations fail to accurately predict electric properties of molecular pairs unless the underlying monomer calculations are reliable. The study suggests that a measure called absolute error of prediction may help gauge the feasibility of using density functional approximations to model electric properties of molecular pairs based on the results of monomer calculations. The study emphasizes the necessity to reassess and verify density functional approximations for predicting electric properties of molecular pairs, especially when transferring from small to complex systems.

Advancements in machine learning have led to widespread adoption of deep neural networks across the industry, particularly in areas where making a precise prediction is crucial. Neurasmus has developed an advanced deep learning-based system for quantifying uncertainty associated with neural network predictions, which can be applied to complex industrial systems. Unlike other models that fail to accurately handle non-deterministic uncertainty, the new system leverages a Gaussian process-based approach combining uncertainty and learning to provide accurate worst-case risk assessment. By integrating the risk analysis into a neural network architecture, the model computes the probability of potential output deviations due to unforeseen inputs or environmental changes, enabling users to make more informed decisions. The system's effectiveness in handling critical safety applications has been successfully demonstrated in the F-35 aircraft simulator and the Remote Controlled Car testing platforms, where it proved capable of identifying and responding to potential hazards.

Markov decision processes are utilized to evaluate the performance of critical systems against failures, and a new objective function, called the Resilience Satisfaction Value, is developed to assess the ability of systems to operate during disruptions. This new function is based on a specification that considers both the frequency of crucial actions and the likelihood of system components operating as intended. Comparing the effectiveness of ReSV and expected reward objectives, through optimal control problems, reveals that ReSV takes into account the value of actions taken under ordinary conditions, whereas expected reward objectives often underestimate the importance of such actions under ordinary system functioning. Additionally, ReSV is shown to be a more stable optimization goal than expected reward objectives when attempting to optimize system performance in general settings.

Dark matter research, particularly through direct detection methods, demonstrates the feasibility of searching for discrete signals within large datasets, a feat achieved through advanced statistical analysis and machine learning techniques. The 2020 'DARK DARKNET' challenge showcased a strapping 1,000+ accelerometers spread across 30 countries, offering a vast array of time series data, which can be interrogated using the same methods employed in direct detection searches, potentially uncovering evidence of dark matter. This paper details the outcome of the challenge, in which participants were divided into two groups: those using time-series data from accelerometers (the 'DARKNET' track) and those analyzing position and rate data as vectors in curved space. The latter group generated novel methods, while the DARKNET track participants developed innovative approaches using time-series analysis. Notably, some participants achieved positive results, with curvilinear group participants claiming signal detection rates of up to 93%, while also accurately distinguishing between various types of dark matter. However, these claims require further validation as the signals found were not clearly defined, and background contamination was likely to have an adverse effect on the signals remaining. Future challenges and research are required to further develop the potential of this type of dark matter search.

We examine global solutions to the equation $\Delta u=\frac{u^p}{\inf_{B_1 \zeta^2}$}+h$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$ with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions, where $p>1$, $\Delta$ is the standard Laplace operator, $\zeta$ is a smooth function in $B_1$, and $h$ is a smooth function in $\mathbb{R}^N$. For smooth solutions, we obtain a boundary estimate related to the Hardy-Leray type estimate. At the same time, when $p>1$ and $\Delta$ is the fractional Laplacian, we study the existence of non-negative solutions to the equation $|\triangle|^\frac{2}{p}u=x^p|u|^{p-1}u$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$ with Dirichlet boundary conditions, where $h$ is a smooth function in $\mathbb{R}^N$.

Our team analyzed images from the Murchison Widefield Intensity Array (MWIFARA) and determined the curvature of the low-frequency radio spectrum in terms of polarization, finding a correlation between this value and the median polarization of sources. Specifically, we discovered that the magnitude of spectral curvature increases until it reaches a certain point, after which it begins to decrease while the polarization of sources reaches its peak. These findings are consistent with predictions from models of spectral polarization that incorporate the effects of Faraday rotation and curvature of the magnetic field, particularly those describing how polarization behaves at the peak of the rotation measure distribution. To further understand these results, we compared them to calculations from a model that assumes a "thin screen" of emission from galaxies, finding some correspondence but also some expected differences due to the inherent assumptions of this model. Ultimately, our analysis contributes to our understanding of the geometry of the magnetic field in galaxies, showing that our Sun lies near the midpoint of a particular distribution.

Operational uncertainty measures defined through extremal properties are tailored to specific tasks, like distinguishing between random samples or approximating inequalities. Several such measures have counterparts that satisfy these properties under categorizations of probabilistic entropy, like $h_\varphi(P) = \varphi(\sum_i p_i \log p_i)$ using $\varphi(x) = x$ or $\varphi(x) = e^x$. However, these counterparts don't capture everything we need to consider when evaluating the security of quantum cryptography protocols. To address this gap, this study develops new operational uncertainty measures applicable to various entropies and probabilistic channels. These measures make use of minimax optimization with a new relative tolerance criterion that enables treatment of unbounded functions. Depending on the tolerance choice, this framework allows the creation of both conservative and lenient variants of existing security definitions, thereby providing a clearer understanding of established conjectures. Additionally, this study introduces a new, conservative definition of minimal uncertainty that is tightly related to maximal entropy. This definition is strictly tighter than previous conservative definitions for several well-known entropy functionals. Furthermore, this study develops functional inequalities that are tight even under the presence of quantum mechanics. These inequalities are an essential part of evaluating the security of quantum cryptography protocols.

The origin of turbulent transport remains unclear even in simple three-dimensional turbulent flows. We used molecular dynamics simulations to study this phenomenon in fluids. Our findings show that turbulent transport can be described as a specific relation between the velocity auto-correlation function and the stress energy spectrum. This is based on a general formula for transport in terms of correlation functions of velocity and stress, where the transport coefficient becomes a specific function of the Reynolds, Waleffe, and Stromguth parameters. It's intriguing to note that in three-dimensional turbulent flows, the transport coefficient can be expressed as a linear combination of the Reynolds and Stromguth parameters, both ranging from zero to infinity.

Conventional techniques for fitting elastic scattering data are often inadequate 
because they don't adequately account for the correlations between parameters, 
leading to extensive parameter error correlations after the convergence of the 
fitting process. In order to rectify this issue, the MINUIT2 program has been 
incorporated into the coupled-channels code, enabling the simultaneous simultaneous 
parameter estimation and correlation analysis. This update not only allows for a 
more reliable treatment of parameter correlations but also significantly reduces 
processing times since it leverages the efficient numerical algorithms within 
MINUIT2.

In the context of blackbody thermodynamics, we examine heat radiation properties within a metallic slab under varying thicknesses and boundary conditions in a finite-temperature scenario. Certain thermodynamic energy quantities, specifically entropy, temperature, and the radiation's Boltzmann constant, are re-evaluated due to changes in the slab's boundary conditions, rendering previous interpretations as being "non-blackbody-like", now instead adhering to the traditional definition of blackbody thermodynamics. Building upon this framework, we address two boundary condition scenarios where the electromagnetic field reflections are absent and then consider the limit where the slab's thickness tends towards infinity, finding that all radiation emanates from an ideal blackbody. Additionally, ideal emitters and absorbers are characterized by specific rules that must be satisfied and are subsequently plotted for various thickness and boundary condition scenarios in a color map. Furthermore, ideal blackbody-like thermodynamics is also effectively modeled using a slab of glass, thus demonstrating the applicability of white papers.

When providing location-based services, users expect their personal data to remain confidential, including knowledge about the presence of others in specific locations. Current approaches for privately querying spatial datasets either guarantee strong privacy or the ability to precisely respond to queries, but not both. To resolve this issue, we have developed a framework that maintains a high level of query responsiveness while upholding strong privacy in the face of dependencies between locations. We began by creating a probabilistic model that models the distance between locations based on given parameters and then established a method for privately releasing this model to a public setting while maintaining precise estimates for distance. We further designed two types of queries, each addressing a different scenario: one that allows prior knowledge of the public dataset, and another that does not. We implemented both approaches using the R\'enyi divergence framework and proved their respective strengths and limitations. Through experiments on real-world datasets, we demonstrated that our approach not only significantly enhances query responsiveness but also does so at a cost that is comparable to existing algorithms.

In various robotics applications, identifying specific locations using 3D point clouds as input is crucial. While network-based methods for place recognition using LiDAR data have been increasingly popular, they typically require access to large, specialised datasets and expensive hardware, such as 64-bit CPUs and high-capacity storage, which can be challenging to deploy on resource-constrained hardware, like microcontrollers. In order to enhance the efficiency of place recognition using LiDAR data on hardware with limited resources, we propose a new point-based approach that utilises a geometric representation of 3D points, comparing them to pre-trained templates in real-time. This method outperforms the state-of-the-art 3D point cloud recognition technique, ADPT, with place classification accuracy of 85.7% and distance to nearest neighbour metrics of 1.53 metres and 2.13 metres, respectively. Moreover, our method significantly reduces processing time, achieving 50 ms to 200 ms per step on various hardware configurations, which is significantly faster than the average 300-400 ms step time of the ADPT method. Additionally, our technique demonstrates strong compatibility with small-scale datasets, such as the 7Class dataset, without the need for extensive hardware resources.

The widespread application of functional connectivity in neuroscientific research has enabled the precise characterization of individual differences and alterations due to various factors. However, the majority of studies have concentrated on intra-individual connectivity while neglecting the influence of inter-site effects, which are pivotal to conveying results across diverse brain imaging centers. Consequently, the present study examines the inter-site variance resulting from population differences in functional connectivity and strives to optimize the reliability of demographic group distinction. Our results reveal that inter-site effects notably impact the accuracy of demographic group distinction. Notably, the accuracy enhances when the demographical distinction is synergized with inter-site effects. Moreover, the accuracy of demographic group distinction reaches its optimum when the inter-site effects are sufficiently diverse. To achieve robust demographic group distinction, the present study advises limiting the inclusion of sites with inter-site effects that are notably similar. Furthermore, the accuracy of demographic group distinction can be further optimized by supplementing with additional metrics like nodal degrees and functional network connectivity patterns.

In computational communication theory, specifically in naming and counting problems, a significant issue arises when a system's stations, labeled with distinct names, request an enumeration of their fellow stations or adversaries to obtain counting information while minimizing data exchange. This has led to the introduction of several challenging problems: the Naming Problem, where a station aims to identify its station labels relative to others, and the Counting Problem, where stations aim to acquire knowledge of the number of stations, all while adhering to limited communication constraints. In this research, we explore these problems in a distributed communication setting, focusing on a binary communication system setup, where data transmission is restricted to 1-bit at a time. Both naming and counting variants are examined; the latter involves either determining the station count or identifying whether the station number falls within a predetermined range. Building upon the work of Beimboift et al. and Garay et al., we demonstrate that the lower bounds for these problems range from Ω(n^2) for the naming problem and Ω(n) for both counting problem variants, measured in terms of the number of stations n. Interestingly, this is complemented by the upper bounds, showing that the naming problem can be solved within O(n^2) and the counting problem within O(n) communication steps. These upper bounds establish efficient solutions for these challenging problems in the distributed communication system.

To rapidly understand and respond to multilingual online inquiries in real-time, fast decoding language models are necessary. We focus on developing and training a single, unified language model to swiftly translate complex, mixed languages consisting of two or more languages. To address the issue that current techniques lack effective handling of mixed languages, we suggest combining the advantages of two existing methods: the positional encoding technique for integrating time-based sequences and the attention mechanism for handling spatially near information. This novel approach enables the model to process sequences of code-mixed text in an ordered manner, thereby differentiating between similar languages. Additionally, we integrate data augmentation and noise contrastive estimation to enhance model training, thereby reducing the impact of noise and distortion. Our proposed method outperforms existing models in translating English-Cebuano and English Hiligaynon code-mixed text, especially under strict decoding time limitations.

Hydrogen selenides in solid form exhibit exceptional tunability of isotope effect by modifying the bandgap through pressure adjustments. Utilizing theoretical calculations based on density functional theory, a study revealed that at low pressure, the contribution of zero-point motion to the isotope effect coefficient in H$_{3}$S and H$_{3}$Se is significant but can be gradually suppressed by increasing the bandgap. It was discovered that the quantum phonological property has a minimal impact ($<$$-1$ eV$^2$) across the entire range of bandgaps in solid hydrogen selenides, in contrast to typical metals. Consequently, the bandgap in these materials serves as an extremely effective regulator of the isotope effect coefficient, making the quantum phonological property accessible over an exceptionally broad energy span. Furthermore, the bandgap predictions obtained through density functional theory paint a positive outlook for the stability of two-phase H$_{3}$S at high pressure and for the solidification of H$_{3}$Se at relatively low pressure. Additionally, the potential for superconductivity at practical temperatures facilitated by the adjustable bandgap in hydrogen selenides has a brighter outlook than similar scenarios with metal hydrides.

Motion planning in complex spaces can be made simple by minimizing the size of the search space with constraints that prioritize obstacle avoidance.
Our approach efficiently generates spatial constraints using recently proposed spatial constraints that consider an object's center of gravity and orientation.
These constraints allow a more compact and constrained environment for planning, resulting in a faster and more efficient search.
We developed a global planner with a 2D grid, using the A* algorithm to find the best path, and evaluated various methods for generating constraints and optimizing parameter settings through simulations in cluttered environments.
Results show our approach outperforms traditional global planners in terms of motion planning, with a more efficient search space and significant speed-up in real-world scenarios.

Research in camera pose estimation has primarily relied on hand-crafted image descriptors like SIFT or SuperPoint. However, these descriptors struggle with complexity and noise, necessitating the development of learned descriptors. Past attempts at integrating learned descriptors into camera reprojecting techniques have led to improved results in controlled environments, but were ineffective in challenging real-world scenarios. We devised a novel deep learning-based descriptor, and integrated it into camera reprojecting techniques via a minimal additional component, enhancing their performance significantly across various benchmarks. The code and a corresponding demo are publicly available on GitHub.

To design MIMO precoders and receive vectors for interference channels where multiple users share the same spectrum and physical resources, the researchers optimized sum-rate and interference management. They proposed two new approaches - one optimizing sum-rate directly, the other tackling interference through group LASSO, which groups weak signal components to enhance individual user performance while mitigating interference for others. The better approach was identified by comparing its performance with traditional methods using simulations and it was found to yield substantial sum-rate gains and improved interference management.

Given a finite harmonic map $\pi$ from tropical curve $\mathcal{C}$ to tropical curve $\mathcal{D}$, the pull-back of the rational function semifield on $\mathcal{D}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ was previously defined but lacked a concrete constructive implementation. Here, we develop such a constructive approach for rational function semifields in relation to tropical divisors and we use this semifield to prove Capelli's theorem for tropical curves.

This research focuses on the quasi-stationary distribution of a two-dimensional Markov process in a finite state space. We establish certain sufficient conditions under which a quasi-st Stationary distribution exists and converges exponentially quickly to its stationary counterpart. Additionally, the study investigates the speed of quasi-stationary distribution convergence in a general framework and provides specific, in-depth analysis for the geometric and birth-death processes.

Recent advancements in higher mass topology have led to new connections between the higher topological versions of knot theory and ocular physics. Specifically, the higher version of the Jones polynomial has been proven to be derived from a higher mass topology approach, and we now expand upon this finding by identifying which part of the mass spectrum is related to the Jones polynomial. The approach also enables identification of ocular versions of other knot invariants and their links to the refined version of the Alexander polynomial. Moreover, the higher mass topology approach to knot theory is integral to the understanding of long-range quantum entanglement in certain ocular systems, and we now provide a simplified yet comprehensive quantum circuit model for certain knot invariants. These findings are made possible by integrating higher mass topology with the principles of 'what you see is what you can say'.

The connection between the structural, elastic, electrical properties, and nematic fluctuations in iron-based superconductors is still a major research question in superconductivity studies. Employing a novel method called elastoresistance, we investigated the nematic fluctuations in two similar but distinct systems, LiFeAs and NaFeAs. Our findings revealed that nematic fluctuations exist in LiFeAs but are remarkably reduced in NaFeAs, coinciding with their varying residual elastic moduli and electrical transport sensitivity. The obtained results can be interpreted within a theoretical framework that attributes the nematic fluctuations to a strain-induced change in the Fe-As bond angle, consistent with ab-initio calculations. Moreover, our study implies that nematic fluctuations can significantly contribute to the anomalous resistance increase at low temperatures by facilitating within- and between-layer electron interactions, ultimately resulting in a more pronounced metallicity in LiFeAs when compared to NaFeAs. The interactions leading to the metal-like behavior in both materials occur at substantially different temperatures and can manifest as a metal-like behavior within the metallic state in LiFeAs and as a transition directly from a metal to an insulator in NaFeAs.

In a specific type of multi-Higgs model where one Higgs doublet interacts with a standard model particle while the other remains isolated, we examine whether it is feasible to have a dark matter candidate that fulfills both physical and theoretical requirements, particularly in light of experiments searching for rare decays and the relic density of dark matter. The study reveals a small window of possibility, existing between decays detectability and non-detectability, and between the correct dark matter relic density and non-relief. Within this considered type of model, we identify the most suitable region for dark matter, suggesting a 225 GeV mass Higgs particle and a 16.7 - 25 GeV mass singlet dark matter candidate within a range of 18 - 55 GeV in the active Higgs doublet's mass. Additionally, we investigate how theory-based restrictions, such as colliders' bounds on multiple vortex formation and disintegration, and model internal consistency constraints impact this proposed dark matter scenario. The research further compares our proposed model with another popular dark matter concept based on a multi-Higgs model.

Building complex materials from individual components requires coordinating tiny particles to achieve a desired outcome, but the challenge is deciphering the optimal arrangement when no pre-existing structure exists. Artificial intelligence has been applied to this problem by using a neural network to learn a direct relationship between the individual particles' arrangements and the materials' properties. However, most studies focus on controlled environments, utilizing pre-set particle configurations generated by exploratory processes, which raises the question of adapting these findings to direct assembly. In our study, we investigate the capacity of AI algorithms to discern between exploratory and directed design processes, differentiate between generated and randomly arranged particle configurations, and adapt these learnings to overcome uncertainty in the input data. We apply a novel, cumulative learning approach, combined with a sophisticated encoder-decoder model, enabling our system to create structured particle arrangements independent of prior knowledge. Furthermore, our results reveal the AI's ability to distinguish between diverse generated configurations produced by distinct rule sets, as well as its capacity for grasping physical laws and its performance in uncertain scenarios. Additionally, our study demonstrates the AI's capability of differentiating between exploratory and directed designed particle arrangements, generated by the AI itself or produced through random processes.

We investigate flavor symmetry in chiral gauge theories with spin 1/2 fermions, 
notably focusing on the relationship between flavor-symmetric confining vacua and 
't Hooft anomaly matching equations. Our analysis applies to gauge theories with 
one or more gauge groups, featuring spin 1/2 fermions that have Dirac or Majorana 
nature and come in fundamental or adjoint representations. Fundamental fermions 
involving two Dirac cones lead to an anomaly matching across different gauge 
groups, including non-Abelian or Abelian cases. A similar result is observed 
when adjoint fermions provide two Majorana cones. Notably, this phenomenon 
emerges in strong-coupling regime of the gauge theory. Furthermore, we explore 
the relationships between flavor-symmetric confining vacua and the constraints of 
Parekh-Samuel-Wyld's quantum defect framework, particularly among SU(2) gauge 
group.

We offer a new approach to solve the Navier-Stokes equations in three dimensions for an infinite number of times and locations. We achieve this by using the Fourier transform to simplify the problem and then solving it through a loop that considers each frequency one at a time. Due to the nature of this loop, we find that the Navier-Stokes equations become a series of smaller, well-formed loops for each frequency. We can then use a combination of advanced mathematical theorems to show that under certain restrictions, the solution exists and is unique. This process allows us to expand the range of possible solutions by removing certain restrictions. We also demonstrate that the solution has a key property where the size of the solution does not continue to grow even as the time and location tend to infinity. This property allows us to further expand the range of possible solutions. We then provide the full mathematical proof for this result in an additional document.

This research introduces a computational methodology to model magnon modes in antiferromagnetic materials subject to temperature-driven thermal fluctuations. Building upon prior work in the field, we've refined our approach by using the finite element method to discretize the continuum approximation of a Heisenberg antiferromagnetic material. We've applied the Rarita-Schwinger equation to derive a temperature-dependent thermodynamic formulation that enables the computation of six magnetic degrees of freedom within the continuum model. We've further developed a temperature-dependent wave function that enables the calculation of various magnon properties, including the bandgap, eigenmodes, and directional stiffness. We validate the developed methodology through its application to a test case where we demonstrate the effect of thermal magnon interactions on magnon modes, revealing a characteristic variation in bandgap and resonance modes under elevated temperatures.

A quantum-inspired protocol inspired by the Bodycentric encryption method, previously developed without a quantitative basis, has been proposed despite its impracticality. This paper seeks to address the issues associated with this protocol, which were previously ignored. The central challenge lies in refining the search for the encoded integer among an enormous number of possibilities. The original proposal relied on probabilistic methods, which prove inadequate in practical applications. To overcome this limitation, this paper suggests replacing probabilistic searches with a quantum-inspired alternative. However, this quantum-inspired modification comes at the cost of reduced transparency and increased reliance on centralized power, as it involves complex computations and stringent interaction with the issuing authority for each encryption and decryption process. To gauge the efficacy of this quantum-inspired protocol, we examine the computational complexity of finding the encoded integer using a quantum-inspired search, subsequently reduced to a form of quantum circuit complexity that utilizes the binary representation of the encoded integer. The resulting complexity is capped at $2.5\cdot\sqrt{L\kappa}$ for each additional decimal place beyond the tens place, with the constant factor 2 accounting for the worst-case scenario of the binary search. Furthermore, this complexity is comparable to that of the most efficient quantum algorithm, which exhibits a similar but slightly lower complexity of $2^{0.5\cdot\log_2(L\kappa)}$ at critical points. The tens place is incurred during each critical period, defined as the duration between successive powers of 10 of the length $

The key to producing innovative and insightful content lies in the ability of Language Models to understand the nuances of language, even in the face of rare words where data is scarce. The provision of sample-based word representations serves as a potential solution to this challenge, allowing the expansion of rare words' representations while preserving their unique characteristics. A new technique is introduced that leverages the capabilities of prompt-based LMs to create mean representations for each word through the average of per-token representations. A subsequent refinement mechanism is put forward to filter out rare words' distinct features. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated by its remarkable performance in two tasks: word meaning similarity measurement and sentence generation incorporating rare words.

Researchers considered a random minimum-spanning acyclic graph created from an independent random matrix containing zero entries and randomly positioned ones. They demonstrated that the extreme weight values associated with this graph converge statistically, with extremal weights of an independent random acyclic graph distributing themselves identically upon the removal of an infinite number of matrix rows. Additionally, the statistical behavior of the extreme weight values associated with all types of minimum spanning trees and acyclic subgraphs was studied, revealing that the extreme weight values associated with a matrix spanned by an independent random binary matrix contain zero ones.

This work highlights the vulnerabilities of vertical Federated learning (VerFL) to privacy breaches. We successfully integrated privacy assaults, such as black-box, white-box, and adversarial attacks, into VerFL, where a hacker can leverage membership inference, boundary attack, or adversarial attack capabilities by feeding slightly modified legitimate training data to each participant or the server. Our experiments on two datasets demonstrate that an attacker can infer membership, find data boundaries, or carry out adversarial attacks with high accuracy across most scenarios, including when the hacker only has limited interactions with the system. To address this vulnerability, we propose two potential solutions, data poisoning, and iterative feature isolation, which can be utilized in combination to significantly enhance the difficulty of membership inference and boundary attacks, although not adversarial attacks. Our code is publicly available on GitHub.

Utilizing the $B$-quark light-cone wave function from the light-conversion $B$ to $p\bar{\Lambda}$ transition, the systematic anaysis of the $B$ to $p\bar{\Lambda}$ decay width, including the effects of light-cone corrections, dark influence of antibaryon fields, and the presence of a strange quark, yields expressions that can be utilized for calculating the $B$ to $p\bar{\Lambda}$ decay width. Additionally, the paper discusses the special case where the decay width for $B$ to $p\bar{\Lambda}$ at zero momentum transfer is used to estimate the mass of antibaryons resulting from dark matter interactions, and investigates how this influences the lifetime of strange baryons like $\Lambda$ or $\Lambda_c$. The study shows that the mass of antibaryons resulting from dark matter interactions, which ranges from a few GeV to tens of GeV, has a notable impact on the lifetime of strange baryons; for example, if the mass of antibaryons is 50 GeV, the lifetime of $\Lambda$ increases by a factor of 20, or the lifetime of $\Lambda_c$ increases by a factor of 5. Furthermore, the influence of dark influence of antibaryon fields on the decay width of $B$ to $p\bar{\Lambda}$, which ranges from a few times $10^{-7}$ GeV to a few

Recent advancements in data-driven modeling have led to improved situational awareness for countermeasures against complex network threats. Nevertheless, the interaction between different entities involved in the defense strategies has been largely overlooked. Our research focuses on resource distribution among various city agencies to effectively combat terrorist attacks, utilizing an agent-based model and two alternative approaches, intuitive and evolutionary algorithms. The results demonstrate that different agencies' allocation of resources can significantly impact defense capabilities, and our evolutionary algorithm is able to optimize resource allocation over time, further reducing the threat. The evolutionary algorithm is then refined into an agent-based model to enable autonomous decision-making, and simulations reveal comparable performance improvements.

A comprehensive examination is conducted on the event horizon of a charged black hole situated within a spherical cavity's confines, along with the cognitive role of the cavity's radius in determining the phase transition process. The existence of two types of phase transition curves is confirmed: one influenced by the electric potential and the other by the cavity's radius, hinting at a deeper relationship between thermal geometry and phase transition mechanisms.

This study presents an innovative bag sampling approach for long document ranking, resulting in enhanced efficiency and accuracy. Inspired by a parallel TF-IDF indexing technique, bag sampling offers speed and versatility advantages over traditional Terravista indexing, enabling segmentation on feature level rather than document level. To achieve this, we introduce a novel loss function and apply bag sampling to the top 10% most distinctive features within each document, utilizing a parallel indexing technique to calculate document similarity based on these selected features, ultimately facilitating faster and more precise ranking. Evaluations reveal an approximately 2 to 4 times speedup and a 0.02 to 0.04 increase in DCG metric compared to Terravista indexing, while bag sampling, Terravista indexing, and Terravista indexing without feature pruning methods achieve a recall of 90.32%, 89.76%, and 88.32%, respectively. Furthermore, our method demonstrates robust performance even under extremely long documents with up to 2,000 features per document.

Semi-supervised node classification in Graph Neural Networks is a well-established task. The labeling process often faces challenges due to the uneven distribution of labels, especially under statistical bias. Traditional pseudo-labeling methods have been shown to have negative consequences, such as reinforcing existing label biases. Building upon this understanding, we present a novel pseudo-labeling framework called the Biased Label Correction Framework, designed to mitigate bias propagation in semi-supervised node classification. Specifically, we integrate a regularization component that encourages diversity among assigned labels, thereby improving the likelihood of correctly labeled nodes. In contrast to existing approaches, we propose to calculate confidence scores based on local representation contrast rather than global properties. The Biased Label Correction Framework consists of two primary components: a biased label correction loss and an entropy regulation loss. The loss is applied to the node representation prior to the final activation function, allowing the model to learn from its biases as part of the pseudo-labeling process. The Biased Label Correction Loss is defined as the sum of three terms: a softmax cross-entropy loss for correcting biased pseudo-labels, a KL divergence loss to measure the distance between the softmax distribution and the true label distribution, and an entropy loss to control the diversity of assigned labels. The Biased Label Correction Framework has been formally named the BC2L framework. Experimental results show that the proposed framework outperforms existing pseudo-labeling methods for semi-supervised node classification, achieving notable improvements in accuracy for datasets with significant label biases.

A novel approach to plasma wakefield acceleration involves using betatron radiation from highly charged particles to accelerate electrons. We have conducted a series of simulations studying beam dynamics in a bunched beam matched to an imprecise wakefield. Our studies, which utilized various particle beam matching methods, revealed that differences in radial size between the accelerator's bucket and the particle beam significantly influence the accelerated electron's performance. Our results show that minor radial size discrepancies can result in substantial particle loss and decreased remaining particle beam quality by as much as three orders of magnitude. The cause of this reduced beam quality can be explained by particle uncoupling in the beam's transverse direction, which amplifies the size of radial perturbations within the beam. Based on our findings, we identified minimal radial size variations and specific matching methods as crucial factors in a successful betatron radiation-based plasma wakefield acceleration stage.

This paper presents a new method for privately learning deep trees, overcoming the limitations of previous work by allowing for a significant increase in dataset size while maintaining performance. The approach involves a two-step process where a preliminary tree is constructed, then refined through a differential privacy process applied to the top tree components. The method is based on an improved application of the DP deep tree algorithm, resulting in smaller privacy budget requirements for larger datasets. The experiment compares this method with other private tree learning approaches, showing that it achieves significantly higher accuracy for large datasets, while maintaining comparable or higher accuracy for smaller datasets, in addition to achieving better expected tree structures. Furthermore, the method is asymptotically equivalent to previous work that applied privacy to individual leaf nodes, with the notable difference being the method's improved expected tree structures. The experiment also highlights the method's benefits in terms of privacy and learning performance, with the notable outcome of a method that simultaneously achieves higher accuracy and less privacy for a large dataset, in contrast to previous work. The outcome indicates that a new method that previously required a smaller dataset size is now capable of a significantly larger dataset size, with the example given of a method that previously required 20% less privacy on a dataset size of 100,000.

This article presents a revised moment-matching algorithm for minimizing the regularized R\'enyi divergence between two distributions, based on a maximum likelihood estimation principle. The proposed algorithm reduces the optimization task into a second-order cone program, enabling the calculation of a more stable upper limit compared to the original divergence formulation. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of the proposed algorithm to a stationary point of the resulting generator optimization problem. Notably, our algorithm has inherent properties ensuring its convergence to a global solution when optimizing the divergence on its own and is adaptable to various distribution families. We provide additional empirical evidence of the algorithm's effectiveness in specific applications.

This paper develops product Dirichlet priors for model selection with conditional logarithmic regression link functions in chain event graphs. Traditional methods for specifying prior distributions through a neighbourhood structure have a restricted scope for model selection with CLRM link functions. To overcome this limitation, two product Dirichlet modelling approaches are proposed - a robust method that sets all neighbourhood structure model probabilities equally (can represent any CGRA model) and a structured method that encodes prior beliefs about neighbourhood structures into a product Dirichlet distribution. These priors ensure model selection consistency and allow for neighbourhood structures to be learned from data. Bayesian inference for the learned models is performed using a stochastic version of the Loopy Belief Propagation algorithm. As an alternative to modelling neighbourhood structures, a score-based approach for model selection is explored. Both methods are evaluated using a synthetic dataset and a real-world electronic circuit reconstruction experiment.

In recent years, the heavy ball method has received renewed interest due to its rapid convergence rate in optimization problems. This study examines the effect of removing damping on the convergence rate of the method when solving strongly convex smooth functions. Utilizing a weight parameter close to zero but slightly greater than zero, we find that it maintains a comparable convergence rate as the original damping-inclusive heavy ball method. Our approach revolves around modifying the Lyapunov function of the method's convergence proof to accommodate the nondissipative variant. This allows us to explore the performance of removing damping in specific problem settings, such as finding the minimum of a quadratic function. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that selecting the damping coefficient carefully can accelerate convergence.

This research explores the algorithms for guidance in navigation, with a focus on robots navigating alongside a wall. We examine how changes in the distance sensor's field of view and its placement influence the resulting trajectories. Our study integrates three distinct algorithms: those based on the arctangent method, rectification, and a technique involving a look-up table. We found that the arctangent method produces the least accurate results, while the look-up table method offers the best trade-off between computation complexity and path deviation from the intended course. Importantly, we identify parameters optimizing the look-up table method's performance that outperform existing approaches.

In superconducting materials handled by light, specific interactions between electromagnetic waves and quasiparticles can occur due to the superconducting gap's influence. Researchers have been using a corrected model of the superconducting gap to explore quantum electrodynamics in a unique context, specifically in a widely studied compound called LaSrCuO and other highly doped ferromagnetic superconductors. This updated model demonstrates that the model's earlier prediction, which showed divergent behavior in microwave conductivity at a specific doping level, was in fact incorrect. Rather, the corrected prediction shows there is no such divergence. Nonetheless, the model's earlier prediction has already led to a potential explanation for patterns of increased sensitivity to microwaves in some materials. Additionally, the model may facilitate discoveries related to phase transitions and the production of entangled states, particularly in experiments involving strontium-copper superconductors.

We investigate the solution space of the anisotropic mean curvature flow with arbitrary speed functions and initialize the flame on a smooth, bounded surface. Our aim is to determine whether solutions exist and are continuous in time for a given initial condition. This depends on the nature of the speed function, which in turn influences the flame's behavior. Our analysis provides a complete theoretical framework for initial conditions that lie within the C^{1,1} category, thereby filling a key theoretical gap in the literature.

Recent breakthroughs in plant movement and manipulation research have been achieved through the use of model-based optimal control techniques, combining plant physiology models with the capabilities of control theory and algorithms. While these discoveries hold great potential for applications in agriculture, pharmacology, and biomedical fields, advancements in this area heavily rely on theoretical botany and physiology. This paper focuses on the design of plant growth and movement models along with the corresponding optimal control strategies using reinforcement learning algorithms. A novel RL model is presented which enables the direct integration of model-based physiological models and does not require a discrete state-space representation. The proposed method also allows for end-effector control that mimics natural stimuli like light, gravity, and touch. Several case studies were conducted to validate the efficacy of the RL controller in manipulating plant movements and growing processes. The results show that the RL approach not only achieves comparable performance to model-based optimal control but also exhibits great potential for handling situations with incomplete state information available.

We previously found that the large-scale structure of simple random quadrangulations containing a single self-avoiding polygon resembles a specific type of Liouville conformal field theory-inspired mesh. This particular mesh did not exist in literature previously, and to better understand it, this paper develops a comprehensive definition. By building upon earlier research, it also demonstrates that the large-scale structure of random quadrangulations containing multiple self-avoiding polygons, along with other types of closed loops, can be described in a similar manner. A key aspect of this paper involves establishing that random quadrangulations featuring these closed loops do exist.
