This achievement is made possible by first introducing a specific type of mesh known as the chordal Liouville mesh, and subsequently developing an innovative approach to create random quadrangulations using specific types of mesh, commonly referred to as uniform quadrangulation ensembles.

High-throughput quantitative image analysis is vital for radiomics, facilitating the identification and prediction of tumor genetics, radiotherapy outcomes, and drug resistance. To accelerate analysis, we need to overcome two main obstacles: (1) significant image processing complexity, resulting in lengthy computation times, and (2) the lack of standardized, automated, and high-throughput protocols for feature extraction, leading to difficulty in comparing results across studies. Our solution addresses these challenges through the development of high-throughput, automated and standardized protocols for radiomics analysis, thereby streamlining the process. We leverage advanced technologies such as automatic feature extraction, deep learning-based image preprocessing, and virtual screening to improve efficiency. Our technique has been thoroughly tested and validated through comparative studies with multiple software platforms, demonstrating its superiority in terms of computation speed and reliability. Furthermore, we have established a standardized, high-throughput protocol for radiomics analysis and made our method available as open-source software to the scientific community. Our goal is to stimulate discussion and collaboration within the radiomics community to advance the field of image-based radiomics analysis.

Our new \J\ \phi\ space calculations for kaon photoproduction, based on the covariant kit, provide the complete differential cross sections for the process \gamma p \to K^+\Sigma^0. The results clearly show the two resonance structures in the cross section, associated with the \Sigma(1385)^0$ and a recently identified \Xi(1690)-resonance, which strongly couples with the \Sigma^0$ and $K^+$ in the direct \gamma p \to K^+\Sigma^0$ reaction. The observed resonance pattern in our calculations corresponds with the experimental data obtained from the CLAS data on the \gamma p \to K^+\Sigma^0$ reaction. The present findings also offer a new understanding of the role played by \Sigma(1385)^0$ and the potential role of a \Xi(1690)-resonance in the process \gamma p \to K^+\Sigma^0$.

The quality of the pre-processing pipeline used in named entity recognition significantly influences the accuracy of the final outcomes. It's crucial to regularly evaluate the pre-processing pipeline to pinpoint areas for improvement, update it as needed, and maintain the accuracy of the NER system. This process inherently demands a separate, reliable measure of the pre-processing pipeline's performance, distinct from the NER model's evaluation. We address this issue by introducing a suite of task-agnostic evaluation tasks for monitoring and improving the pre-processing pipeline's performance. Furthermore, we establish a benchmark database to compare the robustness of our proposed evaluation methods against manual human assessments. The evaluation methods can automatically be applied to various language pairs, streamlining the process of tracking the pre-processing pipeline's progress over time.

In 1929, Epicurus' ancient idea that the Universe is infinite and forever static was reintroduced as a model by Tolman in 1933. This model has recently been explored in a modified form by Zhong [arXiv:1904.03330 (2019)], and in a more extensive study [arXiv:1908.04457 (2019)] it was shown that a static, infinite Universe can be described as an isotropic 3-sphere when certain conditions are met. This research builds upon the work by Zhong to reevaluate the model using the Einstein equations, and it appears that the model does not comply with these fundamental equations. Additionally, we have found that modifying the model to account for time can be achieved through a metric that has been previously studied [Flanagan et al., Phys. Rev. D 79, 021302 (2009)]. This research also sheds light on an alternative interpretation of the model as an emergent combination of dark energy and dark matter, and it suggests that the model's failure to meet the Einstein equations does not pose a problem from a philosophical perspective.

We introduce a probabilistic model that uses a Gaussian variable to represent student preferences by assigning positive or negative scores to possible interactions between students and courses. The model allows us to understand course popularity and individual preferences within a student-body by making predictions based on limited observations of student enrollment. The model's parameters can be estimated using an iterative optimization process incorporating both course and student factors, leading to accurate predictions of unscored courses and identification of relevant student attributes. Our model outperforms existing methods when evaluating predicted scores and predicted unscored courses in simulated scenarios. When applied to two actual educational datasets, the model reveals insights into student preferences at Stanford University and Edinburgh University, respectively.

A mathematical method inspired by Pontryagin's principle is developed to analyze and create Nash equilibrium in vehicle platooning systems. By incorporating a'slack' variable, the proposed approach transforms the finite-horizon equations of a consensus dynamics model into implicit function forms. Subsequently, Pontryagin's principle is applied to formulate necessary conditions for Nash equilibrium, which are demonstrated to align with the existing research on the subject. Notably, the proposed method expands its applicability to infinite-horizon scenarios, achieving a generalizable model capable of handling both with and without constraints on inter-vehicle distances. Moreover, the necessary conditions for Nash equilibrium obtained through this approach facilitate the derivation of a precise identifiability result for the slack variable. Consequently, the necessary conditions become equivalent to the necessary and sufficient conditions for Nash equilibrium, thereby offering a means to identify optimal vehicle spacing in a system of driverless vehicles.

A novel approach called quantized stochastic gradient descent with clipping, dubbed CA-SGD, has been developed for solving logistic regression problems. In this method, the logistic function is approximated by a piecewise linear approximation, achieved by applying clipping to its inputs. Clipping is then combined with quantization, utilizing recently proposed 1-bit and 3-bit encoders and decoders. Depending on the parameter such as number of intervals in the linear approximation, the proposed CA-SGD yields accurate results on various logistic regression datasets, demonstrating convergence rates and accuracies comparable to their fully quantized counterparts. Interestingly, the CA-SGD method converges at a rate of $O(1/\sqrt{bn})$ for large enough clip value and number of intervals, for a fixed quantization bit and data sample size $b$. Furthermore, the proposed approach eliminates the need for a separate quantizer design, an essential component of existing fully quantized SGD methods, and provides a straightforward way to design a quantization schedule as a function of the iteration number. Additionally, the CA-SGD method allows for the simultaneous application of cliping and quantization, an important aspect that can greatly simplify the design of a quantization schedule. Lastly, the effectiveness of the proposed CA-SGD method has been demonstrated on artificial and real-world logistic regression problems with up to a million parameters.

Our task is to verify the authenticity of news headlines by identifying whether they are written by humans or generated by machines. We created a dataset of 10,000 news headlines, with half generated by computers and half written by humans. By gathering micro-agreement scores from human evaluators for each article and training machine learning models on this training set, we aimed to design the best performing models to accomplish this task. Our results show that transformer models can successfully distinguish between human and computer-generated headlines with an accuracy of 22%, outperforming other popular models like recurrent neural networks and bi-LSTM. Among the different architectures we tested, the BERT model achieved the highest accuracy of 23%, making it the top performer in our study.

A multi-fractal pattern of dense packing emerges in a chiral spin liquid when a certain threshold of dense plaquettes with an odd number of edges is exceeded, resulting in a significant gap within this phase of spin liquid. We have found that the critical point at which this gap emerges is unaffected by the presence of any Z2 gauge theory. We have also found that the type of dense packing pattern in a chiral spin liquid changes as a competing interaction of the gauge field changes from its initial state, influencing the gap within this phase of spin liquid.

Antenna arrays with numerous receptors benefit from real-time calibration to ensure stable observations over extended periods, but the effectiveness of this method also makes it sensitive to variations in space. The complexity of explaining the measured effects challenges astronomers, leading some to compare the method with a form of cosmic noise. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the impact of real-time calibration on the stability of arrays with numerous receptors by cross-checking the measurements against mathematical estimates of antenna gain variability. The analysis reveals that the calibration has the overall result of minimizing the fluctuations of receptor gains in arrays where the majority of receptors are equally oriented. However, the predicted noise level derived from the mathematical model does not accurately represent the measured data from the Redshift Search Rookard array. Furthermore, it's suggested that post-event calibration may not completely eliminate the detected variations.

Portfolio optimization is a well-established mathematical method that seeks to balance risk and return, typically achieved by selecting assets with the highest expected returns at a specified risk level. Our research demonstrates the potential for machine learning models to enhance portfolio allocation by learning implicit risk measures. We introduce the autoencoding CGAN, a machine learning model trained to automatically produce a suitable risk metric for portfolio optimization, and evaluate its performance alongside other models such as deep CGAN, Markowitz's traditional method, and stochastic gradient descent. The results show that ACGAN produces more market-like risk metrics that outperforms Markowitz's method in a portfolio optimization context, even surpassing deep CGAN's performance when risk-averse parameters are properly set. Furthermore, we find that ACGAN generates fewer out-of-sample losses than both deep CGAN and Markowitz's methods, and often matches the performance of the gradient risk minimization model after additional training sessions. Consequently, ACGAN appears to be a promising alternative for portfolio optimization.

To maintain consistency in the DGLD relation among Wilson coefficients for different operators, we need to adjust the transition functions $A_{gq}^{(8)}(N)$ and $A_{sg}^{(8)}(N)$ as we go from $N$ to $N+1$. Unfortunately, the VBS scheme's default transition functions $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$ and $A_{sg}^{(3)}(N)$ don't satisfy this requirement, leading to inaccuracies in the DGLD relation at higher orders. We propose a new set of transition functions $A_{gq}^{(8)}(N)$ and $A_{sg}^{(8)}(N)$ that fix this issue and precisely preserve the DGLD relation. We derive these transition functions by matching the QCD evolution operators between $N$ and $N+1$, effectively disassembling it. We recalculate $A_{gq}^{(8)}(N)$ and $A_{sg}^{(8)}(N)$ at two and four-loop orders. We validate the new transition functions against numerical results and the ones provided by autopackage, an automated package. Neural networks, when used for classification purposes, often produce predictions based on inferred models rather than their final optimized state. The Bayesian approach takes this concept further by estimating the probability of a classification being correct along with the probability distributions of potential parameter values. The Bayesian method is particularly beneficial for classifications that involve limited or imbalanced data sets. Recent research indicates that there is a lack of consensus regarding the application of Bayesian neural networks due to complexities in sampling from their posterior distributions. Our study focuses on the computational aspects of approximating the posterior distribution of a Bayesian neural network, especially in terms of accuracy and computational speed. Our research reveals that neural network architecture plays a crucial role in the quality of approximated predictions, thereby stressing the significance of choosing suitable architectures for tasks at hand. Our study is conducted across four different data sets with varying characteristics and a range of methods applied to approximate the posterior distribution, resulting in our code being publicly available for similar research to be replicated.

Despite numerous text-to-image translation techniques and available datasets, generating high-quality human-generated text is a challenging task due to its inherent unpredictability. Our proposed approach involves leveraging the collective knowledge of online communities residing on distinct social media platforms to develop a more realistic and varied corpus of human-generated text. However, accessing and integrating content from different platforms is complicated by various restrictions, such as broken APIs, costly data retrieval, and stringent usage limitations. To overcome these obstacles, we investigated alternative methods of data collection, including manually requesting access to data through email and utilizing available open datasets. Our goal is to create a comprehensive open-language dataset focused on emotions, which aims to revolutionize the field of natural language processing by generating authentic emotions expressed by real people instead of perfect, yet artificial, examples. To this end, we integrated content from Twitter, Reddit, and StackOverflow, ensuring that our data spans a wide range of languages and includes sensitive topics like mental health. Ultimately, we hope that IJUSTTME will drive significant progress in the field of natural language processing by providing a more authentic and varied model of human-generated text.

A new package, TensorLy, has been released to facilitate tensor computation and networking capabilities. The package extends LyMan's capabilities for weighted graphs and introduces a tensor join operation that helps in spectral properties computation and noise filtering in high-dimensional data. A key feature of TensorLy is its ability to automatically generate and solve linear systems using tensor calculus, akin to GraphLy's functionality but expanded for tensor operations. The package's viscosity has been optimized for complex tensor calculations, and it offers a user-friendly API for easy adoption. Several novel algorithms for join-based data analysis have been implemented, along with pre-defined subspaces for tensor decomposition. A comprehensive test suite validates the package's correctness, and a companion Jupyter notebook demonstrates TensorLy's utility in real-world applications. The source code is freely available for further expansions to the package.

The Hubble Space Telescope, operating for over 30 years, has been succeeded by the INSIST space telescope, featuring a larger 2-meter aperture and superior imaging capabilities. Located at the Luret satellite, a joint initiative between CNES and AAI, INSIST has launched with the aim of becoming a leading cosmological research facility. Initially focusing on medium-sized projects, INSIST will expand its scope to larger programs in the years to come. INSIST's extensive improvements have greatly enhanced its imaging capabilities, similar to a Herschel Space Observatory with improved sensitivity and wider spectral coverage. INSIST has integrated various technologies, including a merged design combining optics and the cryogenic cooling system, a large-format instruments, and a mechanism resembling SPIRE, combining a single-lens design with a zoom feature. As the first of a new generation of French space telescopes, INSIST will play a key role in future large-scale astronomy and astrophysics programs. INSIST's first year of operations have marked the successful completion of its medium-sized initial projects, complemented by the presentation of initial scientific findings in this document.

In the analysis of continuous outcomes in clinical trials and research, constrained longitudinal data analysis with constrained estimates is a typical approach that warrants further improvement. Current methods often rely on short windows of data and simple models like the mean to make predictions, leading to inaccurate results, particularly when the outcome changes over time. Furthermore, standard constrained longitudinal data analysis can neglect significant time-varying components of change, resulting in suboptimal clinical trial effect sizes and misleading conclusions. This article details the development of a novel constrained longitudinal data analysis framework that incorporates natural cubic splines to effectively capture the changes over time. It provides a computationally efficient method of constrained data analysis that is easily accessible to researchers through widely available software packages in R. Examples illustrate the proposed technique's utility in determining individualized differences and identifying the extent of changes over time. Lastly, a simulated case study demonstrates superior performance of this constrained longitudinal data analysis over traditional methods.

A novel method inspired by a hybrid of evolutionary algorithms has been developed 
to optimize the configuration of molecules prior to simulating reaction pathways 
with molecular mechanics and molecular orbital methods. The framework's efficacy 
was tested on two alignment reactions, 2-propaniol and trans-2-methylcyclohexane, 
where our approach outperformed traditional methods by significantly enhancing the 
quality of the initial configuration, which in turn facilitated more efficient 
simulation of reaction pathways with accurate results. Moreover, this innovative 
technique is expected to streamline reaction pathway calculations by reducing the 
need for post-processing adjustments.

The connections between nonlinear partial differential equations and discrete problems of varying Laplace or Laplacian operators are well established. Research has established the relationships between these discrete problems and their continuous counterparts through the limit process. In our study, specific estimates for solutions to the discrete parabolic Hessian equations are derived, demonstrating that these estimates align with the solutions to the parabolic equation of prescribed mean curvature. Consequently, this framework allows the formulation of an innovative algorithm for generating zero-level graphics of functions, which can also be applied to the study of issuing menisci in the parabolic context of bubble dynamics.

A common encoding scheme, known as Church encoding, can augment a signature with a specific set of types to replicate any functional expression found in the untyped lambda-calculus. Nonetheless, a particular type of recursive data structure called lists, when subject to a certain form of normalization (normal-order reduction), can circumvent this encoding limitation. This paper first proves that using normalization on lists lists can evade the Church encoding's restrictive type system. To counter this outcome, the paper introduces a novel typing system for Church encoding, known as typing contexts, to reinstate the typing system's completeness. A key component of this new system involves imposing a special type on functions that, when evaluated, produce lists as their last argument, effectively creating a form of subtyping that also includes other, more permissive types. Moreover, the paper addresses concerns surrounding arbitrary arbitrary monomorphic type schemes with a decidable representation and demonstrates that, with the introduction of subtyping, these schemes' types can be restored to ensure the typing system's completeness.

This study introduces a novel concept of Lions-type measure differential, leveraging a measure kernel akin to Lions which incorporates an additional integration operator. Consequently, this leads to the establishment of a generalized version of the classical Lebesgue differentiation theorem for measures. Furthermore, this new notion enables the derivation of two important L\'evy processes' properties. Initially, we determine the conditions under the L\'evy measure exhibits growth relative to the exponential function. Secondly, we identify the conditions under which the double exponential distribution represents the L\'evy density of a time reversal process. The study also explores connections to the integration operators as represented by Riemann, Lebesgue, and Perron.

Consider a topological group $G$ with its underlying group $H$ providing the topology on $G$ except for the properties of the topological space, which are inherited from $G$. Given that $G$ has a separation property, $T$ denotes the family of open subgroups in $G$, which forms a hull-kernel type topology on $H$. This paper explores various separation properties and compactness properties of $H$ based on specific conditions of $G$ or $H$. Specifically, it was proven that if $G$ is a compact group then the topological group $G$ has a separation property. Additionally, the first author and B. Grafe previously established that if $G$ is compact then the hull-kernel type topology on $H$ is compact. Furthermore, the authors of this paper proved that for discrete groups $G$, the hull-kernel type topology on $H$ is compact if and only if $G$ has a separation property.

The advancement of natural language capabilities, along with declining costs of executing database queries virtually, makes it feasible to utilize large databases in the absence of a traditional front-end and back-end separation. However, it is still challenging to execute queries without knowing the database at the beginning. We propose a novel framework that employs a sequence-to-sequence model, combined with an entity and role recognition system based on the DBSchema, to accomplish this task. We evaluate our approach using the SystemUmarNet dataset, achieving an error rate of 1.58%. Significantly, our results demonstrate that this framework can operate effectively without knowledge of the database's contents. Furthermore, we note that the error rate can be diminished by approximately 1% through the use of semantic information.

This study addresses the collision avoidance issue in complex robot environments by enhancing an existing strategy called minimal penetration depth, originally designed for single robot operations. A new approach for real-time estimation of fellow robot speeds and positions is developed by incorporating the uncertainty of predictions. Performance testing in simulated scenarios reveals significant improvements when utilizing predicted uncertainty in avoiding collisions, while real-world testing using four heterogeneous robots demonstrates superior results compared to the traditional method.

The mass-to-light ratios of Andromeda dwarf spheroidal galaxies that rotate are notably low. Among the observed galaxies, Andromeda XXV has a particularly exceptional mass-to-light ratio - roughly five times lower than the majority of its type. Previous studies suggested that Andromeda XXV might be a "dark matter-dominated" galaxy, meaning its dark matter density is exceptional. We investigated the orbital structure of Andromeda XXV to assess its trustworthiness as a "dark matter-dominated" example. Our analysis showed that Andromeda XXV's system is likely a "transitional" type, neither extremely dark matter-rich nor excessively bright. In contrast to prior speculation, our findings suggest that Andromeda XXV's mass-to-light ratio is not exceptional; instead, it resembles several dwarf galaxies that rotate. If Andromeda XXV indeed has unusually high dark matter density, it would be inconsistent with this particular astronomical model. Although the model exhibits notable discrepancies, it generally forecasts that certain galaxies, including Andromeda XXV, possess intermediate dark matter content. Overall, our results indicate that Andromeda XXV might serve as an example of a "transitional" galaxy, rather than an exceptional case, and could provide insight into the relationship between galaxy brightness and dark matter density.

A key technology in 6G, non-orthogonal sequence based grant-free access is being developed as a crucial feature. To ensure reliable data transmission in the uplink stage, a sequence set must be efficiently designed. The conventional approach under "orthogonal sequence matching" has severe limitations, particularly in terms of sequence set size, which can lead to suboptimal performance in sequence length. By contrast, non-orthogonal sequences offer the advantage of utilizing multiple sequences for a single grant, thereby increasing capacity and performance while reducing overhead. In this paper, an advanced method called "non-orthogonal sequence matching" is introduced to explore multiple grants with a single sequence and achieve signal stream bundling. As a result, both throughput and delay-sensitive users can enjoy improved performance with lower overhead. The equivalent theoretical model and minimum mean squared error linear detector have been developed to facilitate simulation testing, which has shown substantial gains in throughput and delay performance with non-orthogonal sequences.

The reduction of cancellations in double products within the Penman-Roots model has led to the development of simplified versions by numerous researchers, with many adopting a constant approximation for the correction factor κ. In this paper, we assess the accuracy of κ's consistent constant approximation, specifically in terms of total enthalpy, heat capacity, and latent heat conversion factors across various temperatures. Notably, this constant approximation is seen to be beneficial for adiabatic dynamics in moist air but fails for dynamic processes involving latent heat. Furthermore, we compare the original Penman-Roots model with its kinetic version and a simplified model based on κ's consistent constant approximation, using cloud in situ measurements and observational data to reveal that the simplified model is more accurate and effective in simulating condensation mass flux, latent heat release, and heat production. Ultimately, we believe the simplified model presents a superior option for everyday weak atmospheric use.

Expanding upon the concept of determinants in idempotent permutative $\mathbb F_1^{\pm}$-algebras, we establish a extension of combinatorial principles. Utilizing this new understanding, we develop an innovative algebraic model for classical M\"obius systems. Additionally, we establish a connection to the traditional theory of matroids, specifically determinant and permanental algebras. It is notable that traditional matroid theorems hold true within this $\mathbb F_1^{\pm}$-algebraic framework.

Recent advancements in dialogue state tracking have been achieved through the use of attention mechanisms in encoder-decoder frameworks. However, the process of integrating attention into traditional confusion networks is still in its early stages. This paper novelly proposes the use of an attention mechanism within a confusion network encoder to support end-to-end dialogue state tracking. Furthermore, the paper suggests the use of a cross-attention mechanism to enable a decoder to attend to the confusion network's output, thereby producing corresponding state vectors. Experimental outcomes have demonstrated that our model produces competitive results on the Dialog-State Tracking Challenge dataset when benchmarked against other underlying encoder-decoder models. This paper is unique in its contribution, as it provides insights into the application of attention mechanisms within confusion networks for dialogue state tracking.

Geometrically significant invariants can be obtained by applying established methods such as regularised summations to the moduli space of vector bundles, where the factor topological field theories are built from bundle maps. This article demonstrates how, for specific map configurations, regularised summations translate into locus-by-locus evaluations, thereby making invariant calculations at a classical level feasible. It further shows that these regularised summations adhere to a fundamental symmetry principle. The article also explores the theoretical framework underlying general factor field theories, discussing the geometric structure of the resulting regularisedsummations, and ultimately establishing a generalisation of the Atiyah-Bott element counting method.

This paper's main objective is to examine how intricate the structure of a general access structure is, when it has a small number of essential groups. In doing so, we first established a lower limit on the complexity of such a structure with n minimal qualified sets, which grows logarithmically with n. Furthermore, we also created a collection of specific access structures - those with only two participants, yet varying levels of sharing information - where the complexity of these structures with m minimal qualified groups grows exponentially with m, given m is greater than 2log(n) for sufficiently large m and n. These findings are then connected to existing research on secure multi-party computation. Ultimately, we discuss the relationship between the complexity of general access structures and their asymptotic behavior.

Quantum systems, due to decoherence, lose their key differentiating feature - interference. Since noise levels differ depending on the measured state's distance from the desired target state, measuring spread or distance to a target state doesn't accurately assess noise levels. Therefore, we develop optimal estimators that utilize minimum Fisher information to provide unbiased measurements of noise parameters. Interestingly, when optimal estimators are applied, differences in noise levels caused by decoherence become evident in systems that were previously indistinguishable. This model-invariant approach can reveal different noise levels even when system sizes are tiny, and it always produces unbiased estimates. By numerically analyzing the spread or fidelity gap between target and random states, we find that optimal estimators yield similar results; however, the fidelity gap is more sensitive to noise parameters than the spread. Consequently, we recommend using the fidelity gap and the fidelity metric as better indicators of decoherence caused spread. Furthermore, optimal estimators can be used to assess and compare different random noise models by developing optimal estimators for the quantum cloning noise, noise in the random unitary decocoherence model, and natural decoherence noise. Our research finds that optimal estimators yield similar results for these models regarding spread or fidelity estimates; however, RUDD noise and natural decoherence noise outperform quantum cloning noise, and natural decoherence noise outperforms RUDD noise. Lastly, we research the spread or fidelity estimates resulting from optimal estimators for various noise models such as Markovian noise, non

Recent studies on toroidal-geometric toroidal tensor products have revealed a wide range of eigenfunctions, which have deep connections with physical phenomena such as Edge Localized Modes (ELMs). Through numerical simulations using a reduced MHD model, researchers have discovered that these Palm Tree Modes (PTMs) can evolve into ELMs through pellet injection. This regime bears similarities to both the ELM suppressed phase through Pellet Injection in INTERACT and the low ELM threshold regime in INTERACT, suggesting that PTMs may act as 'pre-thermal' states in this process. This discovery could help better understand ELMs and develop more effective ELM control strategies through Pellet Injection.

While a Nearest Mean Classifier excels in incremental learning scenarios, its effectiveness when building upon pre-trained models needs further exploration. In our study, NMCC's performance alongside five other state-of-the-art methods, was evaluated using the following criteria: how well each method adapts to new data, how well each method performs compared to the ideal scenario where models are both adapted and initial parameters are preserved, and how stable each method's optimization process is. NMCC, which simply used the mean of all data samples as its classifier, surprisingly performed on par with the most advanced methods in all our tests, while maintaining a remarkably stable optimization process. Furthermore, NMCC, which doesn't modify any existing parameters, consistently outperformed two other methods that modify pre-trained models. NMCC also notably performed on par with the ideal scenario in almost all tests, indicating NMCC's ability to nearly match the performance of the ideal scenario in all tests except when evaluating the impact of parameter freeze on a challenging scenario, few-shot prototyping, and class imbalance.

To fully grasp the extent to, extent and meaning of hate speech, the social and cultural setting in which it is used must also be taken into account. Although hate speech detection techniques have made considerable advancements, they still lag behind in comprehending the social and cultural undertones that give hate speech its full meaning and context. To bridge this gap, researchers have recently suggested incorporating various types of social and cultural data to enhance the performance of hate speech detection models. Despite these efforts, the social and cultural knowledge embedded in language remains difficult to access reliably. Consequently, existing methods rely heavily on available social and cultural data, which may be limited and unreliable. This thesis introduces a new model called SECT, which utilizes a semi-supervised learning strategy that explores the socio-cultural context of hate speech detection. By modeling the socio-cultural context as a markov process, SECT is able to capture both temporal patterns of hate speech and socio-cultural context, allowing it to explore the socio-cultural context effectively even when socio-cultural data is limited. Moreover, SEct is able to segment hate speech and socio-cultural context effectively, which enables it to semi-supervised learning strategy that explores the socio-cultural context of hate speech detection. This approach is unique because SEct is able to explore the socio-cultural context of hate speech detection. This approach is able to segment and learn from both hate speech and socio-cultural context effectively, which is why it is able to perform well on various tasks related to hate speech detection, such as classification,

We examine collective oscillations in connected networks linked by gap junctions, considering the effects of diverse degree-based distributions. Our model utilizes ordinary differential equations to model the voltage trajectories of individual cells and an diffusion equation to model the voltage trajectory of the network's external front. Our approach combines elements of phase oscillations and reaction-diffusion systems, where individual cells represent non-trivial gap junctions engaging in phase oscillations, and a diffusion equation governing the evolution of the network's external front. Our findings demonstrate how altering the width of a degree distribution impacts the frequency and forms of these oscillations. Moreover, our approach offers a new methodology for identifying and validating the limits of stable gap junction oscillations and highlights the significance of degree distribution in shaping these oscillations. This work has potential applications in identifying stable gap junction oscillations in various fields, including neuroscience and biology, and could be extended to account for additional factors, such as spatial variations and noise.

Defining the ideal method to rectify programming errors is a daunting task and a key area of research within empirical software engineering. Existing studies that aim to improve or optimize bug fixing techniques face a particular challenge: they require access to a large number of historical bug fixes that serve as a benchmark. However, such studies are often constrained by the limited availability of data. In this research, in an effort to overcome this limitation, we propose and evaluate a new approach to replicate effective bug fixes. By applying this method to two widely studied bug datasets, we were able to replicate 73% and 85% of bugs exactly as human fixes in two respective datasets, according to two unique evaluation metrics. Furthermore, 94% of replicated fixes were identical to 50% of human fixes in one dataset, and 85% in another. In comparative experiments, replicated fixes performed as well as human fixes across multiple dimensions: precision, location of modifications, the extent of modifications, the necessary number of modifications, and overall performance. Additionally, these replicated fixes allowed us to gain deeper insights into the strategies used by human fixers, which would have been impossible otherwise. In an effort to shed more light on this particular aspect, we conducted a preliminary study among programming contest participants to determine whether human fixers tend to utilize prior examples from the same domain, and found that they often don't. In this research, we were able to replicate these specific human actions and understand how they could inform improved programming techniques.

Inner channel capacity bounds are typically obtained by combining information-theoretic ideas and extremal combinatorics.  A specific bound involves identifying the largest number of interference-free interferences within a given channel configuration.  Generally, this bounding method yields conservative estimates of capacity.  In this research, we propose a novel approach that reframes existing bounds in a more conservative light, enabling the decomposition of the MIMO BC into coupled BC components.  A Beirao da Veiga & Schroeder lemma is invoked to achieve this, along with a new extremal combinatorics result which we call the block-shifting lemma.  Practically, this bounding method offers no advantage over conventional MIMO capacity bounds.  However, it provides a valuable theoretical framework with the potential to revolutionize future MIMO transmission techniques.

This paper introduces coefficients ${{\rm Coeff}_{lm}}$ to analyze angular patterns within a specific region of a particle's transverse momentum spectrum, expanding upon linear flow analysis. Just like traditional flow analysis coefficients, {{\rm Coeff}_{lm}} capture specific characteristics of a particle's movement, but are associated with a broader range of momentum levels. By examining the azimuthal angles in the momentum plane, researchers can utilize ${{\rm Coeff}_{lm}}$ to differentiate the behaviors of fundamental particles and collectivized physics at high-momentum levels. Extending beyond elliptic flow analysis, the coefficients also incorporate linear flow analysis and are highly relevant to the study of collective behavior at high-momentum levels in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Furthermore, studies have shown that optimal flow coefficients can be used to uncover collective behavior in certain processes, like vector boson production, where relevant. By exploiting the uniqueness of optimal coefficients, researchers may be able to observe signatures of collectivized physics even beneath background interference at various momentum levels. Ultimately, the introduction of ${{\rm Coeff}_{lm}}$ provides a powerful new tool for examining the collective behavior of particles and may uncover new physics underlying a variety of collision events.

The application of machine learning in the healthcare sector is becoming increasingly widespread. However, it also raises concerns about the potential for data breaches which could compromise patients' confidentiality. In response to these risks, researchers from China and the United States propose an adaptable framework for protecting sensitive information within healthcare datasets. By formulating risk assessments based on probabilities and using game theory to represent interactive scenarios, they develop an algorithm that not only ensures the protection of sensitive information but also optimizes the overall utility for all parties involved. Through testing with real-world healthcare data, their approach has proven effective in preserving security while achieving optimal utility and improving the accuracy of predictions made by machine learning models.

Recent advancements in AI research utilizing wireless sensing and sensing/communication combined methods have yielded graph neural networks capable of operating independently. However, the graphene-based transmitters used in these models frequently experience outages due to the random characteristics of the pseudorandom frequency signal, resulting in unreliable output predictions. To enhance decentralized GNN predictions' robustness to these errors, we are investigating alternative training techniques. A double Leaky ReLUs activation function is proposed for the decentralized GNN, leveraging its robustness to errors in prediction caused by random signal disruption, thus increasing overall prediction accuracy. To assess activation function performance, we created a synthetic dataset representing a FMCW imaging system's signal, applying perturbations mimicking wireless transmission noise to the input, and measuring output prediction robustness. Experimental results demonstrate the improved robustness of the double Leaky ReLUs variant under various noise levels when compared to conventional models, while achieving output prediction accuracy comparable to its counterparts under ideal signal conditions.

We use a novel approach to define metropolitan areas based on daily location data from cell phones and determine the size of these metropolitan cores. We then examine the relationship between the sizes of these cores and homicide rates within cities, finding a negative correlation. Cities closest to urban centers tend to have lower homicide rates, whereas those isolated from urban areas tend to have lower violence levels and similar crime rates to those in more rural areas. We compare our findings to existing research, attributing the results to the influence of urban cities on their surrounding areas.

Generalizing Nesterov's acceleration technique for linear convergence to stochastic gradients leads to accelerated methods that outperform their non-accelerated counterparts on convex objectives. Our research aims to extend these findings to settings involving adaptive step sizes, typically used in practice. Our results confirm that accelerating stochastic gradients with adaptive step sizes yields a convergence rate of ${\mathcal O}\left(1/n\log(n)\cdot d^{1/3}\log(n)+1/n}\right}$. To achieve this, we establish a lower bound for incorporating Nesterov's acceleration with adaptive step sizes, demonstrating that any method that reaches this convergence rate is also capable of achieving the slower non-accelerated rate of ${\mathcal O}(1/n)\).

Dark matter and energy, which are evident in cosmology, are likely hidden by regular laws of physics. Researchers have proposed a "photonic axion network" model as an alternative to the established dark matter theory. In this scenario, dark matter and dark energy are composed of axion or axion-like particles generating a multitude of faint, distinct spectral lines. These photons, produced through numerous light interactions with dark matter, could be detected in future experiments as a collective background radiation with a high signal-to-noise ratio. To determine the potential dark matter component of this signal, researchers have calculated a "photonic dark matter fraction" and found that it's significant, taking up a substantial part of dark matter, often exceeding 50% with certain ALP properties. This photon signal could be partially absorbed by the intergalactic medium, thereby reducing its observable intensity. Researchers have estimated the dark matter fraction relevant for various experiments and observed phenomena, showing that a significant portion relevant for STO, PTO, and PHEXA could compromise these experiments' ability to accurately measure axion properties. Conversely, a signal relevant for LISA and Gravitational-wave observatories might actually enhance these experiments' capabilities. Researchers have also used QCD data and astrophysical constraints to limit the photon dark matter fraction and thereby set restrictions on ALPs mass and their light interaction rates.

The bosonic oscillator is a fundamental system in both theoretical and applied science, and its linearized behavior is well-suited for describing thermal equilibrium in a wide range of contexts. However, when subjected to non-linear forcing, this simple oscillator can exhibit complex self-oscillating behavior, which is reminiscent of Hele-Shaw flow. Building on existing research into bosonic oscillators and non-linear self-oscillations, we present a new method for creating a wide range of exactly solvable non-linear bosonic oscillators and discuss their potential applications in describing flow in complex geometries.

In robotics grasp planning, achieving a reliable grasp that successfully withholds external forces is a highly challenging task due to the required precision and the diverse nature of objects with intricate surfaces. Past research on grasp planning has typically treated the planning process as a shape-based fit evaluation, where a predefined library of possible grasps is applied to an object model to identify suitable positions. However, these methods often yield unstable grasps that fail to withstand external forces, and the diversity of resulting grasps is generally limited. In contrast, our approach, known as DexGraspNet, employs a data-driven method to directly predict diverse and stable grasps for manipulators with kinematic parameters. Our network takes an object net and a manipulator mesh as inputs, generating a set of predicted grasps along with corresponding pressure distributions at distinct environments. By analyzing predicted pressure distributions at the edge conditions of variously shifting object poses, our approach distinctively measures grasp stability. Furthermore, our training dataset comprises millions of random grasper configurations, ensuring a comprehensive diversity of predicted grasps and manipulation modes. Our evaluation on widely-used grasper configurations demonstrates that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art grasper planning methods in terms of both stability and diversity.

To enhance the quality of synthetic aperture sonar images, the current linear sampling approach will be optimized by substituting its weighting scheme with a more suitable mode choice, resulting in the radiating element being able to exploit phase and amplitude modulation for the desired look direction. However, the initial linear sampling method is not efficient in terms of its point-source function and has limited ability to maintain constant background contrast, which poses a significant challenge for producing high-quality images. Therefore, the paper proposes a new method called rCASPR that leverages the ability of VLSI-based analog circuits to seamlessly implement precise ramp functions, allowing for further optimization of the sampling scheme. By combining this optimized sampling scheme with the constant background characteristic of the previous analog phase imaging method, high-quality images with minimal artifacts are produced, even under difficult conditions where there is substantial side lobe activity. These superior images significantly outperform those achieved using traditional synthetic aperture sonar techniques, where the constant background character has not been utilized before.

Albeit teacher-student learning shows potential in cross-domain knowledge transfer, its extensive computational requirements have hindered its widespread adoption. We hypothesized that reducing computational complexity via channel pruning in student networks would facilitate a more faithful student model learning experience from its teacher predecessor. Building upon this concept, this paper introduces an innovative framework known as Proxy Teacher, which performs an in-depth analysis of proxy variables to derive a proximity measure for evaluating channel importance during the cross-domain knowledge transfer process. Consequently, a more accurate representation of the teacher model is achieved by retaining crucial student channels. Our proposed framework has proven its efficacy on four distinct datasets and benchmark models, yielding superior results compared to the conventional teacher-student learning paradigm and cutting-edge state-of-the-art approaches.

We have identified two new topological invariants which generalize Bierstone's finding that $C^{1}$-smooth linear submersions defined on $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ for $m \geq 2$ are smoothly locally flat. 
One of these invariants applies to smooth linear-like submersions defined on $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ for $m \geq 2$ and has its analog in smooth linear submersions defined on Banach spaces. 
The other one specifically targets linear submersions defined on $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ for $m \geq 2$ and its analog can be found in linear operators between infinite-dimensional Banach spaces. 
Conversely, we have shown that any continuous invariant that would prove that all linear-like submersions defined on $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ for $m \geq 2$ are smoothly locally flat would also imply the continuous invariant found by Perlmutter that characterizes the set of linear homeomorphisms defined on $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with $m \geq 2$. 

Moreover, we have established that local flatness invariance for specific classes of smooth linear submurations defined on $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ for $m \geq 2$ would also imply the continuous invariant found by Perlmutter that characterizes the set of linear homeomorph

Ecosystems that grazing ecosystems are often modeled using temporal delay equations due to the time it takes for demographic events to propagate. The majority of these models have relied on local per capita growth rates, despite demographic factors being influenced by spatial factors. We explore the impact of incorporating non-local aridity, that considers the average water to wet water ratio across surrounding patches, on the stability of these models rather than relying on a patch's own average. This change in formulation modifies the model from a uniform one to one where every patch acts as a source and sink, leading to a variety of behaviors such as patch-by-patch transmission of fluctuations and the emergence of different stable states. When grazing pressure is increased under regular conditions, the ecosystem tends towards a state where it is vulnerable to the disappearance of grass due to the grazing of lavishes and the fluctuation of populations. However, incorporating spatial non-locality has been discovered to increase the ecosystem's resistance to the disappearance of grass due to the grazing of lavishes under the conditions of increased aridity.

In various fields of study, we apply multidimensional data transformation techniques such as PCA, which is widely used either by itself or as a pre-processing step for other methods like classification. We've discovered that conventional PCA is highly susceptible to adaptive input. As a result, it doesn't provide an adequate representation of data that originates from different sources. Furthermore, we've identified a method to manipulate PCA representations, allowing us to attribute most of the variance to a desired subset of variables. We've proposed a new framework, referred to as "parameterized PCA," that enables us to quantify and model the amount of variance coming from different components. We use this approach to better understand parameterized PCA representations and their usefulness in "domain shift" problems, highlighting its capacity to serve as a robust feature extractor.

The target of our investigation is the internal conversion between the $X^1 B_{1g}$ and $^{3}B_{1g}$ states of [Cu$_2$O$_2$]$^{2+}$. Using high-level computational methods that combine relativistic coupled-cluster theory with density functional theory, we analyze the Born-Oppenheimer breaking effect on the aforementioned internal conversion in detail. Both dissociation limits of [Cu$_2$O$_2$]$^{2+}$, [Cu$^+\$O$^+$] and [Cu$^+\$O]$^{+*}$, are identified as extreme cases of Born-Oppenheimer breaking. Furthermore, high-level calculations of Born-Oppenheimer breaking in $X^1 B_{1g}$ state of [Cu$_2$O$_2$]$^{2+}$ indicate that it exhibits relatively small Born-Oppenheimer breaking effect in comparison to $^{3}B_{1g}$ state. In the system of [Cu$_2$O$_2$]$^{2+}$, predicted nonradiative time periods of $X^1 B_{1g}$ and $^{3}B_{1g}$ state of approximately 1-3 ps in conjunction with small isomerization energies of less than 200 cm$^{-1}$ suggest potential importance of diabatic dynamics in [Cu$_2$O$_2$]$^{2+}$ in

High-frequency trading (FHT) technology, underpinned by ultra-fast signal processing, could greatly benefit from quantum technologies, now accessible outside a laboratory setting. The application of quasi-quantum communication (QQC) techniques, combining photonic and electric approaches, could lead to the development of fast and secure FHT systems. This perspective outlines a strategy to integrate QQC into the FHT workflow, capitalizing on quantum signal distribution, storage, and processing advantages. It highlights the importance of reducing latency in FHT, enabling the inclusion of quantum-ready systems, and outlines a plan for implementing this in the algorithmic aspect of FHT. The approach, grounded in practical applications and accessible to those unfamiliar with quantum technologies, aims to facilitate the integration of quantum techniques in FHT algorithms, thereby facilitating the use of quasi-quantum tools.

Recent approaches to online mechanisms for selling items are often based on specific demand assumptions, such as single-demand or addictive demand. In our work, we present a novel mechanism that can handle a broad range of demand types without requiring additional information about prices or valuation functions. This mechanism relies on short messages known as "bids" submitted by buyers, which convey their estimated probability of purchasing each item. We demonstrate that the optimal auction outcome can be achieved by simply sorting these probabilities in descending order and allocating items to their highest-priority buyers. This mechanism is transparent, as the seller needs only know the number of submissions from each buyer. Additionally, its implementation is data-efficient, as the seller can make decisions after receiving a limited number of submissions from an unknown number of buyers. We validate our mechanism's effectiveness by showing that it yields the optimal auction outcome and meets a revenue guarantee. We also illustrate its practical application to multi-item auctions, demonstrating that it can be used to run auctions independently of demand types with only a slight revenue reduction compared to the optimal approach.

To accurately summarize lengthy documents, a system must efficiently identify key points and present them in a condensed form. Current approaches typically rely on two separate components for summary generation and fact-checking, but our proposed RANSRC model unites these functions via an entity-based chain that helps correct factual errors and enhance overall accuracy. By leveraging entity chains as guiding roadmaps, our model can effectively manage and minimize the impact of inaccuracies during the summarization process. Our experiments on the MSRC Paragraph dataset demonstrate that RANSRC outperforms existing summarization methods, validated as state-of-the-art, while our findings indicate that incorporating an entity-based chain helps mitigate factual inaccuracies better than prior remediation techniques.

This paper establishes a new approach to proving the local $n$-dimensional Rademacher differentiability of a function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$. This approach is based on a more general result regarding the differentiability of certain $(n-1)$-dimensional functions that satisfy specific conditions, which are then used to investigate the differentiability of specific $(n-1)$-dimensional functions whose limits along hyperplanes are finite, and to establish a relationship between the differentiability of an $n$-dimensional function and the differentiability of an $(n-1)$-dimensional function whose partial derivatives with respect to one variable are well-defined and satisfy specific growth conditions.

Our research focuses on the development of a non-verbal indicator for Autism Spectrum Disorder identification by utilizing entrainment characteristics extracted from acoustic features present in spoken interactions. We center our investigation around the degree to which an individual's vocal tone synchronizes with others during conversations, as measured by certain spectral and temporal features derived from short-term autocorrelation functions. By testing several features derived from autocorrelation functions, we found that utilizing multiple metrics simultaneously achieved the highest degree of accuracy in predicting ASD diagnosis, reaching a success rate of approximately 89.7% for an optimal combination of these features.

This study develops a comprehensive framework for categorical quantum mechanics alongside a space-based quantum calculus. The construction of categorical quantum mechanics adheres to basic principles, drawing inspiration from Lawvere's approach to axiomatic domain theory and Snyder's work on categorical classical mechanics. In parallel, we define types of spaces that encompass quantum properties and use these spaces to build a categorical quantum calculus. The relationship between the categorical framework and Axelrod, Bisognano, and Henneberger's approach is examined, and we semantically ground categorical quantum mechanics within a topos with a lawless, free partial order.

Recent studies on the composite-fermion wavefunction used ground states of two-dimensional shells with magnetic fields, observing that the energy differences between the composite-fermion and Laughlin states narrow in proportion to $L^{-2}$ as the length ($L$) increases. However, this scaling relation can be misinterpreted due to its similarity to $L^{-2}$, leading to two concerns: (1) whether the previous findings primarily reflect the method of calculating the energy difference rather than the behavior of the wavefunctions, and (2) whether the CFT relative to the Laughlin state smoothly varies with system size. We address these by applying two new methods: one evaluates the energy difference using the exact perturbation theory, and the other directly computes the overlap of the two states. Our results show that the overestimation of the energy difference using the energy perturbation theory follows a $L^{-2}$ scaling, but this does not justify the method's use. Moreover, we found that the CFT smoothly varies with an effective fractional quantum number that converges to $\nu = 1/m$ as $L$ increases, and the overlap scaling with $L$ mirrors the variation of this effective quantum number, while the energy difference scaling with $L^{-2}$ corresponds to the squared magnitude of the overlap at a particular, earlier stage of $L$.

One key approach in glaciology involves a weak formulation of the entire glacial system through a variational inequality. However, the current method lacks a thorough examination of the impact of rigid modes in velocity on the inequality's consistency. This paper uses a theoretical and practical approach to demonstrate that incorporating rigid modes yields an equivalent revised variational inequality with a closed solution set. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of smooth solutions for the revised inequality and provide supporting examples. This revised variational inequality can serve as a foundation for developing stable numerical solutions.

We analyzed the dynamics of massive star-forming galaxies at a distance of z=2.91 through direct observations of their molecular (MGN 1432-4826) and ionized (MGN 1432-4827) gas outflows. Our findings indicate that heavy outflows of ionized gas have a greater impact on the overall gas composition of these galaxies than the observed molecular outflow rates. Additionally, the effects of these outflows lead to rapid gas depletion, which supports the notion that starburst galaxies at such distances are experiencing their final intense episodes of star formation. Furthermore, the observed outflows have a greater effect on the overall gas composition of these galaxies than the rate at which new gas is brought into the system through the process of gas condensation. Our findings also estimate the rate at which the ionized gas outflows are enriched with heavy elements to be approximately 10 times greater than the rate at which the gas is enriched via star-formation processes.

Research into the transverse momentum dependence of the third flow coefficient, $v_3$, of various particles and hadrons has been examined in relation to $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 200 GeV Pb+Pb collisions. The findings indicate that $v_3$ increasing with transverse momentum exhibits a similarity with the patterns seen in the second flow coefficient, $v_2$. A comparison with the Star Light program for simulated central Pb+Pb collisions reveals that the $v_3$ coherence for different particles remains consistent across the full range of transverse momentum, whereas the $v_2$ coherence demonstrates a notable decrease at higher transverse momenta. The relationships between $v_n$ and transverse momenta are explored within the context of two distinct models.

A robotic swarm, comprised of multiple autonomous devices, needs efficient detection and response systems to effectively navigate through their environment. Effective perception is a crucial element in developing a robotic swarm's capacity for adaptive decision-making and action. This research introduces a robotic swarm testbed equipped with wireless sensor nodes and a portable, reconfigurable interface to facilitate robotic perception research. In addition to describing the proposed testbed, we outline a framework for integrating the swarm with a Kalman filter to refine state estimates and discuss its potential benefits, such as improved range estimation and minimal communication requirements.

For vision-language models to understand real-world scenarios, being able to understand how a 2D image relates to 3D geometry is crucial. Currently, computer vision techniques often rely on 2D representations, but research has shown that using 3D geometry can lead to better results. One reason traditional image classification approaches may not be as effective for pre-training deep vision models is that estimating scene geometry can provide more valuable insights. Therefore, this paper puts forth a new idea for pre-training deep vision models using tasks that combine 2D images with 3D geometry. Specifically, this paper uses panoramic images with accurate 2D projections of 3D geometry, leading to several initial experiments. These experiments notably achieved state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet-1K and Visiolabe, surpassing results obtained with other pre-training approaches. Moreover, this paper demonstrates that using these experiments as a form of self-supervised pre-training can also outperform other methods on SimSiam and DINO without needing a large dataset like ImageNet. Lastly, this paper shows that dense pre-training on SIFT flow alongside other approaches can lead to even better performance on Visiolabe and other existing datasets.

This article defines log-harmonic functions on the unit disk by relation to analytic functions, and explores their properties, including the  L^p spaces of these log-harmonic functions. The article also establishes key inequalities within these spaces, such as Minkowski and Schwarz inequalities. Furthermore, it introduces the concept of almost runic log-harmonic functions and investigates their main characteristics.

A novel, efficient algorithm is introduced for calculating Kendall's tau, a non-parametric rank correlation measure. The algorithm's runtime is directly proportional to n log(n) k, where n represents the size of the dataset, and k denotes the size of the set of unique keys present in the two ordered lists. In comparative studies, it outperforms existing methods like the implementation found in Python's SciPy, with substantial speed gains observed for larger datasets.

This work develops a unified theoretical framework that integrates Federated Learning and Local Differential Privacy, leveraging a convex relaxation of the differential privacy constraints and resulting in a dual formulation with LDP characteristics. By making a "local proxy" assumption, a new composite algorithm, FL-REND, is created, combining the benefits of both FL and LDP. This algorithm is shown to be efficient, even in nonconvex problem spaces, and its performance is demonstrated with both synthetic and real-world data sets, showcasing significant improvements in privacy levels, model accuracy, and convergence rates compared to alternative methods.

This project focuses on the advancement of multi-parameter topological data analysis. A novel approach in this field involves utilizing single-parameter topological data analysis to multi-parameter studies by establishing mathematical structures that enable efficient computation. The present work builds upon this concept and uses the single-variable Euler characteristic to develop a multi-variable extension, which can be applied to any semi-algebraic set within the context of algebraic geometry. The desired topological invariants of these semi-algebraic sets can then be derived from the extended Euler characteristic. The study also incorporates a polynomial extension of the extended Euler characteristic, along with an exploration of its key properties and applications. Furthermore, the work presents a novel method for computing semi-algebraic homology using computational algebraic topology tools, and applies this approach to the study of semi-algebraic sets with restricted boundary attributes. The paper's findings were implemented using the OpenEulerChar program, showcasing its efficiency in computing multi-parameter topological invariants of complex geometric objects.

In a pioneering study, **Baldwin's singular perturbation method** was successfully applied to a prominent ecological model, the Lotka-Alexander model, to analyze changes occurring within two interconnected populations. Our investigation focused on the changes at a singular point, which represents the transition from one equilibrium to another, and involved ignoring minor effects near this point, similar to how aerial photographers remove noise from images. Utilizing this approach, we discovered two previously unknown transformations, which reveal how changes affect the curves representing population growth. These discoveries enabled us to simplify complex analysis of population dynamics, including determining stability, identifying phase transitions, and calculating the size of fluctuations. Key outcomes include identifying areas where stability is lost through saddle-node and Hopf bifurcations, mapping the locations of bifurcation points, calculating the size of oscillations, and illustrating how the ratio of these oscillations and the changes in population growth fluctuate.

A novel facet pivot method has been developed for solving linear programming (LP) problems. Utilizing advanced capabilities of modern computers, this algorithm selectively chooses pivot facets based on predicted improvements in the off-the-fence matrix, both outside and inside the current simplex iteration. As a result, the proposed method successfully combines the optimality preserving nature of vertex pivot algorithms with the effectiveness of two-phase pivot algorithms. Through practical testing across a diverse range of randomly generated and real-world problems, it has been demonstrated that the proposed method surpasses first-phase vertex pivot and pivot pivot algorithms, matching the performance of two-phase vertex pivot algorithms only when dealing with deficient basic feasible solutions. Due to its efficiency and ease of implementation, the proposed method is now capable of rivaling the best available pivot-based algorithms for solving LP problems.

We establish a graded analogue of the Quillen-Suslin theory, building upon grade-restricted versions of the theorem without the need for the graded version of the Serre-Swan correspondence. This enables us to derive a graded version of the Chevalley theorem for graded commutative algebras, and provides new insights into the geometric classification of tori in algebraic groups, as well as the study of graded rings and their 'free' modules in the context of algebraic geometry.

The NWA approach employed in top quark studies may lead to inaccurate predictions when analyzing distributions with significantly narrower widths, like those of the $\tau$ nuclino and the top quark itself, compared to an infinitesimally small test particle mass. We've found that incorporating the full width of the particle into a template fit can resolve this limitation and enhance the background challenge in detecting the top quark's charge. Although initially, accounting for the full width won't improve accuracy for the tau nuclino, utilizing the correct methodology according to Bayesian statistics is essential to avoid deriving incorrect conclusions about the model's parameters, even if the results remain essentially unchanged.

Recent breakthroughs in facial spoofing detection have been driven by the expansion of the self-supervised learning framework, specifically for vision transformer models. This paper makes two key contributions: Firstly, it introduces the concept of transferring knowledge from pre-trained vision transformer models using token and vision transformers, breaking new ground in the field's initial approach. Secondly, it introduces a cutting-edge framework known as FiDeTiME, which leverages token and vision transformer models to analyze frequency, spatial, temporal, and temporal-motion features for spoofing detection. This paper validates the FiDeTiME framework's robust performance using the supporting videos from four publicly accessible datasets: Photo, OULNI-IRsys, CAS(MTL)PS, and Columbia3D. Results demonstrate that FiDeTiME surpasses existing state-of-the-art models in terms of accuracy, reaching an impressive 99.70% score on the combined datasets. Additionally, experiments show that FiDeTiME achieves state-of-the-art performance on each individual dataset, with photorealistic detection reaching an accuracy of 99.88% for OULNI-IRsys and 99.70% for Columbia3D, while distillable model shows significant improvements over baseline models and outperforms other relevant models by approximately 15% in depth distortion and 7% in random color.

A crucial requirement for autonomous vehicles is to approximate their environment and predict their surroundings based on available data. Autonomy-focused research into artificial intelligence and computer vision has led to advancements in the development of architectures that enable vehicles to drive independently, especially in complex scenarios where information is limited or full of ambiguity. A key component in this effort is the integration of recurrent neural networks, which allow deep learning models to make use of sequential data and improve the accuracy of predictions and estimates. Furthermore, the application of probabilistic models in autonomous vehicle navigation enhances the vehicle's ability to adapt to uncertain conditions and interconnect with other systems. However, the possibility of fraud and counterfeiting must be addressed, and we present a novel method for validating vehicle location and predicting the presence of obstacles based on the use of deep probabilistic sequences and the imposition of geographical constraints. Our approach involves the combination of a traditional CNN-based architecture for processing images with a recurrent neural network designed to predict the output of a geolocation system. The result is a notable increase of over 4000x in fraud detection accuracy compared to baseline models that do not employ probabilistic sequences, as well as significant improvements in the precision of obstacle prediction and vehicle location estimation. A thorough analysis of the performance of our system involves the use of novel evaluation metrics that focus on the overall robustness of the model.

Evolutionary algorithms have been widely applied in parallel computational systems, incorporating various innovative techniques to enhance their performance efficiency. A novel parent selection approach is introduced, aiming to accelerate search progress within a population by identifying and concentrating on under-explored regions. This strategy is implemented and evaluated in a parallel evolutionary algorithm operating on binary strings, specifically the PSO algorithm, and its efficacy is demonstrated through empirical studies on several benchmark problems, showcasing improved convergence rate and higher success rate compared to the standard PSO method.

The potential for astrophysical neutrino masses to be determined is significant, 
and one particular method involves utilizing microlensing events from the Galactic 
centre to measure the mass of the lensing stars. The analysis involves determining 
the distribution of these stars within the Galactic centre, which can be done by 
analyzing data from microlensing events and using their distances from the Galactic 
centre to estimate their masses through their critical densities. A simulation 
study conducted using these methods revealed that the method can effectively use 
microlensing events to estimate the mass distribution of the Galactic centre, 
particularly when the events are separated by over 0.5 millarseconds from the Galactic 
centre. Additionally, the study found that the method could effectively identify 
outliers in the mass distribution, which could potentially include objects such as 
black holes or giant stars.

We investigate a driven atomic system placed in an optical lattice and driven by a single laser field, which exhibits non-reversible dynamics and a non-Markovian evolution of its Floquet generator under specific conditions. Our research focuses on two distinct regimes, characterized by either a weak or a weakly localized dispersion-like motion, which are both found to generate an infinite latticing potential's coefficient at lower frequencies and give rise to corresponding non-Markovian behavior. Interestingly, we discover that two distinct approaches, either heat dissipation analysis or examination of a system's band structure, can effectively identify and distinguish between these two regimes. Consequently, we establish a method to realize a driven quantum simulator based on an optical lattice and driven by a single laser field that is capable of modeling systems exhibiting non-Markovian, non-equilibrium dynamics.

The effect of Rh content on the metamagnetic cluster size and the by the same authors of Ref. \cite{Sodin2020} previously established freezing temperature in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ alloys has been examined. The Rh content range of $0.052\leq x\leq 0.112$ investigated didn't result in the formation of the B20 structure, with an upper bound of $x\approx 0.112$ established for its existence. Increasing Rh content led to an increase in the freezing temperature and a corresponding expansion of the metamagnetic cluster size. Contrary to observations in other alloys based on rare earth and transition metals, the Rh Rh bonding didn't have a notable effect on the electrical conductivity, low temperature Celentano framework-based electronic structure or the magnetic cluster size. The variation in electronic exchange splitting at the M site had a correlated response with the cluster size, while it remained largely unchanged at the X site.

The first identification of a specific isospecies, 12C-13C, in a source outside of the Sun's atmosphere has been made. This isospecies, called HINSA (Hydrogen Isotopic Neutral Singly-Absorptive), is detected through a specific line in the infrared spectrum. Analysts observed and analyzed data from a device called a telescope, looking at a specific source called G176.51+00.20, and were able to identify both a physical process called vibration and the two most common forms of carbon-13 in the source. These forms, called 12C-13C and 14N-12C, are identified through a specific line in the infrared spectrum. The researchers found that the source contains a specific mixture of the two, called a composition. This is the first time the composition has been measured for outside of the Sun's atmosphere. The researchers also noticed that the source's composition varies across the source's visible boundaries, and recorded the variations.

The use of a device called a factory and a specific line in the infrared spectrum allowed the researchers to identify the two most common forms of carbon in the source. These forms, called 12C-13C and 14N-12C, are identified through a specific line in the infrared spectrum. The researchers also noticed that the source's composition varies across the source's visible boundaries, and recorded the variations.
