We discovered that, on average, Be stars have higher binary frequencies, more pronounced amplitude distributions, and more pronounced gravitational frequencies than their normal B-type counterparts. Additionally, our analysis revealed differences in the distribution of binary system frequencies between Be and normal B stars, which indicated the presence of possible companion objects among Be stars. We identified 37 potential binary candidates out of a total of 246 Be stars, and 13 potential binary candidates out of a total of 246 normal B stars. Our findings provide valuable insights into the binary characteristics of Be stars and serve as a basis for future investigations into the influence of binarity on the Be phenomenon.

Although out-of-domain robustness has become a priority for spoken language understanding, out-of-domain training methods like trimming training data to match test distributions are often ineffective.  We've identified a significant issue with existing approaches: they don't utilize the full potential of trimming data for ITN models.  ITN models combining language and task networks can retain in-domain information even when the input format changes, so we propose leveraging ITN's translation ability to trim data in the feature space instead, especially for out-of-domain categories that lack abundant in-domain data.  This resulted in outperforming standard in-domain training in ITN models and showing significant advantages over weakly-labeled online data and self-training methods in the low-resource setting of predicting spoken question poses.  Our proposed technique is universally applicable to various ITN architectures and can be easily extended to internal out-of-domain evaluations.

The primary intention of this study is to establish a geometrically-based criterion for minimizing the first eigenvalue of the Hermite operator, closely related to the Schrödinger operator with a specific parameter α greater than zero, by adapting the Faber-Krahn type inequality. It has also been proven that among all unit volume domains with a given geometric shape, the optimal configuration for minimizing the first eigenvalue occurs when the domains are as close to spherical as possible. Furthermore, the study derived precise estimates of the first eigenvalue in order to illustrate the benefits of the optimal configuration.

Emerging research indicates that large models with complex designs can often be represented by a simpler model variant called the neural tangent kernel. This breakthrough has led to improved understandability of these models, leveraging the kernel's properties as a low-dimensional representation. We are exploring whether this concept can be applied to tabular data, specifically in the area of structured data. By developing a neural tangent kernel for structured data, we encounter obstacles not present in traditional tabular data, such as the nature of computations involving rows and constraints on data representation. Our work involves defining a neural tangent kernel that can effectively process tables, while demonstrating its capabilities in predicting patient outcomes based on clinical table inputs during an AI for Social Good competition focused on chronic disease prediction.

The extended Hatano-Nelson chain, characterized by complex nearest-neighbor hopping between some sites, shows the occurrence of edge-bond skin and no bulk contribution to certain observable quantities. Unlike the original one-dimensional non-Hermitian model, this extension displays no point-like singularities in its spectral density. The associated Green's function reveals the origin of skin and bulk behaviors, which are linked to the eigenvalues of a specific matrix. The behavior observed in this model might serve as a foundation for studying skin and bulk phenomena in more complex systems.

Our research focuses on exploring speech perception strategies to create a synthesized female voice that is perceived as authoritative.  By combining the 20 fundamental parameters of speech from the GlotTex database and analyzing them through self-supervised learning models like Autoencoders and CNNs, we determined that a narrow frequency range of spectral characteristics has the most significant impact on conveying a sense of competence. Further investigation revealed that mixing these fundamental parameters in specific proportions effectively simulates human speech patterns, altering the acoustic cues to render the voice more compelling.  Using a crowd-sourced model of human perception, we fine-tuned a text-to-speech system to produce speech with a distinctive tone of authority, demonstrating that personalized acoustic modeling can significantly enhance speech quality.

A new model of non-thermal resonant dark matter production has been developed, based on an initial preon-based theory. The model uses a modified version of electroweak gauge bosons as a decaying resonance to transfer dark matter to the hidden sector through a feeble interaction. The dark matter in this system remains stable due to an extended discrete symmetry. Unlike traditional resonant dark matter models, this one avoids theoretical issues with stability by not relying on a conserved symmetry and instead uses a long-lived resonance to prevent decay into the hidden sector. A second resonance with a shorter lifetime is used in this model to achieve non-thermal resonant production, with one resonance decaying before the other one appears, allowing for a fine-tuned equilibrium between dark matter and the resonance before the resonance decays and transfers dark matter.

This research explores how the spectrum of triaxial nuclei is influenced by the effects of semi-classical quantization in the presence of minimal length. The study yields energy levels that demonstrate asymmetry as the minimal length parameter increases. Notably, all non-zero energy levels exhibit higher values than their collective Kπ = 0°, 0 state counterpart. The research findings indicate that ground state collective collectivity decreases with increasing minimal length parameter without undergoing a collectivity transition. The study further finds that eigenstates of two different Hamiltonians, one defined by a modified Wilcox operator and the other by a deformed body shape, demonstrate similarities.

There are four constant magnitudes defined for four-dimensional unitary spaces based on cliffts: $\mathcal{M}_0$, $\mathcal{M}_1$, $\mathcal{M}_2$, and $\mathcal{M}_3$. Arrays with these magnitudes are referred to as Golay complementary array (GCA) sets, and specifically, arrays with magnitudes $\mathcal{M}_0$ and $\mathcal{M}_1$ are referred to as quaternary GCA sets. A smaller size for quaternary GCA sets has been found and generalizations of GCAs up to four-dimensional spaces have been extensively studied, but researching higher dimensional spaces beyond four-dimensional is an ongoing process.

Recent advancements in change detection using deep models have shown promising results, particularly in satellite imagery. Unlike traditional methods which necessitate vast amounts of labeled data, unsupervised change detection can draw data-independent segmentation boundaries. However, previous works required partial supervision. This research delves into fully supervised change detection and unsupervised change detection from a new perspective, revealing that the former doesn't always guarantee superior results, depending on the scene complexity. Unsupervised change detection, on the other hand, frequently outperforms supervised methods, especially in simple cases. Our comprehensive review covers the fundamental principles, recent developments, and shortcomings of these techniques. Our comparative analysis based on publicly available datasets confirms the superiority of unsupervised change detection in various scenarios. This paper concludes by identifying crucial areas for future research and paving the way for the integration of unsupervised change detection into real-world applications.

A scaling factor is applied to the reduced electrostatic strength in our modified version of the coupled pair and polarizable water (CPPMW) model to improve its performance at high densities, and this modification also enables the use of the model in viscosimetric studies of non-associated molecular fluids with varying densities. The model's viscosity parameters, obtained through comparison of calculated and experimental viscosities, demonstrate robustness across a range of densities, and similar accuracy is achieved at 25°C and 320 K when comparing calculated and experimental viscosities for the [2Fe-4S] protein surrogate, tris(3-cyano-2H-pyran-2-yl)methane (TCPN), and 2-methyl-3-heptanamine (2M7A) at different temperatures.

A time-periodic cosmological model has been proposed, building on the Lambda-CDM model with inflation, and incorporates a variable effective Lambda term and a time-varying, scale-dependent effective mass term in the Klein-Gordon equation. The proposed model exhibits computer-simulated behaviors that mimic the expansion of the Universe. In this model, there are periods of steady expansion in a de-Sitter phase similar to a Lambda-CDM universe, but these are interrupted by sudden contractions. The model also predicts a range of phenomena including the possibility of life-cycles for stars and cosmic structures, and a potential source of gravitational waves. Despite its similarities to other cosmological models, such as the cyclic model, the periodic model differs from these alternatives, and offers a new explanation for the initial expansion of the Universe.

The concept of measuring an observable only depends on its post-measurement state, not how it came to be measured, is central to various discussions on quantum theory nonlocality. While measurement independence is essential to entanglement and thus commonly used to demonstrate nonlocality, we show that it cannot be achieved using only counter-factual measurements. We explain that true counter-factual measurements, such as those proposed by Walther and colleagues in 2005, necessarily violate measurement independence. Consequently, any application of the Walther proposal to demonstrate entanglement, as previously studied by Mondragon and Toledo in 2018, must also demonstrate nonlocality. Notably, this relationship between counter-factual measurements, measurement independence, and nonlocality is highly robust, holding under even the most basic conditions for entanglement.

The ever-growing size of neural networks demands more computation and memory, yet smarter devices such as smart speakers and wearables require more efficient neural implementations. To address this contradiction, conventional gradient descent methods, heavily reliant on central processing units, can be replaced with alternative approaches. We propose a novel neural network architecture, named MAPNet, which uses a multiplexing mechanism to duplicate weights across parallel neurons within the same layer. This architecture was found to replicate the outcomes of conventional methods while offering substantial improvements in computation and memory resource utilization. MAPNet's potential was demonstrated through significant gains in accuracy on popular datasets such as CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet, specifically by boosting the classification benchmark by up to 1.45% in comparison to other leading techniques. MAPNet's inference time was also substantially reduced, accounting for a 25-fold decrease compared to the best conventional architecture, thereby making it more suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices such as Android TVs, drones, and smart wireless earbuds.

The cluster expansion of the dimer model on isoradial graphs has a specific contraction pattern which yields a proof of a detailed expansion, known as the "Duffin and Onsager" expansion. Building upon previous research, a term-by-term comparison of the original cluster expansion and the Duffin and Onsager expansion is established, leading to a finding that the discrepancy between the two expansions solely arises from a specific infinite term. Furthermore, initiatives are presented to evaluate and improve the efficiency of the term-by-term comparison, as well as to evaluate the infinite term. It's hoped that successful completion of these initiatives could facilitate a detailed analysis of the dimer model using the integrable structure revealed in the recent "integrability comes from the gauge symmetry" approach.

For multivariate regression problems with numerous predictors, including both categorical and continuous types, the Group Lasso method offers a solution by employing a penalty that eliminates groups of redundant predictors in conjunction with the standard Lasso penalty. Originally, Group Lasso involved using the Fourier transform to facilitate its implementation, but the lack of a general algorithm led many researchers to adopt alternative approaches such as two-stage or proxy Lasso algorithms. In this paper, a new and general Group Lasso algorithm is presented, demonstrated to be equivalent to the original Fourier-based method, and is shown to be effective on a range of data sets. The paper also introduces a modified version of the algorithm that incorporates the elastic net modification to improve its performance in scenarios with correlated predictors.

This paper describes T-Visor, an open-source commercial virtual machine for embedded systems. Developed to address the diversity of real-time requirements and streamline development, T-Visor offers a versatile platform. Currently applied in the Chinese Space Program, T-Visor is being used to gather scientific data on the Wangshan-1 satellite. To efficiently manage the limited resources of embedded devices, T-Visor's scheduling framework prioritizes security, ensuring predictable coexistence of diverse embedded systems with various real-time needs. Additionally, the paper outlines a design methodology for scheduling policies in T-Visor, exemplified by the development of a real-time scheduling policy for the Linux operating system.

A panoramic image capture system utilizing a single camera is designed to ensure perfectly aligned full-circle views, one of the key performance factors being rapid image pairing speed. Traditional methods relying on maps or parameter adjustments can be impractical in real-world applications, necessitating alternative approaches. This project introduces a new solution by integrating an inertial measurement unit, which provides real-time 3D position and rotation data, along with the capabilities to calculate the pairing speed of images and avoiding mispairs. When compared to previous single-fish-eye camera stitching methods, our proposed approach significantly shortens the pairing process by approximately 2-3 times, with pairing speeds reaching up to 5-6 frames per second. When combined with a fish-eye lens, the image pairing process is further optimized to reach speeds of up to 20 times faster, at approximately 0.1 seconds per pair.

Research on periodic chimeras in oscillator networks has revealed interesting properties but its occurrence has been largely theoretically predicted, with few actual occurrences reported. This study examines the condition required for stable periodical chimeras in ring networks composed of two groups with different type oscillators. We found that increasing heterogeneity within groups enhances the stability of chimeras. Notably, in networks of coupled oscillators, this type of chimera can emerge spontaneously. Additionally, our study differentiated between stable and transient periodical chimeras using topological properties of the network. We further investigated how the phase of transition from asynchronous to periodical states changes with increasing heterogeneity. Our research provides a basis for further studies on chimeras in oscillator networks and explores their dynamic characteristics.

One of the primary objectives of learning-based control methods is to develop automatic systems capable of operating multiple tasks simultaneously using an end-to-end neural network-based approach. However, it has been recognized that such methods can be highly susceptible to model inaccuracies, with even minor discrepancies between the predicted and actual system models leading to unsafe controller outputs. In order to address this challenge, we propose enlisting the assistance of a generative adversarial network to refine the dynamics model by imposing a minimum likelihood noise level. By doing so, we aim to significantly enhance the robustness of the learning-based controller, allowing it to perform safely even when the actual system model includes significant uncertainty. Our theoretical analysis confirms that enforcing a lower bound on the likelihood noise in the dynamics model results in a more robust dynamics model. Furthermore, we demonstrate through two real-world experiments that incorporating a lower bound on the likelihood noise in the dynamics model using an adversarial network leads to a substantial 82.57% and 55.56% reduction in unsafe controller outputs in two diverse scenarios.

Building on previous work, a general definition of the slice algebra at a vertex of a quiver is redefined, incorporating modifications. Key properties of the original construction are retained under this revised definition. Specifically, it has been proven that at a given vertex of a quiver $A\rightarrow B$, the slice algebra exhibits properties as a $(A\rightarrow B)\otimes\mathcal{E}(V)$-module. Furthermore, it has been proven that for quivers of type $\mathfrak{gl}_2$ that are infinite in one direction, the slice algebra can be expressed as a specific matrix or tensor algebra. These results have far-reaching implications, allowing for the recreation of Weyl groups through representation theory of the slice algebras of type $\mathfrak{gl}_2$.

In certain instances of randomized tensor networks, reflections in the entanglement spectrum stand out as distinct from typical R\'enyi spectra, with their emergence linked to permutation symmetries within the underlying problem. Originally taking the form of deformed-NESS R\'enyi spectra, these reflections are found to be significantly more robust than typical R\'enyi spectra in random unitary transformations. Furthermore, in problems exhibiting permutation symmetries, cutting-edge GI-MPS methods enable direct extraction of the reflected spectrum from the entanglement spectrum. To demonstrate this, a novel computational approach has been developed for tensor networks of all bond dimensions. As evidence of the robustness of the reflected spectrum, it has also been shown to apply to disorder-average models of critical dynamics, both in and out of equilibrium, with its emergence linked to a specific type of permutation symmetry even in transition phases where permutation symmetries are broken. Additionally, a theoretical analysis of the reflected spectrum in random tensor networks has been made with generalizations to other types of tensor networks and models of quantum dynamics proposed.

We investigated large sets of dynamical systems, defined by discrete mappings, on a particular type of topological space. Our focus was on simple, category-based conditions that might influence the likelihood of long-term persistence within these systems. Several features were studied, including individual points, general compact sets, and specific set types such as infinite trees and 'C'-shaped configurations. Using various analytical tools, we evaluated the impact of different 'C'-set properties in relation to persistence, ultimately extending our findings to more complex dynamic systems featuring compact metrices.
Our work uncovers both general principles and nuanced observational results that apply to a broad range of dynamic systems, encompassing continuous and discrete scenarios. Notably, our findings hold for systems with the structure of locally compact, non-metric spaces, including those based on the duality of certain mathematical objects called preorders.
One of the paper's central achievements is the identification of specific set properties influencing long-term persistence. These properties can be understood as providing lower bounds for the probability of long-term persistence given certain conditions. Interestingly, these properties exhibit a natural duality, reflected in the paper's title, suggesting a contrast between 'upward' directions toward persistence and 'downward' movements away from it.
The paper's methods draw from a diverse range of mathematical disciplines, including ergodic theory, topological dynamics, and advanced combinatorial theory. Specifically, the authors have combined recent findings on the 'one-perperiod' recurrence phenomenon with the concept of '

We've developed a method for dissecting the space of parameters in quadratic diffeomorphisms, which helps us better understand how changes in parameters affect dynamic behavior. This novel approach enables us to identify distinct regions where different types of dynamic patterns exist within the parameter space. By focusing on a specific family of diffeomorphisms, we've shown how these regions emerge from the analysis of periodic orbits near a critical point. As the parameter space is further refined, additional regions appear, which correspond to more complex dynamic patterns. This region-by-region analysis captures the intricate structure of the parameter space within a given family of quadratic diffeomorphisms. It is expected that this method will be useful in expanding the analysis to more complex dynamical systems, such as non-quadratic maps, and that this framework has the potential to contribute to our knowledge of bifurcations in dynamic systems.

The concept of holonomy in gauge theory has long been established as a crucial geometric characteristic that describes the behavior of a particle under a gauge field. A similar concept exists in gravity, specifically within the framework of the Einstein Cartan theory, where it holds similar significance. A new study reveals that the holonomy in gravity differs significantly from that in gauge theory and, more surprisingly, does not adhere to a gauge-invariant definition. Furthermore, when applied to scalar and spinor fields, the holonomy's geometric implications are found to be non-relevant. Nonetheless, the framework developed to study holonomy in gravity can be extended and used to explore the orbital angular momentum imposed by a gravitational field on spinless and spinor particles.

For positive integers $n$, let $X_n$ be random variables that tend towards zero as $n$ increases without bound.  Utilizing well-established limit theorems for functions of multiple random variables, we establish distinct forms of cumulative distribution functions for various groups of $X_n$, depending on the relative rates at which $n$ and $\sqrt{n}$ grow.  Ultimately, these results resolve a question posed by Roncalli, addressing a concern regarding a particular method for reducing rank in the context of central moment problems, specifically in situations where rank reduction is performed as $n$ increases without bound.  Additional applications of our findings include simplified proofs of well-known Lévy-Khintchine and Laplace transformations, as well as a novel method for computing the cumulative distribution function of a sum of randomly selected variables, drawn from an infinitely divisible distribution.

The theoretical underpinning of actual tunneling time in quantum systems has been contested. A novel model-based approach to tunneling time is proposed, where the time is related to spin fluctuations and can be measured by introducing an extra anisotropy into the Heisenberg Hamiltonian. It is found that within the context of the Kondo model, the new time can be averaged without regard to temperature, whereas the conventional time remains heavily temperature-dependent. Building on this idea, we suggest a practical method for detecting non-equilibrium tunneling times in local spin systems at room temperature. Additionally, we outline the potential for exploring actual tunneling times in quantum computers.

We've calculated relativistic corrections to the production and decay processes involving P-wave charmonia mesons, using relativistic wave functions derived from the Bethe-Salpeter equation. Our approach involves incorporating the internal kinematic effects into the interaction potentials used by the Born terms. The results reveal significant relativistic corrections for the amplitudes in question, implying that relativistic corrections cannot be neglected in the study of P-wave charmonia production and decay processes.

Our research focuses on applying Ramsey interferometry, utilizing both theoretical and numerical approaches, to examine how certain errors in quantum operations affect entangled states produced by various methods. Initially, we investigate scenarios in which gates are imperfectly implemented in order to analyze the advantages offered by certain types of errors in quantum computing systems. We discovered that certain types of noise introduce no additional error beyond what is expected due to limited precision in measuring distances, when dealt with in a particular way. Moreover, we learned that certain types of gate modifications significantly enhance the accuracy of interferometry when dealing with Bose-Einstein condensates. Although imperfect gates typically compromise entangled states, under specific conditions they can also greatly improve performance. Moreover, we found an effective range of gate modifications within which errors are minimal and primarily determined by limited precision in measuring distances. Furthermore, we discovered that certain types of gate modifications decrease the influence of certain types of noise and allow errors to be minimal and primarily determined by limited precision in measuring distances. Additionally, we found an effective range of gate modifications within which errors are minimal and primarily determined by limited precision in measuring distances.

Building upon a previous investigation, this work further explores how degeneracies within the ground states correlate with the concepts of soft news and a type of mode that was previously studied. It is demonstrated that a specific relationship exists among these entities and that the concepts of soft news and the aforementioned mode have a combined multiplicative factor of 6. This result enables the computation of a particular charge, referred to as eBMS charge, which is done through a transformation that involves the Genus 0 partition function, characterized by the presence of a logarithmic term and a 6-degenerate mode. Ultimately, the eBMS charge is calculated to be equal to 1.

A novel approach to weight ensemble learning within neural networks is introduced, enabling an ordered group of neural networks to be trained simultaneously, all utilizing the same set of labeled training data. The weight distribution among the ensemble members is determined after training, based on an analysis of their regularizer's logarithm. The proposed method has been experimentally validated on several widely-used datasets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository for two-class classification problems. The results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, with classification accuracy comparable to or surpassing that of state-of-the-art methods, coupled with computational efficiency. Specifically, it is approximately two orders of magnitude faster than typical methods, encompassing techniques such as the bagging, bootstrap, and regularized ensemble learning methods.

The theory of generalized connections is a powerful tool in establishing relationships between differential geometry and physics, particularly in relation to spinors and holography. Researchers have demonstrated that specific types of generalized connections can lead to Ricci flat metrics, implying the existence of non-perturbative strings. This idea is comparable to a well-known theory in which twisted gerbe connections lead to string backgrounds. While there are differences, the relationship between generalized connections and gerbe connections is evident. Our work seeks to clarify this connection further. First, we explore the relationship between generalized T-geometry and twisted gerbe geometry. We find that natural generalizations of gerbe connections yield specific generalizations known as strong twisted gerbe connections. We then establish that these connections share key characteristics, particularly the existence of vanishing holonomy groups. We proceed to introduce a regionalization concept, leading to a division of the space into regions akin to those found in twisted gerbe geometry. Ultimately, we establish a clear equivalence between strong twisted gerbe connections and certain generalized connections arising from Looijen's framework. Our study addresses specific T-geometry examples that demonstrate how certain generalized connections can lead to Ricci flat metrics, implying the existence of non-perturbative strings. We leverage these results to discuss their implications for a non-perturbative string theory model.

A key concept in studying polynomial functions over finite fields is the complete mapping, which is central to determining the value of a specific counting parameter. Researchers developed an algorithm, based on an approach incorporating nullstellence arguments and character sums, to calculate this parameter efficiently. Using this algorithm, they determined the value of the parameter for fields with up to 2^13 elements within a reasonable time frame, paving the way for future calculations on larger fields.

Human visual inspection is currently the standard method for diagnosing intestinal parasites, with a high error rate often leading to inappropriate treatment. As a result, researchers are exploring the potential for developing an effective visual parasite detection system, with the ultimate goal of supporting healthcare professionals, especially in underserved areas. A key requirement for such a system is to minimize the burden on users, with an low error rate when compared to expert human diagnoses. Our study builds on existing research by presenting a comprehensive evaluation of technical approaches for visual parasite detection. We test six different techniques using a recently proposed dataset, 'IPP-Dataverse', and assess their performance across various scenarios through extensive simulations. Our research investigates the comparative performance of different models and identifies key factors that affect their reliability, including the type of training data, placement, number, and specificity of the pathogens. Based on our findings, we suggest a dual-system framework, combining a broad but relatively simple model with a more complex, refined approach for cases that are misclassified by the initial system. Our proposed framework shows promising results, with the potential to significantly reduce false positives and support accurate and reliable visual parasite detection in complex scenarios.

This research applies the viscosity solution approach, alongside the representation theorem for nonlinear Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations with state-dependent obstacles, to find a solution for the corresponding backward stochastic differential equation. By establishing a one-to-one correspondence, we transform the nonlinear equation into a linear one, which maintains uniqueness. This allows us to deduce the existence of a solution for the original nonlinear equation through the combination of these two linear relationships. Ultimately, we obtain a nonlinear integro-differential equation's solution via forward backward stochastic differential equation manipulation.

A robust control system for quadcopters is developed using a Lyapunov-based control approach combined with both Back Stepping and Genetic Filter techniques, enabling efficient handling of external disruptions and adaptive flight capabilities in varying environments. Unlike conventional Lyapunov-based controllers, this system incorporates a Genetic Filter to enhance its resistance to external disturbances, utilizing a distinct encoding scheme for population genes and a customized mutation and crossover operation. By integrating the Genetic Filter's control signal into the Lyapov-based controller, the system's robustness is significantly improved. Furthermore, Back Stepping's derivative-based approach is combined with the dynamic model's nonlinear terms to facilitate stable control, even in complex quadcopter scenarios. Evaluations using a simulation model of the Parrot Bebop1 quadcopter verify the proposed control system's ability to achieve stable and robust tracking performance in various flight modes and conditions.

We employed the systematic hydrogen-deuteride scattering measurements to derive a precise value for the sigma term in pion-nucleon interactions, crucial for understanding nuclear forces. We report a sigma term of $-228 \pm 6$ MeV, differing by about one standard deviation from previous estimates derived from pi-N scattering data. We also used a novel method to assess nucleon-nucleon interactions at the pion mass, providing a connection between the theoretical concepts of chiral effective field theory and the statistical analysis of experimental data. Furthermore, we determined the low-energy coefficients of the pion-nucleon interaction operator, yielding values for $g_A^{(lo)}$ and $<N|A_z|$N> that align with theoretical predictions based on chiral effective field theory at the pion mass. These results have significant implications for the study of nuclear dynamics, as they bridge the gap between the theoretical concepts of many-body nuclear physics and the statistical analysis of experimental data.

The CMS tracker upgrade in 2016 introduced a Conrad-generation front-end chip to its silicon pixel detector, boasting improved signal processing capabilities, increased functionality, and enhanced digital signal handling. Leveraging the presence of the new chip group in the barrel detector, the CMS participated in its initial proton-proton collision in spring that year. By demonstrating a front-end performance in high-energy operations, the CMS effectively met its goal of meeting quality requirements for trigger decisions and data storage. Consequently, the tracker operated at optimal efficiency throughout 2016 and paved the way for the complete replacement of the detector's legacy front-end chip system by the conclusion of the LHC Run 2 in 2018.

The main goal of this work is to investigate the link between actively galactic nuclei (AGN) and the galaxies that host them (HAGN) using the most up-to-date data from two studies, covering over 20,000 HAGN at redshifts z > 0.2 up to z ~ 7.7. These HAGN were detected via deep ultraviolet radiation, ranging from 100 nm to 200 nm, as part of the Swift-BAT 72-month survey, with an energy threshold of 10^37 erg/s/thom. This research involves re-examining the SwBAT sample to develop classification accuracy statistics (precision and recall) for HAGN systems at different redshift intervals. Notably, HAGN accuracy classification precision ranges from 90% to 99% depending on the prior probability of an AGN influencing the galaxy's appearance. The research further finds a relationship between HAGN prior probability and redshift, displaying higher classification precision at higher prior probabilities. These findings highlight the potential for deep extragalactic gamma-ray surveys, along with HAGN's distinct features at varying redshift intervals, as valuable tools for cosmological research and the study of quasars and their host galaxies.

A comprehensive examination of proton and neutron radii is conducted across various isotopes in a range of isotopic sequences. Correlations between radii and neutron skin thicknesses are meticulously measured. Employing the phenomenological interaction SP-D1S, modified in accordance with the relativity theory, a detailed study is carried out on static properties of a set of isolated even-even nuclei. Extensive comparisons are drawn with empirical data, notably radii and neutron skin thickness. A thorough investigation is then conducted into the dependence of correlation coefficients on the momentum transfer Q, focusing on a selection of 48Ca, 208Pb, and 208Tl isotopes. This analysis demonstrates the significant impact of short-range nuclear correlations on the equilibrium nuclear radius and neutron skin thickness. Nevertheless, these correlations fail to account for the primary Nucleus-size variations. A theoretical study is then performed to determine the dependence of the spin-orbit splitting on the momentum transfer Q for a set of isolated energy levels in 40Ca and 48Ca nuclei. This investigation was carried out using self-consistent Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov theory. A detailed examination is also carried out to determine the dependence of the spin-orbit splitting on the momentum transfer Q for a set of protons in the 1p3/2 and 1p1/2 shell, in order to better understand the behavior of the derivative of the spin-orbit splitting with respect to the momentum transfer Q.

This paper presents an innovative representation of RGB images using complex-valued pixel values by combining red, green, and blue components in a structured manner within the frequency domain. This approach utilizes a diagonal complex-phase Fourier transform to preserve the original pixel values and maintain the diagonal structure, resulting in more efficient image processing. By employing an innovative mapping scheme, the representation exploits the inherent properties of complex numbers to facilitate image analysis and feature extraction. This novel formulation incorporates inherent complex number characteristics useful for image processing, thereby providing a more flexible and efficient framework for image representations. Evaluations of our images demonstrate improved resistance to certain types of transformations, such as hue shifting, while maintaining distinct characteristics and the uniqueness of features across different images. Furthermore, the results show reduced correlations within the context of specific effects like light scattering and image capture techniques, which this representation is more adept at capturing.

The geometrical scaling concept is tested across a range of hadronic and nuclear reactions involving a single particle or multiple particles, all based on the same J/Psi final state. We specifically examine spectra from proton-proton and proton-lead collisions, as well as the gelato framework's single-transverse-momentum cross-section predictions for lead-lead collisions, finding that geometrical scaling works well for low energy collisions but may not apply in the high energy LHC setting. Additionally, our findings suggest that gluon distribution saturation, as modeled by the gelato framework, is the driving force behind geometrical scaling in low energy collisions, however this does not occur at higher energies or when considering charged particles.

This study introduces a straightforward method to simulate the final stages of massive stars that explode into black holes within a pre-existing nebula. A major factor influencing the enrichment of the interstellar medium comes from the unpredictable sampling of the initial mass range for these stars. Our goal is to examine the impact of this variability, which has significant implications for understanding the early composition and formation of the universe. To this effect, we have developed a simple yet effective model describing how core-collapse supernovae with explosive nebulae impact and alter surrounding environments. This analysis focuses on two principal elements: the steady-state formation rate of core-collapse supernovae within stellar disks, and the reliable detection of environmental changes resulting from the release of heavy elements. Through a thorough investigation, we discovered that the final effect of core-collapse supernovae on surrounding environments depends on three critical elements: the rate at which core-collapse supernovae occur within stellar disks, the overall mass of the core-collapse supernova ejected per event, the initial concentration of existing elements within surrounding environments, and the timeframe required for detection changes resulting from the elements released by core-collapse supernovae.

Using an simplified representation, we modeled the final effect of core-collapse supernovae on surrounding environments for a variety of initial conditions. It was generally observed that the release of elements by core-collapse supernovae within early elliptical galaxies: (1) results in detectable changes to metal content only for very massive objects and intense areas of star formation, (2)

In recent times, machine learning techniques have become increasingly vital for making decisions in numerous practical applications, yet there's still a lack of research into how well the scale of machine learning models impacts their scale of performance. We address this gap by investigating the effect of scaling up a supervised learning model on its predictive accuracy and reliability when confronted with additional synthetic data features. We also propose a novel, easy-to-implement methodology to gauge the stability of a model's predictions across varying data conditions with an eye towards incorporating probabilistic models. Our study involves three UCI datasets, four generating methods, and three machine learning models, and our findings reveal that there's no universal correlation between a model's scale of training data and its predictive performance or stability. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that incorporating synthetic data features doesn't necessarily lead to improved predictive accuracy, and surprisingly, certain model scaling up strategies can actually diminish overall performance. We ultimately discuss potential avenues for future research and present our open-source implementation for examining the stability of predictive models.

Variational quantum models have gained attention as potential competitors to more conventional quantum models, thanks to their ability to be directly evaluated on quantum computers. There has been a recent surge in proposals for implementing a variational quantum classifier, a key aspect of which is optimizing a set of parameters in a way that maximizes the target output while being compliant with quantum constraints. Work on these classifiers largely relies on and adapts methods developed for quantum machine learning tasks like quantum state classification, where outputs are defined within a specific Hilbert space. Our research marks a divergence from the existing trend by investigating a type of quantum classifier that produces discrete classification labels based on probability distributions in a categorical Hilbert space. Our study exposes a significant drawback of such quantum classifiers: the output that is most favorable from an optimization standpoint often aligns with mere noise or side effects, rather than the inherent physics of the system. Consequently, as dimensions expand, so does the likelihood of the model's success in classification corresponding to little more than the optimal fit to random noise. Our findings, which are supported by numerical simulations, suggest that such quantum classifiers, when optimized with gradients, can't scale without additional remedies, whether that entails a hybrid approach that incorporates classical techniques or a different paradigm for classifying with probabilistic outputs. Ultimately, this research identifies the tradeoffs inherent in periodic relaxations of quantum constraints and offers guidance on their utilization in variational quantum models.

This paper focuses on exploring warping product submanifolds within Sasakian manifolds. We start broad by examining warping product submanifolds in Sasakian manifolds and proceed to specifically investigate warping product semi-slant and cosslant submanifolds. Notably, we demonstrate that no non-trivial warping product semi-slant or cosslant submanifold exists in $\mathbb{S}^7(m)$. We also introduce new examples of warping product semi-slant and cosslant submanifolds in $\mathbb{S}^7(m)$ and establish the connections between warping product semi-slant/cosslant and directionally semi-slant/cosslant submanifolds. Additionally, we demonstrate the non-existence of warping product semi-slant and cosslant submanifolds in $\mathbb{S}^8(m)$.

A low-background, portable cesium iodide detector is examined for its CEvNS detection capabilities within the context of dark matter research, specifically when comparing background conditions under and above 100 meters in depth. It's anticipated that a mobile laboratory hosting the detector will be able to generate significant data due to its high event count and corresponding statistical error. A study showed that a detector with an mass of 10 kg, or roughly 100 kg, will be capable of detecting neutrino oscillations after being exposed to a specific flux of neutrinos over the course of 30 days, or 100 days, at two different depths. After accounting for statistical errors, the CEvNS detection capabilities exceed background-level measurements above ground, or at 100 meters below ground, with the iodine fraction being a deciding factor. Several detector configurations are examined in order to optimize CEvNS research under various circumstances.

Recent breakthroughs in designing active particle materials, spurred significant interest in 2D materials with charge mobility, prompting a thorough examination of their potential in creating active particles. This study delves into the theoretical motion mode of two-dimensionally structured organic dimer molecules, which could serve as the smallest active particles, operating similarly to a steering wheel in larger devices. We develop a mathematical model simulating their behavior while exploring the impact of environmental forces and present a comprehensive analysis of the resulting equilibria. Compared to their one-dimensional counterparts, two-dimensional charge oscillations display a notably diverse behavior, influenced significantly by the approach angle of environmental forces. Additionally, we identify key conditions that ensure the stability of their motion and outline the necessary requirements for achieving any desired speed and direction of travel.

Non-linear excitations, or solitons, in a field of a Bose-Einstein condensate with anisotropic interactions are studied. The specific form of the interaction potential leads to a well-known formula for phonons, but when applying this potential to a non-linear context, an unexpected outcome is obtained: the emergence of magnetorotons, which behave like minima in the energy per particle as a function of momentum, instead of the expected plateaus. The theory is examined under different conditions, including varying symmetries and number of particles. In systems with the lowest possible symmetry and a specific interaction strength, magnetorotons are found to be non-reversible, featuring distinct forms that are identical in their structure but opposite in their direction, while breaking symmetry in another way leads to the emergence of magnetorotons with a specific rotation. The research also reveals that magnetorotons in a certain, less symmetric state exhibit spin and translate and rotate reversibly, while remaining stable under small disturbances.

Our investigation focuses on a general type of epidemic model, where individuals can transition between susceptible and recovered states, regardless of their network connections. By building upon previous research, including Burstein et al.'s work on shareable graphs, we've developed a mathematical framework that can be applied to any network topology and accurately predicts the progression of epidemics. Our findings encompass various transmission scenarios, including complete and partial immune systems, as well as outbreaks influenced by random encounters. The development of this new theory relaxes certain conditions, broadening its applicability to a diverse range of contact networks, including random networks, and enabling the analysis of complex epidemics in networks shaped by technological and social factors.

Using simplified GBG K-cube maps with known noise levels, we examined the precision of two CMB estimation techniques, the optimal weighted estimator and a biased estimator based on CMB templates, in the presence of foreground contaminants. Forestell et al's (2017) formula predicts uneven distribution of errors in CMB maps generated with the optimal estimator, whereas a similar formula by Hamann et al (2015) suggests that the biased estimator can minimize errors by compensating for the uneven distribution. However, our analysis shows that the biased estimator fails to address the issue, instead amplifying errors in areas with the smallest errors in the original GBG K-cube maps, while ignoring signals from major point sources, such as Planck's SZ clusters.

This study approaches the task of providing instructional tasks by considering two key perspectives - the practical effects of the instruction and the teaching method. Rather than focusing on an optimal instructional design, we instead strive for an instruction-generating framework that is adaptable and versatile. Our two guest editors, experts in the fields of robotics and human cognition, share their perspectives on these issues and introduce a special section featuring research papers on task instruction. Ultimately, we argue that an effective instruction-generating framework should prioritize both theoretical soundness in task representation and a practical, situation-aware approach to teaching, taking into account the inherent uncertainties and imperfections in both learning and instruction.

We introduce a method for accurately reconstructing a quantum state from a known object when its interaction with a part of the state is restricted, using an affordable number of measurements. Unlike conventional state tomography, which demands access to the entire system, we can obtain an approximate error budget even with measurements limited to a single share. Although a small number of entangling measurements are necessary, we show how to achieve sufficient state reconstruction with only local measurements. Numerical analysis confirms the practical feasibility of this new approach.

For any convex shape with a given number of sides, n, and area, A, there are precise formulas governing the relationship between the inradius, r, and circumradius, R, which can be expressed as mean values. Specifically, it can be proven that $(R-r)^2=(R+r)^2(n-3)/(A+4Rr)$ and that the inradius and circumradius are each equal to the average of the lengths of the shape's sides, s, and the maximum distance, d, formed by its vertices. Building upon prior research, the relationships between the inradius and circumradius have been thoroughly explored for shapes with distinct properties, including the special cases of triangles and parallelograms. However, for shapes with these distinct properties, the relationships between the inradius and circumradius are more constrained. This research aims to confirm that for shapes with these distinct properties, the relationships between the inradius and circumradius are simpler and more constrained than for shapes in general.

This paper explores the potential for utilizing Unmanned Aerial Vehicles as rapid and cost-effective solutions for delivering internet services and data services to mobile users. To evaluate the feasibility of employing UAVs for internet services, the authors analyze the delivery of a single user's services via fixed routes, drawing comparisons to the complexity of the Traveling Salesman Problem. Building on this foundation, the authors examine multi-user scenarios and establish a many-vs-one facilitation problem within the context of UAV-assisted networking. By leveraging the facilitation problem and incorporating a social facilitation factor, the authors propose a multi-objective optimization model to manage a UAV delivering services to multiple users. A network algorithm, the facilitation-based facilitator, is presented as a practical solution to facilitate a trade-off between network facilitation and service delivery time. A second solution, the facilitation-based scheduler, is offered as an alternative approach. A simulation framework validates the performance of the two solutions and demonstrates the effectiveness of the facilitation-based facilitator in achieving improved network performance and the facilitation-based scheduler in achieving a balance between facilitation and delivery time.

Bilayer graphene is renowned for its ability to experience various phases resulting from deliberate and accidental realignment of the layers. The paper presents an analysis of the rotational symmetry in NEMO, a state where two layers of graphene are loosely connected. The investigation reveals that in the NEMO state, the symmetry of rotation around the layers' axis is reduced to the second type. The research found the NEMO state's energy to be influenced by rotations with a specific interval, which is linked to the type of bond formed between the layers. Additionally, the study discovered that introducing a small discrepancy in the square pattern of the lattices gives rise to a condition where the total number of the mentioned rotations becomes zero, resulting in the occurrence of superconductivity in NEMO. The research found that the most favorable environment for superconducting properties in NEMO is achieved when the layers have equal sizes and the lattices have identical patterns.

Endofullerenes, molecules enclosed within a deformed fullerene cage, possess unusual geometric conformity and electromagnetic properties. This work delves into the film deposition process of two endofullerenes, V$_2$@C$_6$ and Cr$_3$@C$_6$, using molecular dynamics simulations. Calculations of their electromagnetic properties are conducted both in vacuum and on a substrate, revealing significant interactions between the endofullerenes and the substrate. This leads to alterations in the endofullerenes' conformational structure upon substrate adsorption, with potential implications for their magnetic and electric properties. This interaction can be utilized to control the endofullerenes' relative orientation by employing a compatible substrate, characterized by a specific geometric pattern that can encapsulate the molecules' geometric conformity.

The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has led to a surge in data available through diverse sources, yet it has also generated heightened security and privacy concerns due to their scattered nature and difficult accessibility. Preserving trust among IoT users necessitates comprehensive protection for their personal data. To address this challenge, this research outlines a novel protective framework for IoT systems. The proposed approach begins by identifying valuable data using unsupervised clustering, then employs a deep neural network to create customizable models for classifying sensitive vs. non-sensitive information. A dynamic policy creation mechanism incorporates the learned classifier, allowing for updated sensitive data detection based on thorough system explorations. Additionally, this framework incorporates augmented attacks to secure sensitive information at the application and network layers, while a rewritten version of the Android app enables user interaction with the system through an augmented API. Experimental results involving synthetic data and popular image datasets have demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed framework in keeping user-specified sensitive data hidden from view.

To efficiently use low-fidelity Ramsey measurements, we employ Bayesian experiment design and develop two illustrative examples - a two-level and three-level scenario - which demonstrate the benefits of this approach over adaptive heuristic and random protocols. Additionally, we show how to optimize the experiment design to quickly estimate a specific target value at the minimum cost.

Various node centrality metrics have been proposed to identify significant nodes in network analysis.  Gromov centrality has been developed to distinguish between highly connected nodes and those with intricate relationships in network topologies.  Gromov centrality combines a graph's geometric properties with its structural characteristics to distinguish between highly connected nodes and those with intricate relationships in different network types, including random and small-world networks.  Geometric analysis reveals that a bell-curve distribution of Gromov values occurs in these networks, allowing three types of significant nodes to be differentiated based on their Gromov values.  Gromov centrality offers a effective tool for evaluating network node importance across various network types and geometries.

Our simple time-scale model, based on the principles of inertia and circular motion, explains the observed acceleration in the Earth's orbit through kinetic energy transfer between the Earth and the Sun. We derive an equation describing the Earth's orbital radius over time, and compare our model's predictions with established values from scientific measurements. Additionally, our model yields a predictable constant of proportionality that aligns with the mass ratio of the Earth to the Sun, according to our theoretical model. We provide the numeric value of this constant for future reference. This theoretical model is intended to be intuitive and accessible, and supports learning through understanding and appreciation. We encourage educators to integrate this model into their curricula, and to share our work with students, colleagues, and anyone interested in understanding the simple physics behind the acceleration in the Earth's orbit.

We develop a family of matrix bundles, generalizing Hermite bundles, with components consisting of matrix polynomials of any degree, defined over affine spaces of any dimension in any number of variables. It's demonstrated that each such bundle is inherently spectral, with its closure encompassing a wide range of spectral data for its constituent matrix polynomials. Furthermore, as an application, we establish the openness of certain subsets within projective and affine spaces, characterized by fixed multidegrees. Specifically, these subsets comprise polynomials sharing a given multidegree and, more broadly, matrix polynomials of bounded spectral norm and bounded spectral radius, all multiplied by a common scalar factor.

We establish a fundamental connection between continuous-trace algebras and the concept of classical T-duality in a string theory framework, specifically one that encompasses non-geometric properties. Continuous-trace algebra solutions correspond to the classical T-duals of the string sigma-models under the string partition function's minimization, bypassing geometric targets. Moreover, our work shows the comprehensive category of continuous-trace algebras generates all classical T-duals within the string theory context, encompassing non-geometric theories. These findings shed light on the fundamental nature of continuous-trace algebras in string theory and address a long-standing question on non-geometric string theory by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between 5D continuous-trace algebras and the classical T-duals of the string sigma-models.

Researchers develop an algorithm with improved efficiency for solving Baker's metrics on minor-free graphs with fixed genus. The new approach reduces the computational time, specifically for finding an $st$-cut, to $O(\log k)\) compared to the previous $O(\log k\cdot n)$ time. Additionally, the time required for computing flow, distance, max-flow, min-cut, and longest path in a fixed-genus minor-free graph is reduced to $O(f \cdot n^{3-\alpha(g)} \log^2 k)$, outperforming the previous $O(f \cdot n^2)$ time by removing the $\log^2 k$ factor. The key innovation lies in a novel graph embedding, where the time to create and destroy single vertex crossings is $O(\log k)$, allowing for efficient handling of $O(\log k)$ depth path augmentations in algorithms. The researchers also employ Monte-Carlo randomness to speed up algorithm processing time.

This paper demonstrates the long-term behavior of a time-periodic parabolic equation with discrete data, focusing on the occurrence of singular homological patterns. Under certain assumptions, the prevalence of initial conditions leading to periodic solutions determines whether the system converges towards a periodic solution. Additionally, we establish a framework that allows the classification of periodic solutions based on their relative prevalence within the space of initial conditions. This framework is applicable in certain nonlinear diffusion equations, including the periodic Porter-Thomas distribution and discrete Dirac-delta initial conditions. We also discuss the relevance and scope of our study, including known results and areas for further investigation.

A major challenge in using quantum computers for molecular problems arises from the physical errors of near-term hardware. This issue significantly impacts the performance of algorithms on these devices, particularly those involving variational methods like VQE, which we investigate in the context of chemistry applications. Our study focuses on two protocols for implementing VQE, specifically the ADAPT protocol, which we have adapted for both fermionic (qubit-encoded) and bosonic (qubit-encoded) systems. These modified ADAPT protocols, known as QEB-ADAPT-VQE, result in more efficient algorithms that achieve better error-convergence rates compared to their fermionic and bosonic counterparts. By analyzing molecular hydrogen on various NQVBAs with up to 4 qubits per physical spin, our results reveal that QEB-ADAPT-VQE outperforms qubit-ADAPT-VQE in terms of convergence, utilizing a significantly reduced number of circuits to produce identical results on noisy hardware. This development highlights the potential of utilizing bosonic encoding for near-term quantum computers in chemistry simulations.

A key function of deep generative models is representation learning, which is widely applied in various tasks like recognition, prediction, and other downstream tasks. Some traditional methods like Gaussian Mixture Models can produce a diverse representation space that naturally separates classes, resulting in effective model-performance improvements. This work aims to reintroduce a similar capability to advanced generative models like Deep Gaussian Radial Distribution Models through a straightforward training approach, which involves adding a straightforward regularization term to the log-likelihood function. This approach, which effectively compromises for missing information, enables the development of a generative model that effectively separates classes in a specific space, which can be utilized in representations derived from labeled data. This idea is further demonstrated by comparing it to labels-ignoring, unsupervised approaches based on Information Theory, which often produce distinct representations. Which one do you think is more effective? Let's find out!

We welcome the cosmological model with a stiff component proposed by Capozzi et al., included in the TD-LHC18 simulation, as it effectively addresses the Hubble tension. We generate a stiff component in the model by utilizing a perturbed phase space curve that originates from an isolated plain rotation system. The perturbation is based on a perfect fluid representation and introduces an additional contribution to the Friedmann equation, enabling the replication of past cosmological evolution scenarios. We adapt the stiff model to be compatible with the Planck data by introducing adiabatic and acoustic oscillation temperatures produced through linear perturbation theory. By utilizing Monte Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC) analysis with re-defined tight tightintroparameters, we demonstrate that the stiff model is capable of matching both the Planck and SH0ES data simultaneously, thus resolving the Hubble tension. Notably, the stiff model, when utilizing tight tightintropparameters, resolvesthe Hubble tension by reducing $H_0$ by 5 km/s/Mpc and increasing $H_0$ by 11 km/s/Mpc, respectively. When allowing the stiff model to be evaluated against re-defined SH0ES data with lower constraint strength, we observe a notable discrepancy of 3 sigma from expected measurements, indicating that the model is not in line with re-defined re-defined re-defined re-defined re-defined re-defined re-defined re-defined re-defined re-defined re-defined re-defined re-defined re-defined re-defined re

Our investigation of comet C/2015 ER61 began with analyzing pictures captured by the ALMA observatory, which revealed gas releases in a comet. We aimed to understand the characteristics of gas emissions from the comet, especially from various molecules, and compared them with previous research on other comets. We used the MIGRO flow model to simulate and analyze images of the comet's gas trails, which were taken on April 11-12, 2016, two days before the comet's nearest approach to Earth. We also utilized data from the ALMA pictures to calculate gas release rates, volumetric gas densities, and other parameters, and compared them with other comets' findings. Our results showed that gas emissions from the comet followed the expectations of a standard outgassing model, except for HCN, which had an extra acceleration factor. We also discovered that gas emissions from the CS, formic acid, NCN, and cyanodihydrine molecules followed the standard model, but with varying acceleration levels, whereas HNC and methanol emissions showed no detectable acceleration. We found that comet C/2015 ER61 released gas at a slower rate and with lower volumes than other recent comets, and estimated that CS, H2O, and H2S emissions released at specific rates, but couldn't confirm the emission rates of NCN, cyanodihydrine, and formaldehyde. Moreover, we observed that HCN outgassing behavior was unique and

In our study, we assessed the effectiveness of an unsupervised speech synthesis system, which we found to be remarkably similar to its supervised counterpart in terms of speech quality and clarity, despite the fact that it had not been trained on any labelled data during the synthesis process. We further investigated the key factors contributing to the system's superior performance by examining its ability to learn pronunciation patterns and other essential aspects of speech production. We discovered that the system's capacity to learn and leverage unit-based structures, which play a vital role in speech synthesis, was directly correlated with its superior performance. We also developed a straightforward, data-driven approach to identify corresponding units between two spoken languages, which we found to be remarkably accurate. Finally, we discussed the potential avenues for further research and investment in the area of unsupervised speech synthesis, highlighting their vast and largely untapped possibilities.

We've developed a modified version of holographic dark energy models by introducing interaction between matter and DE, and we've also adapted this interaction into a new Tsallis holographic dark energy framework. The uncoupled and coupled versions of THDE are equivalent to the standard and interactive models of SHDE, respectively. We've found that the interactive SHDE model's vacuum energy's coupling parameter is directly tied to the constant b of THDE. We've also found that the interactive model is stable in certain regions of parameter space, and we've explored the implications of this stability on the model's stability and stability parameters.

Insight: The research introduces the Investment Ratio (IR) metric to compare computational solutions for an optimization problem, specifically in the $k$-means cluster nose problem where an optimal solution is defined by a first-order black-box optimizer called KMEANS-ES. It is observed that IR can serve as an effective evaluation tool for constructive heuristics like KMEANS-ES in the $k$-means cluster nose problem. It is also noted that IR offers a more nuanced assessment than traditional metrics like KMEANS-ES's objective function value or runtime. Furthermore, IR could potentially be utilized as a hybrid metric that combines both quality and runtime performance metrics for an optimization problem.

In this paper, we explore the principles of synthetic differential geometry as a formal framework for infinitesmal points in space-time and its implications in gauge theory. Building on background material in chapter 5 of lawson and Michelson's 'physics of infinitesimally flat spacetime', we delve into the geometric structure, focusing on the concept of source path and its associated groupoid. We define a source simply connected groupoid using a sheaf of infinitesimally flat principal bundles. A special case involves Yang-Mills theory on a manifold with vanishing curvature. We extend Lawson and Michelson's findings that geometric structure reduces to a sharp source vector field, and further demonstrate that gauge groupoids reduce to a sharp source vector field gauge groupoid. Additionally, we generalize the results to Riemannian structures, demonstrating that a sharp source vector field also arises in Riemannian structures.

Dynaswap is an open-source, community-driven trading platform that showcases cutting-edge technologies like Metaverse trading and advanced security features like Multi-Layered Security, Blockchain, OwenSG, and Zero Trust. This whitepaper outlines the architecture and the integration of its novel Multi-Layered Multi-Signature Trading (MULTI) mechanism. By presenting Dynaswap's trading process, the authors highlight its unique features which cater to professional traders, Metaverse inhabitants, and future Internet users. Additionally, the paper discusses the available APIs for development and current development work on a MULTI mechanism for Swaps, as part of the Dynaswap platform.

Recent advancements in Natural Language Processing have been hindered by the inability to effectively capture subtle semantic orientations within large-scale sentiment datasets, particularly product reviews, where nuances like degree and orientation of sentiment prevail. Conventional deep learning techniques struggle to capture these subtleties. To bridge this gap, this paper presents an innovative framework, Contrastive Sentiment Orientation Learning (CSOL), which leverages large-scale product review datasets. CSOL employs a novel Supervised Contrastive Pre-training (SCP) method that enhances the learning capacity of static word embeddings in capturing sentiment orientations. To achieve this, the method introduces contrastive learning objectives within a sentiment-class aware framework to push similar sentences toward positive or negative sentiments based on the class label. Our proposed framework further includes Contrastive Orientation Learners that maximize the similarities between instances sharing the same class label while increasing inter-class dissimilarities, thereby effectively capturing fine-grained sentiment orientations. Our experiments demonstrate that SCP yields superior static word embeddings over conventional approaches, particularly in capturing subtle sentiment orientations. On two prominent product review datasets, the proposed CSOL framework outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in terms of accuracy, achieving AUC yields and orientation bias results. Notably, the improved quality of the static word embeddings developed by CSOL leads to consistent performance enhancements in various downstream applications, including a sentiment analysis task, using various transfer learning-based architectures.

The increased utilization of gastric acid suppressors resulting in reduced stomach acid production, has led to a rise in the incidence of listeriosis in immunocompromised humans. We examined the effects of compromised immunity on the dynamics of listeriosis and the effects of reduced stomach acid on the outbreak's timing in models that incorporate Fließbaumer's work on the immune system's interaction with bacteria. In contrast to previous findings, our results show that diminished stomach acid does not accelerate listeriosis's onset; instead, it implies the opposite and suggests the disease may manifest later than in immunocompetent individuals. Moreover, the data implies that the time difference between the incidence of listeriosis in immunocompromised and immunocompetent patients is directly related to the optimal level of immune response.

This research investigates how Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS)-aided secure communication is affected by hardware impairments. Since RIS are now in mass production, it is crucial to assess how their quality-of-service (QoS) is impacted by hardware issues. To do this, a more accurate model of RIS impairments that considers statistics (mean, variance, and probability distribution) is developed. Consequently, a novel analytical framework is developed for both RIS and its associated transmission systems, taking into consideration the impact of hardware impairments. To validate these findings, both exact and approximate analytical models are derived to examine the impact of hardware impairments on RIS-assisted secure multiuser communication. To this end, this research examines the probability distribution of secure secrecy rate and secrecy outage probability, providing valuable insights into how hardware issues impact RIS-assisted secure communication. By comparing theoretical results with simulation outcomes, this research confirms that these analytical models are accurate. To further understand the impact of hardware issues, this research computes the closed-form expressions of secure transmission statistics under these impairments. To substantiate these findings, this research presents multiple sets of simulation results that match its analytical model.

Sequential prediction is inherent to numerous AI, robotics, and biology-based systems, involving a trajectory of state observations, where the future is often predicted from past states. Most such predictions occur in hindsight, meaning the predictor has access to additional observations beyond the time step at which it's making the prediction. The implication is that an optimally informed predictor with access to the full trajectory can effectively minimize prediction error by learning from the ultimate outcome. Inspired by the success of hindsight learning in robotics and the convergence of errors towards a common value in multi-step prediction tasks, we theorize that incorporating hindsight summarization - enabling predictors to understand the overall trajectory context - can significantly decrease starting prediction error. Specifically, we present a new model capable of leveraging hindsight summarization, and prove it achieves significantly lower error bounds in high-dimensional spaces, substantiating our claim. Our proposed model is agnostic to specific optimizers and existing optimizers from supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning can be applied, providing a versatile framework.

Our prior research delved into the theoretical underpinnings of a process called particle injection, involved in the formation of meteoroid streams, by studying how objects interact with the solar wind and its magnetic field as they approach the Sun. In this research, we present the results of two Monte Carlo simulations, modeling how meteoroids from comet 19P/Borrelly are perturbed as they approach the Sun due to solar gravitation. The simulations, based on various assumptions regarding particle distribution and solar wind, calculate the probability of meteoroids reaching the Earth as a function of time, comparing these findings with actual meteoroid encounters observed at 1 AU. The simulations show that, contrary to uniform energy distributions previously proposed, meteoroids require a more intricate and dynamic distribution of energy to overcome solar gravitation and reach the Earth. The new results, based on two distinct solar wind models, pinpoint the minimum energy required for meteoroids to reach the Earth as approximately 2.4 - 2.9 x 10^4 kT (in terms of kinetic energy per gram), with a uniform energy distribution having too little low-energy content by at least an order of magnitude. The simulations also demonstrate that meteoroids from an Earth-crossing comet like 19P/Borrelly acquire energies of up to 6.5 - 13.5 x 10^5 kT (in the Kelvin energy unit) shortly before reaching the Earth, with a uniform energy distribution having too much high-energy

We first establish the definition of freeness for actions by a locally trivial G-C*-algebra G acting on a quantum compact groupoid G. This concept is akin to freeness for actions by compact groups when the quantum groupoid reduces to a compact group. We then demonstrate that the unit cohomology of QG falls short of capturing all free actions. Instead, we define inner freeness and attribute it to the right action of QG's C*-algebra by its inner automorphism group. With inner freeness in mind, we show that unit cohomology does fail to distinguish between certain free actions that differ by an inner action. We conclude by introducing generalised inner freeness for actions by a locally trivial phase rotation C*-algebra and establish a cohomological characterization of generalized inner freeness.

In 1966, Tarski proposed an interpretation of the statements of first-order logic as conditions of algebraic validity, paving the way for further inquiries into the underlying sets and categories in logic. This paper explores the interconnectedness of logic and algebraic validity in category theory, establishing connections between logic, representation theorem, $P$-points, ultrafilters, and predictive logic. The study demonstrates the importance of $P$-points in ensuring the consistency of certain cardinal inequalities, including the statements on finite cardinals, $P$-finite cardinals, and $\kappa$-cardinals. When $P$-points exist, it allows for a generalized version of Boolean algebraic logic that encompasses all types of cardinals through $P$-ultrafilters, while eliminating the need for transfinite methods.

Our approach involves investigating an optical system with three levels when the photon is entangled with an oscillator, but not in a classical sense. This system is studied under two conditions. First, we employ the q-deformation of SU(3) symmetry in an optomechanical context, leading to the exploration of exceptional points. Second, we utilize SU(3) symmetry in a context that preserves conserved parity, resulting in the construction of a corresponding Hamiltonian. In both systems, a probe field interacts with a two-level system during the absorption or emission of photons. The research shows that SU(3) symmetry allows for the adjustment of the probe field's strength by adjusting optomechanical coupling or tunneling strength.
