Furthermore, SU(3) symmetry facilitates the control of the absorption-emission process through the purposeful manipulation of optomechanical coupling or tunneling strength.

In the field of nuclear physics, dipole rotational modes are gaining attention for their role in describing structures within nuclei that rotate rapidly. Various studies have demonstrated that a specific type of rotational mode, the R-negative state, can be crucial in understanding the internal makeup of these complex structures. Unlike their R-positive counterparts, the R-negative states generally have lower energy and stronger interactions with other particles, making them more prone to being influenced by the surroundings. A new research framework is being developed to describe the R-negative states and provide a standardized way of analyzing these rotational modes across different types of nuclei, thus enhancing our understanding of the emergent dipole rotational structures within nuclei.

This research compares the numerical solutions of a nonlinear hyperbolic conservation law in one dimension from two approaches: a neural network method and a classical Runge--Kutta approach, enhanced by an approximate Riemann solver. We focus on a model that features a discontinuity capturing the essence of wave interactions, including contact discontinuities and rarefactive and compressive shock waves. We employ the SSPL scheme, known for its approximate Riemann solver and strong stability enhancement, which maintains stability even in the presence of flammable numerical fluxes. Its high-order extension with the classical Runge--Kotta method produces a second-order accurate solution at the expense of slightly reduced wave smoothness. A neural network solution, obtained via the \V-RNet method, offers a high-order accurate solution under specific assumptions. Notably, both methods are able to represent contact discontinuies and rarefactive and compressive shock waves accurately. We also demonstrated that the solution from the neural network method matches that of the classical approach up to a four-order accurate approximation, with some minor differences likely resulting from numerical artifacts.

The LUXe3 experiment plans to utilize the Electron Ring at DESY to measure the elastic scattering cross-section at the precision of $10^{-9}$ mb, by doing so, it will be possible to gain more insights into the physics of QED and the properties of atoms as well as enhancing our understanding of the physics beyond the standard model by crossing the threshold of detection sensitivity to the Higgs boson decay into a photon pair. In order to achieve its research objectives, the experiment requires an upgrade of its current experimental setup, which involves three key areas of enhancement. Firstly, in order to increase the precision of its measurements, the experiment plans to utilize a newly developed gas chamber, which has been specifically designed with its research in mind. Secondly, in order to increase its photon detection capabilities, the experiment plans to install an upgraded module of an energy-based detector, which has been equipped with amorphous silicon sensors, as a result of this the experiment will be able to achieve its research objectives quickly. Thirdly, in order to increase its precision of measurements, the experiment plans to utilize an upgraded system of data read-out, which could be linked to the presence of electron-positron pairs. In this document we will be investigating the proposed system of data read-out for the experiment.

This research focuses on exploring an unconventional platform for observing the Unruh effect in a timelike context, utilizing an adjustable $q$-system. By deriving a set of q-deformed Klein-Gordon equations that describe the detection of Unruh modes by different Cavities in the Unruh space-time, we reveal how the Unruh effect can be implemented for timelike observers through the use of time-dependent q-deformed Lambiase systems. We further investigate the timelike Unruh effect in a Schwarzschild background and establish connections between our findings and recent research on their thermodynamic properties.

This research presents two innovative EE techniques that overcome previous difficulties in applying this method to non-English languages, which often lack relevant training data and high-quality annotations for similar, English-based NLP tasks like semantic parsing. Our first contribution is a cross-lingual training strategy that utilizes unsupervised EE models to produce robust word embeddings that capture general linguistic patterns, which can then be fine-tuned in target languages. Additionally, we developed a multi-task training method that combines two EE sub-tasks, one of which is cross-lingual and helps reduce noise and improve the model's ability to generalize. Our experiments, which included three languages and a leading EE model, demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach, resulting in top-tier performance and notable improvements on the GT2BES dataset for Besney language modeling.

In a proof that relies on a specific assumption, it can be shown that a certain positivity property of Chern forms implies Griffiths' original positivity conjecture for forms in positive characteristic. This more general form involves mixed Chern and chiral Chern forms. The original assumption requires further exploration, but it can be disputed using examples from a specific surface that has a singularities structure resembling the case when k=2 and a specific transversality condition is met. The example also raises doubts about the validity of a more general conjecture related to positive characteristic forms in a K\"ahler manifold.

Simulating the effects of relativistic scattering from the accretion disk in high-mass X-ray binaries, our research reveals that this mechanism could significantly reduce coherence between light curves in different energy ranges. Our predicted soft-to-hard energy delay agrees with previous studies, but our current model doesn't reproduce the exact phase lags observed in certain sources. One possible explanation is that the accretion disk in such systems is likely fragmented, preventing a unified description with our present model. Nonetheless, our research provides new insights into a feasible mechanism responsible for coherence loss in high-mass X-ray binaries, and future observations with more advanced instruments could help confirm this hypothesis. Moreover, our study highlights the potential for direct coherence to become negative, as well as the existence of frequency-dependent features that may appear as discontinuities in wavelength-dependent analysis.

By incorporating a non-abelian version of the aether invariant into thermodynamics and Casimir theory, researchers gain insights into non-abelian radiation and potential implications for high-energy physics beyond the standard model. The proposed modification to thermodynamics leads to a generalization of the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law, which differs from previous predictions. Similarly, incorporating the aether invariant leads to an alternative calculation of Casimir energy, which may also account for modifications to the stress tensor reported in loop quantum gravity.

Our proposed model simultaneously analyzes sentence structure and meaning, and when trained on three distinct languages, it highlights a shared phenomenon in which words tend to be co-ordinated or co-referential in conjunction with typical linguistic patterns in each language. Conversely, when the model is trained on each language separately, these common tendencies yield distinctive variations. Furthermore, this model's joint predictions exhibit a pronounced and consistent trend of gradually increasing uncertainty in both syntax and semantics that parallels existing theories of linguistic information density, and its joint modeling compares favorably to separate models in terms of both linguistic understanding and text prediction accuracy. Finally, an investigation into the scope of applicability reveals that this model's joint framework is effective for understanding and generating text from multiple languages with differing word orders.

Radioactively driven transients formed by compact object mergers could be visible across a range of luminosities from 10^38 erg s^-1 to 10^42 erg s^-1, spanning two decades of variation. By employing a universal radio efficiency and similar energy dependencies, researchers have developed a model to predict appearance patterns of these transients and their potential surface features throughout the explosion phase. It's anticipated that a significant portion of transients with moderate to high luminosity will transform into red supernovae type IIN, while those with less brightness may appear as yellow supernovae or faint gamma-ray bursts, potentially accounting for a significant portion of unresolved kilonova events. The model also suggests that about 5-50% of long gamma-ray bursts within a specific luminosity class may actually be radioactively powered transients from compact object mergers.

This research aims to understand the formation of tidal features stemming from galactic interactions, as observed in the underlying $ \chi^{2}$-best fit dark matter distributions within galaxies. We examine the satelite cross section model and apply it to a detailed set of N-body simulations, as well as two distinct sample sets: a sparsely selected group of 97 galaxies, known as ATLAS$^{^{3D}}$, and a extensively selected group of 927 galaxies, known as ATLAS. The research shows that tidal features are prevalent in interacting galaxies, as indicated by both observed galaxies and dark matter distributions, as a mean $25\pm5\%$ of the disk flux resides within these tidal features. Furthermore, the occurrence of tidal features, as predicted by the satelite cross section model, correlates positively with the galaxy's mass, as evident in both N-body simulations and observed galaxies. However, the satelite cross section model overestimates the size, as measured in kiloparsecs, of tidal features within galaxies. Additionally, the satelite cross section model fails to forecast tidal features, as observed in late galaxy counterparts, to adequately address tidal features, as observed in some early galaxies, to sufficiently explain interactions between galaxies' processes.

The Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation suggests an alternative approach to general relativity, addressing several longstanding challenges in astrophysics. Our study demonstrates that this theory can overcome the Radiation Problem associated with massive star formation. This problem stems from the conflicting nature of radiation emission and absorption laid out by Einstein's emission and absorption laws. These laws are pivotal to understanding how stars emit and absorb light, as utilized across numerous astrophysical applications. Although researchers acknowledge the limitations of these laws, deemed fundamental by Einstein, we reveal that they possess hidden ambiguities. This resolution yields a streamlined method for calculating stellar energy output, along with principles for stellar structure and evolution. This framework is capable of handling the physical processes present within extremely hot stars, encompassing those identified by Wheeler, Weinberg, and Icko in the 1950s and 1960s as well as additional advanced concepts. This simplified approach is even extendable to the vast expanse of the interstellar medium. Consequently, we are able to rewrite the equations for stellar structure and evolution in a straightforward, unified format, providing a foundational understanding of massive star physics across space and time, as an alternative to the conventional magnetic models. Furthermore, we utilize this theory to gauge the potential role of gravitational waves in the universe, revealing an entirely new understanding of celestial phenomena.

Within the last ten years, researchers have observed a connection between Fast Radio Bursts and the environments of galaxies hosting supernovae and active galactic nuclei. To improve understanding of the physical origins and radio emission processes in Fast Radio Bursts, researchers should be able to locate their host galaxies with high precision. Achieving this requires pinning down the burst's location in three dimensions, facilitated by observations with multiple telescopes simultaneously capturing the burst's radio signal. Although significant progress has been made, fast radio burst localization remains restricted by the speed of data transfer between telescopes and the radio emission models used to predict their locations. To support the search for these elusive bursts, researchers should be able to locate the burst's location in real-time, informed by predictions from computer simulations and a comprehensive understanding of the observational process. To showcase this process, I have implemented a novel visualization tool, available at github.com/kgruber/fast-rayleigh-distance, that allows researchers to generate an animation based on the burst's speed and observers' positions, calculated using the speed of light and the burst's triangulation boundaries, known as the Rayleigh distance.

The growing demand for complex laser systems such as CPA and NLO systems drives 
the need to improve numerical simulations to accurately model these systems and 
their interactions. However, detailed models are often hampered by numerous 
interactions and physical processes involved. To fill this gap, a set of Python 
tools, called PyALMA, has been developed to facilitate the building of detailed 
physical models and Monte-Carlo based simulations for advanced laser systems. 
These tools include features such as a nonlinear crystal calculator, a photonics 
library, and a 1D wave propagation engine with numerous solver options. Furthermore, 
the framework offers a dynamically configurable architecture, enabling easy extension 
of the code and its applications. PyALMA's versatility also extends to its integration 
with various existing frameworks and libraries, such as ApoPy, Yoof, and MySTEEML, 
as well as its plans for future collaboration with the CPA laser community to develop 
a set of reference models to assess the performance of CPA laser systems.

Visual Commonsense Question Answering, a task that requires both visual and logical reasoning, has received growing attention in the NLP community. Our work addresses it by adapting the MAGIC framework, originally designed for text-based external knowledge sources. The MAGIC framework incorporates magic cards that represent knowledge and logic, allowing them to be organized in a sequence and executed one at a time. For VCQA, we've introduced new magic cards that interact with the external knowledge based on image features. The MAGIC model then uses an image encoder to get feature embeddings that guide the selection of magic cards and their ordering. Our model can automatically learn the weight of each magic card for each input image without parameter adjustment. The MAGIC model has outperformed previous state-of-the-art models, achieving a significant improvement in an exact match metric on the GEMbench benchmark. Our analysis using an interpretability tool confirmed that the MAGIC model's magic cards capture the task-specific features and logical operations.

We introduce Delegated RingCT, a highly efficient RingCT variant for Monero and its variants, such as RingCTDX. Delegated RingCT achieves this efficiency by minimizing the size of the compact signatures added to the blockchain and has two key benefits. Firstly, it significantly speeds up transaction verification on the network, making Delegated RingCT transactions verify $6.35\times$ faster than RingCTDX and $12.92\times$ faster than Protocol 3.0. Secondly, its low peak memory usage during the verification process makes it suitable for low-powered devices, with Delegated RingCT being up to $25.6\%$ more efficient than RingCTDX. This makes Delegated RingCT an advanced protocol not only for Monero but also for future Quantum-resistant variants.

A method is described for making precise measurements of small discrepancies in the track patterns followed by particle beams in circular accelerators. These discrepancies arise from various sources, including the distortion caused by interactions between beams and the magnetic fields generated by accelerator components. A method for quantifying and analyzing these discrepancies is presented, as well as a simple way to estimate how interactions between beams distort track patterns. Experimentally measurable effects of beam-beam close orbit differences can be detected through precision measurements of closed orbit discrepancies, and predictions are provided for how interactions between beams distort track patterns in specific accelerator configurations.

To address the complexities of modeling history-dependent plasticity and damage in solid mechanics, we need to accurately describe material constituents found in structural and geotechnical engineering. This includes soils, granular materials, and even soft biological tissues, which often exhibit physiologically driven evolutionary processes. One major challenge in computational modeling is capturing these processes effectively. For instance, traditional approaches typically require significant data storage or 'ghost' arrays, which can be impractical for large-scale simulations. Furthermore, existing data storage methods may not be suitable for real-time modeling applications. This research presents a novel approach to modeling memory-intensive material processes by leveraging continual learning. This method enables the modeling of material processes using progressively increasing amounts of memory over time. It utilizes a unique ensemble technique that fine-tunes previously acquired knowledge and adapts it to new situations. We've developed a simple yet efficient implementation of this approach using basic tensorflow routines and the non-linear viscoelastic model for one-sand model, before extending it to a more complex model of granular materials. Our results, show that model accuracy and memory consumption exhibit a pattern where an initial rapid improvement in predictions and memory consumption plateau once a sufficient number of past material states have been incorporated. This behavior is in line with the characteristics of other machine learning models. We also discovered that including at least five past material states is typically enough to achieve accurate results, which presents a significant finding since most geometric problems typically require at least 5-10 history steps.
