In-Plane Spin Polarized Monopole Excitations in Dirac Spin Liquids have been found using projected entangled pair states methods with a triangular lattice, in conjunction with a p x + p y wave function. The acquired evidence supports their role as a hallmark of Dirac spin liquid phases, distinct from gapped valence-bond solid states. Furthermore, a previously established account for a system of interacting spin-1 particles based on statistical methods has been validated through comparison with our results obtained through PEPS.

A quantum system featuring the combined $Z_3$-broken and $Z_6$ symmetries is examined on a one-dimensional lattice, where the $Z_3$ symmetry stems from a three-site lattice environment and the $Z_6$ symmetry comes from a six-site environment. Three distinct models, incorporating bosons, fermions, and the interplay between bosons and fermions, are studied to analyze the breaking of the $Z_3$ symmetry in the many-body limit. It's observed that the more temporal sites the lattice has, the stronger the $Z_3$ symmetry is broken. Additionally, the research reveals a phase transition from an ergodic to a non-ergodic phase, which happens when the $Z_3$ symmetry isn't broken. This finding makes the initial models suitable for testing theories about system dynamics where the $Z_3$ symmetry isn't broken, as well as developing approaches to break the $Z_3$ symmetry freely.

To investigate the magnetic competition in non-collinear orders, a next-nearest neighbor Heisenberg model is used on a specific type of crystal structure called the simple antiferromagnetic structure of $\sqrt2$Xo compounds. The compounds in question, Cr$_2$Al and Mn$_2$Au, exhibit distinct magnetic properties including incommensurate and ferromagnetic ordering at specific points within the model. The study finds that varying two key parameters leads to various magnetic configurations including a type of order known as skew ferromagnetism, and another type known as the Kitaev magnetism. The study further estimates the potential for these different magnetic properties to occur in other $\sqrt2$Xo compounds, where X representing elements can vary.

A novel approach, termed the $\mu$-model, has been devised to enhance thermal transpiration modeling in rarefied micro-flows. This polyatomic gas model incorporates the moment equations of mass, momentum, and energy using a concise solution for polyatomic mean heat capacity as a function of temperature. As a result, the $\mu$-model efficiently handles polyatomic gas thermal behavior, analogous to monatomic gas models, and effectively simulates thermal transpiration across various scenarios with high accuracy. Notably, the $\mu$-model models thermal transpiration for gases such as hydrogen, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide with correlation errors less than 1% even in slanted, horizontal, and vacuum environments. Furthermore, the $\mu$-model offers a simplified alternative to complex nonequilibrium gas models, thus providing a valuable tool for rarefied gas flow engineering applications.

Existing solutions for few-shot semantic parsing rely heavily on having a large amount of unsupervised text data, but our approach takes a different direction by utilizing unsupolved text data and external knowledge sources like databases and wikis to aid in the learning process, specifically for the dependency parsing and state transition graphs used in the system. This change in approach allows for better performance when given limited positive training samples, and particularly when the system is introduced to new categories not seen during the initial training phase. Additionally, this approach's novel retrieval method can identify and prioritize the most relevant information from vast databases and wikis to aid in the learning process. To better this approach's efficiency, a novel word embedding technique is introduced, using word sense indentity to bring together related words from the external knowledge sources, but this comes with increased computational costs. Consequently, a mechanism was introduced to balance the efficiency and performance of the system. This approach was tested and evaluated on the SEMISAME benchmark, leading to significant improvements in the state of the art for few-shot semantic parsing. Results show an almost 7 point gain in the micro-precision score when given limited positive training samples, and particularly when the system is introduced to new categories not seen during the initial training phase, when compared to the standard approach used in existing solutions.

Thin, radiation-resistant sensors, implemented in various advanced technologies with integrated readout electronics, are essential components of modern particle physics tracking systems and detectors.  Two recently developed technologies - the Depleted Monolithic Active Pixel Sensor (DMAPS) and the AC-coupled Low Gain Avalanche Diode (AC-LGAD) using a high-resistivity silicon material, are being utilized in cutting-edge particle physics experiments.  Characterized by high signal robustness, the DeMAPS/DMAPS system can track charged particles in challenging environments, while thin, high-microscopic displacement rate sensors, facilitated by AC-LGAD technology, are distinguished by their powerful photon detection capabilities.  Research personnel are presenting the latest advancements in experimental settings of the SHiP experiment, specifically focusing on DeMAPS-based pixel sensors, as well as on-track time resolution measurements for AC-LGAD detectors, which are being evaluated under high energy proton particle beams.

Our detailed examination of the low-mass AGN 2XMM J123103.2+110648 began with a comprehensive look at its X-ray spectra using Chandra and XMM-Newton data across multiple observations, followed by a broad-spectrum spectral analysis spanning several wavelengths. 2XMM J123103.2+110648, located at a redshift of 0.029, is characterized by a power-law shape consistent across different energy ranges and significant hard X-ray emission compared to predicted black hole seeding timescales. Its spectral data show no notable gas absorption beyond the Milky Way, although neutral gas is detected in UV observations at a column density of $\approx 6.5 \times 10^{19} \mathrm{cm}^{-2}$. Using the broad-spectral data and energy ranges, we applied different models including those for comptonization and applied relativistic reflection analyses of hard X-ray spectra. Our results suggest strong reflection strong reflection dominance over comptonization processes and a highly inclined system with a blackbody emission component indicating ongoing comptonization in a hot accretion flow. Moreover, flares observed in XMM-Newton data were also detected in UV and optical bands with frequencies ranging from 2 to 5 per day. Using multi-band photometry and spectroscopy, we verified that the system is primarily powered by an actively accreting supermassive black hole rather than any stellar activity. The interaction between stellar winds and magnetic fields creates distinct magnetospheres around certain types of stars. Magnetohydrodynamic simulations predict that these magnetospheres can resemble a type of celestial phenomenon called a wind rossiter-McLaughlin effect. However, the exact shape and properties of magnetospheres around specific types of stars, such as B-type magnetic stars, remain relatively unknown. Recent observations have revealed the presence of magnetospheres in the vicinity of these stars, but the available data is limited. Our team conducted an observational analysis focused on the B-type magnetic star, HD243138, and its wind-magnetic field interaction. We utilized specific astronomical instruments to measure the effect of phase on certain spectral features and determined that this effect is primarily caused by the presence of a stellar wind-magnetic field interaction. Our observations further suggest the presence of a stellar wind with a speed of approximately 1000 km per second. We compared our findings with the predictions made by an existing model, and the phase effect observed did not fully conform to the shape and properties predicted by the model. Our study reports the presence of a stellar wind-magnetic field interaction in the vicinity of the B-type magnetic star, HD243138, and highlights potential discrepancies between the observed properties of magnetospheres and those predicted by models. Our research also indicates the need for additional observations and modeling to further understand the characteristics of magnetospheres around B-type magnetic stars.

The intertwining operators concept is explored through oscillator operators in a one-dimensional space, yielding novel results expressed in terms of Weyl-Even and odd P-operators. Building upon these findings, connections are drawn between the introduced kernels and known representations of creation and annihilation operators. Additionally, the study delves into functional analytic properties of the operators in question, culminating in a consideration of their potential unitarity.

We analyzed data from HiGeSS for 25 galaxies with low metallicity found outside the Local Group, measuring their total infrared flux and Hi spectra, and also obtained H30α emissions for a subset of these galaxies. We used the corrected Hi line and modified Pu '13 method to estimate star formation rates (SFRs) based on Hi and infrared data, respectively. We further compared our Hi-based SFRs with those calculated using Hi and H30α emissions, revealing a significant underestimation of SFRs derived from H30α compared to infrared fluxes in low metallicity galaxies (-0.4 dex). This discrepancy is not found in typical galaxies, highlighting the need to adjust SFRs derived from Hi emissions when comparing to those obtained from infrared fluxes in dwarf galaxies or low metallicity systems outside the Local Group. Additionally, our analysis indicates that the mass of neutral hydrogen in galaxies with low metallicity is primarily formed through the interstellar medium, yet our data also suggest that a small portion of this gas exists in diffuse filaments along the galactic disks. We developed a formula to calculate the column density of these filaments using the Hi bias and the optical depth at 21-cm transition. We discovered the filaments hold 30% of neutral gas and the bias is around 1.5.

We investigate the class of topological spaces that support continuous minimal group actions. Our focus is on a specific type of action, commensurable to the infinite dihedral group. The dihedral group, with order 2n, is generated by rotations (order n) and reflections (order 2). Our study reveals that such actions on compact, metric spaces are not rigid within their equivalence class when n equals any given integer. In contrast, we've shown that actions of a different type, commensurable to the infinite dihedral group but generated by elements of order 2, exhibit rigidity. Our work also demonstrates the rigidity of certain cyclic actions and has implications for hyponormal C*-algebras.

In recent years, kernel-based techniques for projection have gained attention, particularly in various applications of data analysis. This research aims to evaluate the convergence properties of kernel-based methods for solving parametric projection and compare them to classical approaches like Galerkin method. We examine the convergence behavior of the kernel-based methods in relation to the smoothing parameter of the kernel. The results demonstrate that kernel-based techniques can surpass parametric methods when an optimal kernel with an appropriate smoothing parameter is utilized. A proposed ensemble kernel bridge method is also presented, incorporating multiple kernels to mitigate the choice of the smoothing parameter. The proposed approach is tested and verified on three distinct types of problems: a benchmark problem, a Poisson equation, and a multi-dimensional periodic diffusion problem. The results confirm the effectiveness of the ensemble kernel bridge method in improving convergence and alleviating the impact of kernel parameter choice.

This study introduces an observer designed for a particular nonlinear class of systems, encompassing classic deterministic epidemic models. By utilizing a novel observer with adaptive transformation and fractional filter components, accurate estimation of key system states can be achieved. Theoretical analysis has confirmed the observer's convergence to the true states through practical Lyapunov stability arguments. Furthermore, simulation results validate the theoretical findings and demonstrate the proposed observer's effectiveness in estimating critical parameters such as infection rates and population densities for complex nonlinear epidemic models.

Knowledge graph embeddings, which allow for representation of entities and their relationships in a usable format, have gained significant interest from the research community. Conventionally, the focus has been on improving temporal knowledge graphs, where fact-based relationships are reflected across different time stamps. Unfortunately, existing models using transfer learning to embed these graphs still struggle with accurately capturing temporal connections. We propose TKE, a new method to enhance temporal knowledge graph embeddings by retaining context information through a Temporal Context Retrieval module. We evaluate our approach against superior non-transfer and state-of-the-art transfer learning-based temporal knowledge graph embedding methods, demonstrating that TKE consistently achieves superior results across various evaluation metrics. The advancements made by TKE set a new benchmark for temporal knowledge graph embeddings, and we conduct thorough experimentation to verify its efficacy. Notably, we examine its application in a real-world setting, specifically detecting temporal connections in documents. The source code for TKE is openly available on GitHub.

We successfully implement stable Kerr-lens mode-locking in a monolithic, ultra-compact optical cavity featuring a Si$_2$O$_3$ waveguide and a Ge$_2$As$_2$ photonic crystal fiber for the signal path. The structure allows for integration of the pump source, a photodetector, and a spectral analyzer within a compact enclosure of merely 25 cubic centimeters, as demonstrated using a solid-state pump laser operating at 1535 nm. By leveraging the native Si$_2$O$_3$ waveguide and employing appropriate waveguide filters, we achieve a tunable center wavelength of approximately 1550 nm with a 3dB bandwidth of about 5.3 nm. The incorporation of a 45-micron-diameter Si$_2$O$_3$ waveguide serves to significantly reduce mode-anisotropic losses and facilitate the construction of a stable Kerr-lens mode-locked laser, as this anionic oxide waveguide exhibits comparable thermal and refractive properties to the laser's germanium-based fiber. Moreover, our work showcases the first development of a Kerr-lens mode-locked, frequency-comb semiconductor-based optical oscillator capable of generating ultra-stable, ultra-low noise 10-fs pulses, as this achievement is facilitated by the incorporation of a frequency-stable, 340-MHz sub-PSB-level laser source with a linewidth of merely 10 kHz. As online federated learning gains momentum, reducing participant computation costs becomes a growing concern, despite the existing literature primarily focusing on reducing the time required for each participant's computations.  To address this issue, we examine the communication expenses in asynchronous online Federated Averaging for multiple participants.  To achieve faster communication while preserving data privacy, we introduce a partial-sharing-based approach, which allows participants to send only the necessary information for their updated models.  The proposed method is efficient not only because it reduces the communication costs at the participant end but also because it minimizes the storage requirements at the server end.  The effectiveness of our method is mathematically proven by showing that under specific conditions, the error convergence under the partial-sharing-based approach is identical to that under full data-sharing.  The proposed method is flexible enough to be combined with other acceleration techniques for Federated Averaging, and through experiments using artificial data, we demonstrate that it can achieve a 65% reduction in communication costs while still maintaining the same convergence as the full data-sharing approach, thereby enabling participants to save time and the server to minimize storage costs.

We investigate the theoretical aspects of solar energy production using thin silicon films within nanophotonic frameworks. Our focus is on the optical properties of these films when utilized in structures comprising a silicon nitride base, placed between two external mirrors, one being a reflective photonic crystal structure made of silicon, and the other a reflective metal layer. The results indicate that by selecting an optimal thickness for the silicon nitride film, and employing a photonic crystal back reflector, its optical absorption can be enhanced compared to a flat silicon film, and also compared to a system consisting of a flat silicon nitride film paired with both a flat silicon and a metal reflector. It is discovered that the controlled reflection of the photonic crystal back reflector at the silicon nitride/silicon interface enables a notable enhancement of the absorption profile of the thin silicon nitride film over a broad range of wavelengths. This effect arises from the interference in the film's optical properties caused by the photonic crystal reflector, accounting for approximately 86% of the enhanced absorption. Consequently, a thin silicon nitride film of merely 50.7 nm thickness is able to efficiently absorb a substantial amount of power from incident white light, making this setup appealing for efficient thin-film solar cells.

The paper's objective is to derive specific functions that govern the behavior of the exponential map on the complex plane. This is achieved by applying the dynamics of the exponential map to distinct subsets and using it to find particular solutions of the Cauchy-Riemann equations, which in turn enables the construction of appropriate monogenic functions. It further explores some underlying relationships among these functions, as well as their connection to the trace formula and the spectrum of harmonic numbers.

This paper introduces a new construction for high-dimensional expanders, which are expanders with the property that filtered degenerate matrices have large trace norms. Building on this, we use tensor products to create high-dimensional expanders based on existing construction expanders. We apply these expanders in two areas: developing a quasi-MAP Monte Carlo method that reduces sample complexity, and designing robust hashing schemes that guarantee distance preservation even under attack attempts.

The structure of the ground state and excited states for the Gd$^{3+}$ ion chain in GdInO$_3$ were investigated using both density functional theory and spin-polarized mean-field approaches. By minimizing the energy, the DFT method determined that the ground state is a cubic lattice with an inverted spin configuration. Through a spin-polarized mean-field calculation, it was found that the ground state multiplet $\Gamma_8$ splits into $\Gamma_8$ and $\Gamma_7$ sub-configurations. Additionally, mean-field results match the expectations of a Hartree-Fock-like behavior. Mean-field results also revealed that the energy differences between various configurations and combinations of $\Delta E($\Gamma_8$-\Gamma_7)$ are substantial. Using these results, the EMPIRIC code's RPA calculation treated the influence of electron excitations on the $\Gamma$-point susceptibility $\chi_{GG}$ as small. Furthermore, the Metropolis algorithm was employed to sample the variations of the mean-field Hamiltonian, leading to the determination that the magnetic susceptibility at the $\Gamma$ point is paramagnetic. It was found that the magnetic energy term $\mathcal{E}_{M}$ negatively correlates with the coupling constant $J$, while it positively correlates with the exchange parameter $J$ and the inverted spin configuration. Finally, the free energy calculation revealed that the ground state is cubic, and there is an energy gap of approximately 1.22 e

Our research examines various methods for representing nodes within sparse networks, leading to the innovative proposal of Sum of Normalized H-order Adjacency Matrix (SNHAM). SNHAM involves calculating the sum of normalized adjacency matrices resulting from different order graphs generated by a random walk, under the constraint of a fixed number of steps. Diverging from traditional methods, SNHAM orders nodes based on a unified score that incorporates the views of all generated order graphs. The SNHAM approach offers improved representation accuracy for homogeneous and inhomogeneous networks, outperforming existing node representation techniques in our empirical studies.

A novel pill activation device with two connected chambers has been developed to enhance low-vapor-density gases and improve its overall design. 

The objective of this research is to study the mass transport within the chambers using computational models based on the principles of molecular kinetics. 

We have optimized the pill design to accelerate vapor density within the chambers and minimize the processing time required. 

Several factors have contributed to the improvement, particularly when utilizing a two-chamber approach instead of a single, broadened chamber design. 

Additionally, the placement of the chambers relative to each other significantly impacts vapor density at various stages: initial design allows faster processing in the initial stage, whereas the initial design yields better results in the final stage. 

We have also found that the presence of heat transfer significantly boosts processing times, leading to the recommendation to maintain temperatures consistent within both chambers. 

The models have successfully predicted the trends of vapor density using three distinct pill designs, with each having unique characteristics that favor specific design approaches. 

We estimate that the accelerated growth factor can reach up to 4.7, and the design could potentially reduce the processing time required to achieve a target density by up to 5 times. 

The average error between the model's predictions and simulations in a test case is found to be approximately 0.06 or less. 

the models show a consistent correlation between processing time and system size or temperature. 

We believe that these low-cost devices have the potential to revolutionize the storage of high-dense gases

Computer simulations of optical communications with high signal count and complex polarization schemes would benefit significantly from simplified models of optical interference. Traditional methods for calculating optical interference in these systems are often computationally too expensive. We introduce an approach that utilizes the Kramers-Kronig reciprocity relations to create a more straightforward, phenomenological model of optical interference relevant to systems using polarisation-multiplexed formats. We found that a standard Gaussian shape effectively approximates the predicted intensity autocorrelation function, allowing for a reliable method to determine the model's parameters. The introduced model was validated by comparing its results with accurate quantum mechanical simulations and experimental data from a test bed featuring a large number of interfering paths. We show that this simplified model enables the computation of optical interference in complex systems with thousands of polarisation-multiplexed channels, making it a valuable tool for designing and evaluating emerging multi-core, mode-division multiplexed optical communication systems.

Image fusion technology has become a critical component in various sectors such as remote sensing, virtual reality, and video streaming. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of cutting-edge image fusion techniques that utilize multi-scale and detailed information. These novel approaches are expected to enhance the accuracy of fire detection and other image processing applications. This paper provides a comprehensive review of existing image fusion techniques, assesses their performance using a standardized fire detection dataset and metrics, and discusses the challenges and limitations of the field. It exposes a previously unidentified issue where state-of-the-art deep learning-based image fusion techniques tend to produce high false-positive rates when imaging fires. Consequently, a new multi-scale pixel-wise decision-making strategy is presented to improve the accuracy of fire detection by incorporating the strengths of various fusion techniques. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach, outperforming existing image fusion methods, including those based on deep learning, in terms of accuracy, using the fire detection dataset. The accompanying code is accessible via a public GitHub repository.

Diagnosing mental health using social media data poses unique challenges compared to traditional physical checks, primarily due to its unstructured nature. Decentralized, observational, and informal data collection methods used on social media platforms require innovative and data-driven approaches for accurately diagnosing mental health. Present methods often struggle to achieve high classification accuracy for individual users, thus we propose a decentralized system utilizing Markov chain algorithms to aggregate and accumulate user data for enhanced diagnostic capabilities. The results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in providing accurate mental health diagnoses while maintaining user anonymity.

The worldwide outbreak of COVID-19 brought about a significant increase in infections and deaths, leading to the adoption of unique lockdown strategies in various countries. A different approach was required to manage the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic, which is a highly contagious virus causing respiratory infections that can be deadly. Our research focuses on a mathematical model representing the suppression of epidemic waves through a combination of hospital and healthcare facility actions, individual social behavior, and limited lockdown policies in a mobile population. The study builds on a previous framework by Saez and Gilkey, which described a system's response to lockdown tactics, and incorporates distinct control methods such as contact tracing, testing, screening, early treatment, and social distancing. Our results illustrate how the measures taken by hospitals and other institutions can supplement lockdown policies in reducing epidemic waves, thereby minimizing the pressure on healthcare systems.

This research is focused on the interplay between the Isoscalar Giant Monopole Resonance (ISGMR) and the Isoscalar Giant Quadrupole Resonance (ISGQR) in heavily deformed nuclei. We have employed a microscopic method utilizing the Hartree-Fock-RPA model to investigate the coupling between these two resonances as it pertains to nuclear collective excitation. We found that the degree of coupling depends on the level of nuclear deformation and, when present, it can significantly impact the ISGMR energy structure by causing it to shift towards lower energies. Additionally, our findings indicate that the coupling leads to an intermingling of ISGMR and ISGQR densities which in turn enables the coupling to occur. We observed this intermingling most clearly in regions of high deformation, and we also noticed a specific effect where the ISGMR density becomes split into two distinct components - one that overlaps with the ISGQR and another that lies outside of it. Lastly, our study demonstrates how this coupling affects the peak widths of the energy distributions (collected from the densities of ISMR and ISGQR) and reveals how this phenomenon can be utilized for learning more about nuclear collective excitations in isotopic series of neutron-rich nuclei.

This research involves examining the fine-grained, microscale movement patterns of a solid piece called a disc, which is subjected to a predetermined force and also experiences a "sticky" area where movement is impossible. Similar to studies on stick-slip phenomena in mechanical systems, this study investigates how the presence of the "sticky" region affects the pattern of movement and the areas the disc occupies during these cycles of sticking and sliding. In contrast to prior research, this study focuses on smaller-scale dynamics, known as "stick-and-slip" phenomena, which are characterized by rapid changes in the disc's motion paths. Additionally, this study develops a mathematical model that takes into account the "sticky" area and uses numerical methods to identify and classify different patterns of movement, which are then compared to a similar system with no "sticky" areas to understand how the disc's movement patterns change as a result of sticking and sliding.

The most effectively traded markets are also those with the least obstacles and highest liquidity levels of course, however the intricate nature of financial markets means actual trading costs and market conditions often diverge significantly from their ideal state. This chapter will explore how the presence of hindrances like processing fees, limited liquidity, and other obstacles can be accurately quantified and factored into a trading model, which in turn enables an adaptive framework for developing customized strategies tailored to the specific market conditions and costs associated with each security. The result is a versatile and versatile model capable of handling various magnitudes of trading costs across a broad spectrum of financial instruments. The algorithm's ability to adjust to changing market conditions ensures its decision-making processes remain transparent and easily auditable at all times.

Understanding user intent is vital for delivering personalized experiences, and intent inference has become a cornerstone for guaranteeing user safety in recommender systems. Previous approaches to intent inference were often inflexible, not able to adapt to implicit user actions such as clicking through filters, and required a lot of manual work. This paper introduces a new model called Intent-f, which learns intent in a more collaborative way by using the collective intent of all users sharing the same attribute, like two people from the same city sharing the same interest. This model uses neighbor-based intent inference, where Intent-f's training process emphasizes similarity in shared attributes and group-based intent alignment. During inference, Intent-f's learning process is reversed, translating Intent-f's shared attribute group-based intent alignment to specific user intents. This model's key feature is its ability to identify intent through filtered clicks, requiring no labels whatsover and not relying on explicit user intent. Experimental results demonstrate Intent-f's superiority over current research and its ability to identify intent accurately, even when users click on filters randomly.

The reducible double confluent Heun equation can be simplified into two separate Heun equations, and we do this by making a change of variables that involves only two parameters. By choosing specific values for these parameters, certain instances of the reduced equation become holomorphic within specific regions of the complex plane, leading to non-singular solutions at those points. Two distinct sets of parameter values result in two different types of solutions: one set leads to a solution that is regular within the entire complex plane excluding the origin, and another set results in a solution that has a specific type of asymptotic behavior near the origin. By further transforming the equation, we can make the solution look like a particular type of special function, and we provide explicit formulas based on two distinct types of series reversion. One of these transformations connects the double confluent hypergeometric function with an unusual type of generalized hypergeometric function, and the other connects the double confluent hypergeometric function with a different specialized Fourier series type of hypergeometric function.

In low-rank matrix recovery, PCA is proven to work well for certain types of incoherence conditions and weighted combinations of data, including weighted PCA, which involves combining signals with distinct structures. When these signals are weighted and combined, PCA still successfully recovers the original matrix under specific conditions. This is demonstrated in two scenarios: (1) when the weights stabilize and distribute the data evenly, (2) when the weights cancel out and the data is evenly weighted, resulting in PCA's ability to recover the original matrix. In both cases, the limits on PCA's performance are similar and more restrictive than what is previously known for equally weighted data. This research offers a new understanding and a stronger baseline for comparing PCA to more sophisticated methods, such as maximum likelihood estimation, which is shown to be less effective in certain scenarios. Additionally, PCA's effectiveness is shown to be a'sharp' threshold phenomenon, where it successfully recovers the original matrix below a particular threshold and fails above it.

Recently, it was found that certain classical systems without symmetry still exhibit fractional boundary states. This work shows that these states can also appear in systems that exhibit symmetry but have a constraint that complicates its formulation. Two examples of such systems are discussed - a loop quantum gravity model and a rotating string model - both of which share similarities despite their differing backgrounds, but share a common property of having a symmetric connection and a complicating constraint. Furthermore, a new approach was developed to formulate the evolution of a particle in a circular representation of quantum mechanics, which shares similarities with the aforementioned examples.

We've analyzed potential discrepancies in decay patterns between the Standard Model and certain rare $B$-meso decays that involve the $\Lambda_b$ baryon. Our study focused on two specific types of decays, $\Lambda_b^0$$\to$$\Lambda negative charge particle$ and $\Lambda_b^0$$\to$$\Lambda^0 K^-$, utilizing the LHCb experiment's data. To increase detection reliability, we considered multiple decay pathways and employed a novel method of $\Lambda^0$ tagging based on the time distribution of particles emitted from the $LR$ vertex. The analysis found no evidence contradicting the Standard Model, resulting in the establishment of a 68% confidence level limit on the anomalous branching fraction ratio for a particular decay mode. This research has imposed constraints on several new, effective operators in the low-energy $SU(3)_F$ theory, thereby reducing constraints on $\mathcal{B}(\Lambda_b^0$$\to$$\Lambda negative charge particle)$ relative to the $\Lambda_b^0$$\to$$\Lambda^0 negative charge particle$ mode. Moreover, we've demonstrated that sensitivity to lepton flavour universality violation in $b$$\to$$l^+$ transitions can be significantly enhanced by studying the $\Lambda_b$ baryon's decays into vector and pseudo-vector leptons.

Research on networked control systems (NCSs) has gained significant momentum, and its applications have been recognized as promising. However, the reliability of an adaptive controller based on networked information has not been thoroughly explored. This study focuses on the dynamics of multiple adaptive algorithm iterations and reveals that their behavior follows stable patterns. Specifically, we analyzed 12 distinct adaptive algorithms and found that 7 exhibit linear system behavior that can be managed with appropriate compensation, leading to enhanced stability and resistance to failures. Building on this understanding, we developed a novel controller based on Bass' algorithm for NCSs, leveraging its stable-resilient properties to create a comprehensive framework. Furthermore, we identified key factors influencing the performance of this new controller and verified its efficacy using simulations.

This research presents an image classification framework based on a variety of pre-trained models, which demonstrates a classification accuracy of 96.73% on the NTU RGB+D dataset and 94.94% on its xtreme form. The proposed framework utilizes a combination of pre-trained models as feature extractors, with different architectures including VGG, ResNet, Inception, and others. By selecting five basic models and 28 composite forms, the framework achieves optimal performance with a specific configuration, consisting of two composite models. Furthermore, the study includes a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed framework's performance across 60 distinct human action types.

The widespread occurrence of complex networks in both natural and engineered systems has established them as a significant area of study across numerous disciplines. As a result, an open analytical toolbox was created, combining discrete and continuous tools, to aid in understanding complex systems and their behaviors. This comprehensive toolkit is designed for use by both experts in network science, researchers, and students, to support their work. A corresponding set of tutorials, available online, offers step-by-step guidance for getting started with the toolkit.

The heatwave that Australia is experiencing has sparked severe wildfires nationwide.
Wildfires in the southern hemisphere of Earth are primarily driven by similar climate-induced factors as those in the northern hemisphere, leading to the degradation of local biodiversity.
Yet, the extreme fires bring about a unique evolutionary opportunity.
A recent study focuses on the interplay between ecological and evolutionary processes under the intense heat of the wildfires.
The researchers used a complex model of metapopulations, accounted for demographic changes, and applied natural selection and genetic diversity metrics to understand the dynamic interactions between population survival and their genetic makeup.
The analysis shows that higher temperatures, a larger population, and greater sensitivity to temperature and genetic diversity lead to a higher likelihood of ecological and evolutionary convergence.
Ultimately, the study's findings emphasize the critical need for comprehensive conservation efforts that account for the intricate connections between ecological and evolutionary processes, especially in the face of catastrophic climate events like the widespread wildfires in the southern hemisphere.

Machine learning-based speech representation models are now widely used in a range of applications, but they have a critical security flaw. They can be easily manipulated by an adversary with various levels of expertise, which is why it's essential to understand how to effectively defend these models against such attacks. In our study, we've limited our focus to adversarial attacks on speech representation models and developed a new system to generate adversarial examples using human speech. Our research involves three different types of attackers with distinct levels of knowledge and a range of challenges, including an anonymous attacker who doesn't know the specific speech representation model being used, a professional attacker with access to the model's architecture, and an advanced adversary who has access to the model's training data. Our analysis shows that all three types of attackers are able to successfully target speech representation models, using either unpaired or paired speech as the input, using our newly proposed methods. Our results also reveal key features of the generated adversarial examples, including their similarity to regular speech, the impact of their length, and the effectiveness of different detection methods in identifying such attacks. Our study not only provides valuable insights for future research but also highlights the critical need for more effective security measures to protect speech representation models from such threats.

Decentralized finance (DEF) has recently gained significant attention, with Automated Market Makers (AMMs) being a cornerstone of DEF, enabling users to swap tokens on the blockchain. They work by using a pricing curve computed from a weighted average formula, but the curve has inherent inaccuracies due to its reliance on limited parameters. Our study delves into the characteristics of this curve, showing how its inaccuracies affect users. We found that the pricing curve has inherent flaws, impacting arbitrage costs, investor surpluses, and the trade-off between liquidity and arbitrage. Our investigation also uncovered additional flaws, revealing that the pricing curve has inaccuracies when accounting for arbitrage costs and its impact on the game-theoretical equilibrium of the Pools-Arbitrageurs system. These findings will contribute positively if used to identify areas for improvement in the current AMM model.

Causal inference has a established connection with information theory. Recent advancements allowing for the evaluation of a causal conclusion's reliability have focused on incorporating these principles. We introduce an innovative measure, the E-value, capable of assessing the robustness of a causal conclusion in the presence of missing data. This new measure is equivalent to the fraction of targeted probability distributions within a specific parameter space, where the causal conclusion remains valid. We develop an algorithm for estimating the E-value using data and explore its relationship with other crucial concepts such as probability coverage and confidence levels. Our study also includes a thorough examination of the E-value's asymptotic properties. We illustrate the practical application of this new measure through both theoretical analysis and practical examples, showcasing how the E-value can facilitate a more thorough understanding of a causal conclusion by considering multiple assumptions simultaneously.

The extended quantum plane $\mathbb{C}_q\left[x^{\pm 1}, y^{\pm 1}\right]$, incorporating elements of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries, is presented, and its relation to the $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-module algebra $\mathbb{C}_q\left[x^{\pm 1}, y^{\pm 1}\right]_{\Lambda}^{(m)}$ is investigated. The ring of invariants under the action of the center $Z(U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2))$, and the degenerate case of the quantum plane when the action of $Z(U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2))$ simplifies, are discussed along with the generated integrals of motion. A study on how $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries introduce weights and multipliers is also performed. Furthermore, the effect of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries on the highest weight $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-modules, the module-algebra $\mathbb{C}_q\left[x^{\pm 1}, y^{\pm 1}\right]_{\Lambda}^{(m)}$, and its dependence on the parameters $q, \Lambda, m \in \math

The emergence of Blockchain technology has significant implications for data security and privacy within the context of Internet of Vehicles (IoVs). Notably, a public ledgers system for IoVs holds promise of safeguarding user privacy by ensuring that shared data are anonymized and distributed securely. Nonetheless, existing solutions that combine public ledgers with IoVs are vulnerable to anonymizing attacks, thereby compromising user privacy. In this research paper, a novel solution addressing these vulnerabilities is proposed, which incorporates a cutting-edge deep neural network-based anonymizing system to enhance resilience against anonymizing attacks. Furthermore, the proposed approach utilizes a local discriminator to validate the integrity of smart contract nodes and promotes data security within the public ledgers framework. Performance evaluations utilizing real-world data validate the efficacy of the proposed system.

Using our fragmentation functions for heavy quarks, we have analyzed the strange meson production in $e^+e^-$ annihilation, specifically for mesons $\mathrm K^*$, $\phi$, $\rho^0$, $\rho^+$, and $\rho^-$. Our fragmentation predictions for heavy quarks are compared with experimental data collected at the B-factory Belle collider. We find that the fragmentation of heavy quarks to strange mesons is significantly higher than to non-strange mesons, with an exception for the fragmentation to $\rho^0$ and $\rho^-$, which is lower than expected. Furthermore, the fragmentation of beauty quarks to $\phi$ is notably lower than that of charm quarks to $\phi$. Our results are in line with experimental data, providing an accurate description of $\mathrm D^*$ and $\Lambda$ production. We also provide the first theoretical explanation for the $|\bar{d}/\bar{u}|$ ratio, influenced by the wave functions of mesons and the quark masses. These calculations are in agreement with experimental meson production data, thus validated.

Evaluating the effect of programmer error on program misuse is crucial in understanding why certain programs, even those designed by experts, utilize insecure encryption functions despite being aware of their vulnerabilities. By contrasting the interface of popular Python, Java, and C crypto libraries used by experts across three fields - web applications, cryptography, and network programming - this study identifies significant variations in API design that contribute to a higher likelihood of accidental misuse in Python due to its intuitive design. The comparison reveals that Python's ease of use, reflected in fewer functions and clearer naming conventions in its crypto library, initially appears beneficial, however, leads experts to overlook the significance of secure encryption mechanisms. As a result, this study suggests that an appealing and user-friendly interface can inadvertently encourage experts to make critical security mistakes by hiding relevant security considerations. The findings suggest that conscious designer choices can have unforeseen consequences and should be taken into consideration when designing interfaces to prevent security vulnerabilities. The study's source code is available for review at https://github.com/explore-applied-security/expert_study.

Three-dimensional image reconstruction from two-dimensional data like images, scans, and feeds has significant cost and time implications when applied across large areas. In particular, using aerial images to create high-resolution 3D models of small areas is feasible but becomes impractical for larger scales due to the volume of data and high processing times. To enhance workflow efficiency, multiple smaller areas can be processed in parallel, but effective partitioning is crucial to ensure fair workloads and efficient use of resources. Therefore, this research aims to develop an algorithm for optimal division of 2D image data into smaller sections with varying sizes, which can then be processed independently and in parallel, minimizing the overall processing time. In a practical application, this algorithm was tested using UAV-captured images and showed promising results in reducing computation times and improving fairness across different workloads.

A method for enhancing the recovery of reflection coefficients from near-surface data is developed by framing the recovery process as a sparse synthesis-based inverse problem with a non-uniform and non-convex synthesis model. Utilizing the fact that major subsurface reflection coefficients are typically compacted, we apply a non-convex optimization to obtain original wavelet coefficients, specifically, to maximize their p-hold and soft-masking terms while constraining them within a pre-determined range. Through numerical experiments involving synthetic and real data, we showcase the efficacy of this novel approach in specific land-terracotta geophysical applications.

The situation is examined where a Mobius transformation of the unit disk maps the Bergman space's  L_p norm onto the Moebius invariant Banach space BMOA_p for 1 < p < 2. It's demonstrated that the compactness of the mapping T_g involves the compactness of T_g in BMOA_p, a concept proven to be consistent in the range 1 < p < 2. Building on these findings, the mapping T_g is investigated for its compactness within BMOA to BMOA_p for 1 < p < 2 and its connection to B(M(g,B_p)) in BMOA_p. The case when p = 2 is left unresolved.

A recent study demonstrated the use of low-energy wavefunction overlaps to compute conformal data for specific quantum spin chains with SU(2) symmetry. Building on this work, we now apply the same method to calculate conformal data for certain SU(N) spin chains with extended N=4 fluxes, which necessitate utilizing gauge-symmetry-invariant operators to achieve this goal. Furthermore, we calculate the critical exponents for a representative model featuring SU(3) spin chains with N=4 flux and obtain analogous results for spin chains with N=2 fluxes in comparison. Additionally, we conduct an experiment to map the phase diagram of the N=4 flux model using the density-matrix renormalization group method.

Traditional machine learning techniques for part-of-speech tagging fail when they encounter unfamiliar words, since they are based on patterns recognition. Our approach integrates set-valued prediction into neural networks, enabling them to provide a range of possible tags for unknown words along with confidence levels for each option. As a result, our model can either choose one tag or multiple tags, depending on the level of confidence provided. We tested our model's performance using Wikipedia and Treebank datasets, and the outcome showed that it offers more accurate predictions than existing models, accompanied by a more reliable measure of uncertainty. Moreover, our model's level of uncertainty can be utilized as a criterion for quality assessment and word classification.

To determine if a sequence of non-negative, separately continuous demand functions converges to a continuous demand function, we must establish that the sequence's limit function is non-negative and satisfy a specific condition known as homotheticity. This result has significant implications in various fields, including general equilibrium theory and the study of externalities. Meanwhile, the question of whether a sequence of homogeneous, non-residual demand functions converges to a homogeneous demand function remains an open inquiry in the field of theory of specifications.

In smart cities, people's lives are increasingly intertwined with urban services delivered through IoT deployments, which necessitate reliable, real-time monitoring beyond traditional human interaction. To effectively manage these smart cities and IoT infrastructures, an unambiguous and continuously updated picture of city and IoT element conditions is essential. Unfortunately, existing monitoring systems often struggle with the ambiguity and uncertainty inherent in manually specified requirements, hindering effective service delivery. To address these challenges, this research introduces a groundbreaking framework for monitoring smart cities and IoT deployments, which leverages AI and fuzzy logic to rapidly develop and deploy inference models, allowing for seamless adaptation to shifting requirements, straightforward integration with diverse city and IoT data sources, and providing actionable recommendations in both predictive and real-time contexts. The proposed framework has been effectively implemented as a prototype, which has been successfully tested and validated in real-world settings across two distinct domains: smart transportation and environmental monitoring.

To mitigate noise in near-term quantum computers, we've developed a method to adapt the variational quantum eigensolver algorithm for calculating ground states and eigenvalues of complex Hamiltonians. This adaptation incorporates a noise-reduction scheme that limits error propagation, thus significantly improving the accuracy of its results. Our research includes a detailed explanation of this approach, along with numerical experiments that demonstrate the significant efficiency and accuracy gain provided by this protection mechanism.

Under the conditions of $R_{<\omega,\infty}>$ on a regular category or $L_{<\omega,\infty>}$ on a topos, we can guarantee the existence of meaningful results including cartesian images and suprema within categories that include a finite partial order. Specifically, for categories with a finite partial order, we can confirm the existence of meaningful images and suprema within categories that include a finite partial order. These conditions not only apply to categories that include a finite partial order but also provide new information about categories that do not have a finite partial order but have other desirable properties such as n-permutability.

Using satellite data from Metop, wind speed, wave height, and frequency data from BUFR, we investigate the occurrences of extreme events such as damaging winds and large wave heights. We apply an improved version of the main effect method to identify areas where severe weather is more likely to happen. By using maximum likelihood estimation, we quantify the distances over which extreme weather is more likely to occur. Specifically, we analyze how wind speed and wave height correlate with each other, and how they conditionally correlate with Metop wind speed. The results reveal that severe weather phenomena typically fall within a 1000 to 5000 km range, but large-scale areas of 5000 to 10000 km can also be affected. Furthermore, we discover that the occurrence of extreme wave heights within a given area is more dependent on wind speed further away from that area than it is on wind speed closest to that area.

Within the realm of visual-language partnerships, determining how texts and images relate to each other is vital, yet defining and measuring visual-content relevance remains a challenge due to the absence of standardized criteria. Our solution involves refining the pre-trained CLIP model by incorporating Visual-guided Texts, words learned alongside images during pre-training, to serve as labels for cross-modal comparison. This results in an enhanced CLIP model, Vision-CLIP, capable of accurately differentiating visual content based on single words rather than entire images. Specifically, fine-tuning Vision-CLIP on Visual-guided Texts yields an 87.5% accuracy gain over the base CLIP model on the VGG16-birds-1k benchmark, while also performing strongly on other benchmarks like VGG16-1m and VGG16-Rubik. Notably, our model can effectively analyze a bird's identity simply by looking at a small patch of its beak. Moreover, we discovered that using Visual-guided Texts as labels significantly boosts the model's capacity to recognize images, even when those images were viewed during pre-training was not possible. This was possible due to the Visual-guided Texts learning to represent the visual contents that were easily identifiable, thereby serving as a reliable and precise image descriptor. In other words, they function as a tiny, image-based dictionary. To facilitate further research, we will be sharing our Visual-guided Texts and the resulting Vision-CLIP model with the research

In the context of matrix inverse estimation, where the goal is to find the best fit for a given set of measurements, noise level and direction of perturbation when data is imperfect, researchers have considered different approaches. When assuming symmetric noise, a specific optimal direction is suggested, but this consensus is disputed by new findings which show that different norm minimization methods yield distinct, opposing optimal directions under asymmetric noise conditions, leading to a divergence in solution outcomes. Furthermore, when dealing with a range of noise levels, rather than a fixed value, optimal solutions exist and are linearly related, suggesting that averaging these disparate solutions may be beneficial. Lastly, as an application of matrix inverse estimation, we examine the inverse of the Hadamard matrix, specifically focusing on its columns and drawing connections to other areas of study, such as deep neural networks and sparse modeling.

By linking derived functors of local systems of abelian groups with certain types of Mackey functors, a key aspect of equivariant stable homotopy theory, the text establishes a crucial corollary. Furthermore, the text demonstrates how Flum's work on equivariant rational homotopy theory can be utilized to create a category of "rational" Mackey functors.

We show that the zero submodule of local cohomology relative to a prime ideal
is directly related to the existence of a specific test function that indicates the
F-rationality of a local ring. Furthermore, our results provide the exact composition
of three key modules, one of which appears in the local cohomology theory and the
other two are related to symbolic cohomology, over a prime ideal. Additionally, we
prove that the depth of the zero submodule of local cohomology relative to a prime
ideal equals the symbolic multiplicity of the prime ideal when it serves as a reduction
modulo a parameter. Lastly, we establish a connection between the zero submodule
of local cohomology relative to a prime ideal and the parameter test for F-rationality
in local rings with a single imperfection.

The use of deep learning in radiology has become increasingly prominent, despite many models failing to meet expectations when used internationally due to differences in data imaging methods. To address this, the developers of a Python library called highdicom are merging imaging metadata standards with the advanced capabilities of Python's scientific community. By integrating tools like the DICOM standard and PyDICOM, highdicom facilitates the conversion between metadata formats and the extraction of key information, ultimately enabling the seamless integration of ML models across various country-based datasets.

Diffeomorphisms play a vital role in maintaining the integrity and specifying properties of the event horizon in general relativity, particularly when applied to asymptotically flat spaces. We investigate and confirm that they indeed leave the horizon invariant, albeit in a manner dependent on the stage of penetration into the horizon. We further explore how the equation of motion for charged black holes is reflected within the horizon framework and how the inner product of perturbations, primarily driven by mass and charge perturbations, varies across the horizon, specifically highlighting a key functional based on this inner product and charged black hole parameters. We demonstrate that this functional is finite and its expression can be determined through a mode analysis of perturbations near the horizon.

Our results demonstrate that deep learning models with carefully optimized splice and deep architectures can improve performance in spliceomics-based cancer classification tasks. A DNA classification task was used to validate the transferability of splice signatures learned from a more complex classification task involving multiple cancer types. Analysis of these signatures revealed both known and unknown regions of DNA, some of which are linked to cancer-related biological processes across different cancer types, as revealed by enrichment analysis. The undirected graphical model used for analysis noted significant connections to cancer-related genes and pathways, providing novel insights for further scientific investigation.

A transition from an insulating to a metallic state occurs in doped 2D Hubbard models with a finite correlation coefficient, as demonstrated by the absence of a spectral weight gap and the breaking of a specific sum rule that describes the transition.  This change happens quickly as the temperature decreases and can be split into two parts which differ in their behavior, each representing a distinct type of excitations in the system.  One part corresponds to a type of excitations that behave in an orderly fashion in terms of the exchange of momentum, the other part corresponds to a type of excitates that behave in an orderly fashion in terms of the exchange of holes, both of these portions exhibit breaks in their respective sum rules.  Further separation of these portions reveals that the breaks in their respective sum rules occur at different temperatures, as well as hinting at the idea that the breaks in spectral weight may occur in an orderly fashion as well.  Complementary studies using exact diagonalization of finite systems also confirm that the breaks in spectral weight occur smoothly and continuously during the transition from an insulating to a metallic state, and that the breaks in spectral weight may occur in an orderly fashion as well.

We have intentionally introduced a collective framework for constructing time-reversible symplectic integrators of Hamiltonian systems with a Lie-Poisson structure, aiming to extend existing methods that only work with linearly momentum-covariant integrators. This new approach naturally retains coadjoint orbits and Casimirs, and can seamlessly incorporate collective phase space preservation, making it a viable option. Our method provides a promising way to develop reusable multiple shuttle tools, enabling local modifications to smooth flows, and may have applications in solving partial differential equations. To demonstrate its capabilities, we have successfully implemented and tested our approach for two Lie-Poisson systems and two fluid models, achieving good results.

To compare various algorithms for detecting planets in microlensing events, we conducted a simulation study. We employed several methods to dispose of 20 common known planets within a portfolio of 100 microlensing lightcurves. The algorithms then indicated potential planets, and we compared their performance across a range of criteria, including accuracy rates, the ability to identify existing planets, and relevant detection parameters. The results revealed that discovering planets with lower mass ratios requires different approaches than those with higher mass ratios. Further analysis involved fitting models to the lightcurves to recycle detectability parameters, yielding consistent results and demonstrating the importance of eliminating common known planets effectively to enhance detectability. The most recent public software for microlensing analysis was also evaluated, with our study revealing that it struggles to detect planets with low mass ratios, primarily due to issues related to eliminating common known planets.

We create an explicit solution procedure for the most straightforward form of an implicitly defined approximated conservation equation, a method which can be extended to more complex approximations as well. This paper primarily focuses on the approximated conservation equation $\partial_t u + \Delta \Phi(u) = 0$ using the exponential time integration method. Our new approach contrasts existing solutions which convert the approximated equation into its fully implicit approximate solution, leading to a system of linear equations that is equivalent to our direct solution approach but much slower due to increased dimensionality. Additionally, we introduce an extension that combines our approach with the exponential time integration method in a way that maintains explicitness even when the approximated equation is highly accurate. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach with various approximations and even work with schemes that involve approximated flux limiter functions.

The perspective of a bank is explored to examine the issue of predicting default loans. Focus is placed on developing accurate models to forecast NPLs for a pool of existing customers, as well as exploring ways to differentiate between defaulting and non-defaulting clients. Various machine learning models are tested, including a random forest approach, a gradient boosting model, a support vector machine, and a neural network, using data from approximately 900,000 clients. Results indicate that a random forest model offers the best combination of predictive ability and data resilience, particularly when using a 12-month time frame for the NPL forecast. Moreover, with nearly complete data availability, nearly perfect differentiation is possible between defaulting and non-defaulting clients in the dataset, achieved through various feature sets and models. Ultimately, findings suggest that a neural network-based model, trained on detailed credit application features, can successfully mimic the judgment call made by an experienced credit officer when evaluating a new customer for loans.
We present novel $q$-analogues of chromatic symmetric functions for $B$-partitions, establishing connections to $q$-hit numbers and $q$-elementary symmetric functions through intriguing identities.

In recent years, various techniques have sought to mitigate the orientation challenges inherent in deep network training, such as using steady and orientation-insensitive image representations. A novel method for combatting orientation issues is presented in this research, where Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs) are employed to enhance the robustness of deep network-based image representations to orientation changes. The research indicates that Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs) achieve an optimal balance between a reduced number of filters to learn and increased robustness levels. The research further showcases the efficacy of LGFs in enhancing deep network-based image representation robustness by using the ST-LCNT model on the SHILAB, CUB-200, and ILRS datasets. The results reveal a substantial improvement in classification robustness in these datasets with the incorporation of LGFs.

The relative fundamental lemma serves as a key corollary to the orbit convergence theorem, significantly bolstering its implications across various mathematical scenarios, notably including the study of reductive group algebras and their properties. Furthermore, this lemma has crucial applications within the context of building blocks for relative algebraic tori and iterated root subgroups, with implications extending to the study of orbital integrals, as well as the construction of relative tori through a process of ind-scheme ind-etalification. Notably, as part of the developing "Diacu-Mumford program", this unitary relative tori construction will have far-reaching implications in the field of topological application, notably within the study of the quotient space of MMOD by its commutative Lie algebra. Thus, the proof of the relative fundamental lemma is pivotal in this broader mathematical framework.

Our point of departure begins with the distillation of the renormalization group formalism into a framework that illuminates how current RG trajectories can be derived from the combinations of heavier and lighter quark masses. By utilizing this approach based on the MSbar scheme, we generate a set of one-loop matching coefficients for the transitions between heavy top and charm quarks and their lighter counterparts. Additionally, our analysis involves analyzing various decay processes such as $t\to t$, $t\to c$, $c\to c$, and $c\to u$ along with deriving formulae for the wave function and mass renormalization, all up to one-loop order in QCD.

A sublinear time, almost linear time algorithm is proposed for coloring a graph's edges with up to $k$ colors when the graph meets a criterion for its degree difference. Specifically, the algorithm requires input parameters $\epsilon > 0$, the number of desired colors $k$, and an integer $\Delta \geq 2$, subject to the condition that the ratio of a vertex's maximum and minimum degree in the graph $\mathcal{G}$ deviates from 1 by at most $1/\sqrt{3}$. As a result, the algorithm offers edge-colorings that use at most $k$ colors, with an indicated running time of $O((k+\log n)(\frac{\log n}{\log \log n})^\frac{2}{3}(1+\frac{\log \log n}{\log n})^\frac{2}{3})$ and a constant $\epsilon>0$. Furthermore, the algorithm has a known approximation ratio of $1-\epsilon$, and it is known to take $O(k(n^{1+\frac{2}{\log \log n}})(\log n)^{-2\frac{\log \log 2}{\log 2}})$ time when $k$ is not a perfect power of two. Additionally, the algorithm has similar edge-coloring properties as a previous algorithm proposed by Fox, Straszkiewicz, and Zivny, with comparable running times and degree difference criteria.
