This article delves into the weighted Bergman spaces over the unit disk, focusing on the polynomials and power series that compose these spaces and examining necessary and sufficient conditions under which they are comprised solely of orosztochstvennyh polynomials, in relation to specific growth conditions and with respect to their Cesaro and Laplace transforms.

This research paper introduces a versatile, open-source framework called ClinDI for training Deep Learning models that use clinical data and image material to make a diagnosis. ClinDI focuses on demonstrating the potential benefits of integrating clinical data into AI models for accurate virus and pneumonia detection. The framework's first application involves a multi-task model that combines chest X-ray analysis to detect COVID-19, influenza, and pneumonia, which delivers a high degree of precision with an AUC of 0.923. By leveraging its capacity for incorporating diverse clinical datasets, ClinDI was able to enhance the sensitivity and accuracy of the model by 12% and 7%, respectively. Furthermore, the study develops a new baseline for single-view chest X-ray diagnostics with an AUC of 0.913. ClinDI features a user-friendly, modular design that enables easy data preparation, model integration, and deployment, and is designed to support a wide variety of pre-trained models by using a uniform data interface. The software's open-source code facilitates its easy replication for various tasks, while its user-friendly design makes it suitable for developers, clinicians, and research institutions.

As the popularity of low-earth orbit communication satellite megaconstellations increases, the need for more efficient satellite design arises. In an effort to minimize costs, reducing the overall size of a megaconstitution while maintaining its functionality becomes a crucial consideration. The main concern lies in avoiding collisions and maintaining clear line-of-sight communications, which can be achieved by implementing minimum space occupancy orbits. The concept of MiSO orbits was first introduced as a means to restrict satellite formations to specific areas of space, thus allowing for tighter control over the overall formation size. The usual approach to defining MiSO orbits relies on computationally expensive methods that are poorly suited for megasatellite designs. In this study, a new framework for defining MiSO orbits using alternative optimization methods is presented along with the introduction of a software tool called miso-formation. The results show a significant reduction in computation time, making it more feasible to design and analyze the formations. Furthermore, the results demonstrate the capability of alternating optimization to closely approximate the results of more complex algorithms and the effectiveness of the miso-formation tool in generating physically realizable MiSO orbits that allow for substantial size reductions of megaconstitutions.

In mesh generation, manually configuring regional mesh layouts can be a time-consuming task. To streamline this process, we propose an automated system for generating quadrilateral meshes based on given data. The proposed method starts with a T-mesh construction that allows for straightforward and efficient quad layouts. Subsequently, an algorithmic process is employed to convert the T-mesh into a full-fledged quadrilateral mesh. The method further incorporates a detailed analysis to assess and ensure the quality of resulting meshes. The proposed approach excels at linearly refining initially smooth meshes, achieving high-quality quadrilateral meshes with exceptional properties. Notably, it operates within a reasonable time frame even for intricate domains. Additional experiments are also presented to demonstrate the method's capabilities and optimizations.

When evaluating the validity of statistical models, p-values are utilized as a measure of model performance. They're typically derived under the assumption that the data follows a specific distribution, but this isn't always the case. In the context of bivariate normal distributions, p-values can be approximated by comparing simulated values to the data, using either random quantities or density estimates. This paper introduces new techniques for approximating p-values in scenarios where the data doesn't follow a bivariate normal distribution. It also presents methods for combining p-values from multiple directions, thereby assessing the overall validity of a statistical model. These novel approaches are exemplified through a real-world study of aircraft stall and upset incidents.

A method based on QED's $S$-matrix approach is developed to calculate QED boundary conditions on black-hole spacetimes with arbitrary metrics, which cannot be treated with the traditional Kruskal metric in the asymptotic region. Although certain non-asymptotic regions of these black-hole metrics are similar to those found in Schwarzschild spacetime, a new approach is necessary for the study of black-hole physics with arbitrary couplings and masses. We derive a set of rules for calculating QED boundary conditions on mirror surfaces within the black-body horizon of the black-hole spacetime through the $S$-matrix approach, which is validated for various couplings and masses and also extended to the case of double null coordinates. We further utilize this new method to study "quasi-photons" - particles of arbitrary mass coupled to the electromagnetic field - and examine the influence of back-reaction in the case of a massless scalar quasi-photon, which yields a finite "tunneling" amplitude. Consequently, a new interpretation of the "tunneling" amplitude in the context of back-reaction has been developed.

The study provides a spectral analysis of unstable equilibria in the Navier-Stokes equations using feedback controls, focusing on the geometric properties of Navier-Stokes dynamics near unstable configurations. It demonstrates the exponential stability of solutions under full-state local feedback control when the operator is a Maxwell iteration, but does not apply to biharmonic operators. Additionally, it shows that unstable dynamics can be stabilized with targeted feedback controls localized in a small neighborhood, as small as a single control point, near certain types of unstable configurations.

Mind mapping tools can be visually impressive, offering a comprehensive understanding of concepts and their connections, as seen in products such as Xmind, XMind, and MindMeister. However, these commercial tools come with a subscription cost. A free, open-source alternative is provided by Mind Mapping Tools like Freemind (Java-based, with a dated user interface) and MindMeister (with limited, paid features). In response, we've developed LitMind, a free, open-source software, written in Java, featuring a modern UI and enriching ideas with linguistic insights. LitMind incorporates a dictionary that draws from definitions sourced from Lexopen, a trustworthy and legible dictionary that covers both English and Spanish dictionaries, ensuring that Mind maps are filled with accurate, readable definitions. LitMind enables users to automatically enrich their mind maps by integrating external data sources such as Wikipedia, enabling them to understand the broader context of noted ideas and concepts. With its integration of lexical semantics, LitMind delves into the subtleties of word meanings, including synonyms, antonyms, and more. Additionally, LitMind allows for automatic enrichment using user-provided keywords, including technical terms and part-of-speech specifications, as such as "Mobile network operator" and "NOUN" respectively. Using this data, LitMind automatically suggests relevant words, such as "3G," "4G," and "skyscraper," displayed along with their definitions, synonyms, and antonyms.

The use of explanations to clarify black-box models in recommender systems has seen significant advancement, with a focus on understanding and interpreting the decision-making processes of users. Despite existing measures for evaluating the quality of explanations, little research has been carried out to assess the reliability of models that produce these explanations, with reliance on methods like backcasting and post-hoc approaches being shown to be vulnerable to flaws. Backcasting relies on user feedback to reconstruct the features used by a black-box model, but is susceptible to inaccuracies, with post-hoc explanations being based on the predictive capabilities of the model, with a large gap often existing between the two. By applying a robust formal assessment framework, our study reveals the shortcomings of current explanation and evaluation methods, with our framework consisting of an evaluation phase that uses public data and a testing phase with simultaneous access to the same data. Using this framework, our findings indicate that existing measures for evaluating explanation quality and model reliability are inadequate, with a proposed new metric being developed to address this issue, with future research being needed to improve the understanding of the relationship between the quality of explanations and the reliability of models that produce them.

Research on how the macroscopic electric shape of an electric field influences the electronic properties of a two-dimensional electron system is ongoing. Yet, achieving control over this electric field with pinpoint accuracy remains difficult. Our study discovers that by integrating a thin capping layer with an adjustable work function into a semiconductor structure, we can precisely control the electron density and the location of the surface Fermi level. We employed two types of capping layers, InAs and In$_{0.81}$Al$_{0.19}$As, which exhibit minor differences in their electron subband occupations. Our findings reveal that only the capping layer containing indium is able to move the surface Fermi level as far as 10 nanometers below its initial position. We also observed a significant decrease in the electron density as a result of forming two-dimensional ferromagnetic domains. We were able to achieve the highest domain control with the assistance of the indium-containing capping layer, resulting in a domain period of 50 nanometers.

This paper provides new results on robust learning. Firstly, it proves the minimal radius of a query needed to perform robust learning within a given class of concepts - this involves challenging any algorithm's ability to distinguish between two datasets that may or may not contain an instance of a concept. Secondly, it shows there are different minimum radii of a query that achieves this robust learning within the same class of concepts. Lastly, it categorizes several important concept classes based on the largest possible radius of a query that may still allow for robust learning within those classes.

The FS-2 algorithm, a derivative of the Sinkhorn algorithm, accelerates optimal transport computations by leveraging the Nyström method to approximate pairwise distances in any given dataset. It calculates an efficient estimate of the pairwise distances in subspace, using only the k nearest neighbors, thus significantly reducing computational resources, especially in dealing with large scale datasets. FS-2 incorporates this approximation into a simplified two-step procedure for solving the dual problem of the Sinkhorn algorithm, while maintaining its dual-dialogue proximity property. Consequently, it guarantees the convergence to the true OT solution under the same conditions as the Sinkhorn algorithm. FS-2 also introduces a heuristic termination criterion, which limits the number of iterations by minimizing the last change in the transport plan. Experimental results show that FS-2 surpasses the Sinkhorn algorithm in efficiency, particularly when dealing with complex datasets.

The characteristics of the companion to AU Mic, a low-mass AE star, are largely unchanged due to weak mass loss through its atmosphere. However, powerful solar flares cause a brief increase in the system's mass loss rate. Using observations from the James Webb Space Telescope, we analyzed the mass loss rate from AU Mic's companion with unprecedented detail. This process allowed us to refine our understanding of the mass loss process in binary systems with intense stellar activity. Even with the precision of the JWST, direct evidence of mass loss from AU Mic's companion was challenging to confirm. Instead, we identified subtle gas patterns in our data, suggesting mass loss occurs at a $\approx 2.6 \times 10^{10}$ g s$^{-1}$ rate, slightly lower than previously predicted. This finding implies any accretion onto the companion is likely to occur at a lower efficiency than previously estimated. During the JWST observations, the mass loss rate remained steady at $\approx 10^{8}$ g s$^{-1}$, similar to previous Telescopes. Future data from the JWST will determine if the mass loss rate consistently remains steady between observations.

We offer a comprehensive explanation for the phenomenon where radiation pressure creates a warped matter environment that results in a substantial, direction-dependent force known as radiation friction. This effect significantly alters the motion of particles in a medium that generates a lot of radiation, such as in the formation of relativistic jets from black holes. We apply our findings to understand the movement of particles in astrophysical jets produced by black holes and nuclei. Our study marks the first occurrence where particle motion has been shown to significantly impact the characteristics of flows in multiple phases.

This research introduces an enhanced ensemble approach tailored for handling imbalanced datasets that combines multiple under-sampling techniques. Three novel classifiers, specifically Majority Vote, KNN, and SVM, are proposed to address the issue of class imbalance, as they are less affected by minority class overfitting. In contrast to traditional oversampling methods that introduce artificial examples into the dataset, the proposed method extracts a reduced representation of the majority class to balance the distribution of data points. Unlike other under-sampling methods that randomly remove majority class examples, the presented method employs K-means clustering to identify and remove minority class examples. We claim that this method can successfully preserve crucial information in the minority class without compromising its distribution. Experimental evaluations using 29 UCI datasets and 33 UCI datasets with random forest and AdaBoost architectures demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in handling imbalanced datasets.

Twenty-five unique Southern QSOs at redshift values above 6, discovered through heterodyne Owens Valley Radio Observatory radio observations, were found along with seven previously identified QSOs from the South Pole Telescope survey (z>6) which also met specific radio and infrared criteria. By incorporating multi-frequency spectral analysis, the spectral energy distributions for fourteen newly discovered QSOs and seven previously identified ones were created and subsequently used to calculate their bolometric luminosities, absolute magnitudes, and Eddington ratios. The QSO sample spans a wide range of absolute magnification from 44.3 to 17.4 and 10^30 to 10^33 Jy on the log-log scale. The QSOs in this study exhibit a mean bolometric luminosity of 4.4 x 10^30 erg s^-1 and 1.6 times the Eddington limit. The QSOs' luminosity distribution shows comparable properties to prior studies and a mean luminosity comparable to twice the predicted luminosity from the gamma=2 power-law model at z=6. The QSOs' luminosity and Eddington ratio tend to decrease as lookback angle increases. Future radio observations are necessary to define the relationship between radio and mid-infrared emission in QSOs at z>6.

The interplay between quantum dots and superconductors offers a chance to explore unordinary quantum systems, which has motivated numerous studies using the Andreev scattering process to analyze the quantum dot's behavior. Despite this, there's still a lack of understanding in controlling the quantum dot's properties to characterize the superconductor's energy landscape. Our research reveals that a quantum dot can serve as an efficient sensor to describe the superconductor's interfacial energy spectrum by manipulating its transmission coefficients. Our findings show that the quantum dot's charge neutrality point and critical charge value correspond to two significant points in the superconductor's energy landscape, known as the 'adding gap' and the 'adding gap's threshold value. Through Andreev analysis, we find that these three values are related to different parameters of the superconductor's energy spectrum. By using the Green's function formalism and solving self-consistently any of these three parameters, we can precisely calculate the interfacial density of states ( DOS$_{if}$) of the superconductor. Benefiting from recent advancements in growing quantum dots around nanoscale materials, our theoretical predictions offer a potential route to experimentally verify the superconductor's energy landscape through transport measurements. Furthermore, our research expands the previously proposed dephasing time approximation by providing a general expression for the quantum dot's phase relaxation time in terms of different elements of the self-energy matrix.

Our investigation centers around the formation of shocks in two-dimensional, isentropic magnetohydrodynamics and their non-linear interactions.  We begin by re-examining some well-established properties of 2D isentropic hydrodynamics regarding the physical space behavior of two-dimensional simple waves, specifically the contraction properties which serve as a fundamental foundation for understanding and modeling the behavior of shocks.  Although these contraction properties have some useful applications, they become unreliable under certain specific shock configurations.  We then proceed to explore the application of water waves, which results in more accurate estimates of shock sizes, but also raise additional valid concerns about shock dynamics, prompting an investigation into the broader class of inviscid shallow water equations.  We also touch on a related mathematical challenge related to smooth wave interactions in various inviscid fluids and their potential connection to magnetohydrodynamics.

The objective of perpetual view generation is to create an endless, horizon-to-horizon video sequence depiction of a scene observed from a fixed vantage point, accounting for both camera motion and occlusions resulting from objects in the scene. Building upon the CVPR 2020 paper, this code supplement provides detailed implementation details for two neural network-based solutions for this challenge, alongside a benchmark evaluation protocol on the widely accessible Waymo driving dataset.

In large-scale systems, model predictive control consistently produces optimal outcomes but is hindered by the computational difficulties of repeatedly solving the constrained optimization problem. Research has focused on reducing computational demands, such as using the Koopman operator to approximate system dynamics or applying special structures in constraints. While Koopman-based approaches can offer computational advantages, they typically generate multiple local suboptimal solutions, and the most suitable solution must still be determined. We propose a novel method that leverages the Koopman operator in a different way - by utilizing it to generate multiple candidate solutions simultaneously. We apply the Koopman operator to generate a set of trajectories from an estimated model, and then apply constrained predictive control to identify the best trajectory while considering constraints. This results in a significantly faster approach than conventional MPC, enabling real-time application on high-dimensional systems. Our approach also allows for control inputs to occur at discrete intervals, and includes an estimator to account for any model discrepancies between the estimated model and the actual system dynamics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in reducing computational requirements of conventional MPC by conducting experiments on several examples, and further verify the performance of our approach using a real-time control environment.

The Lagrangian formulation, with its intrinsic connection to the physical state of a fluid, naturally lends itself to computational methods that preserve geometric invariants. Although Lagrangian calculations are unaffected by by flow-directed numerical dissipation, they still experience some quantification errors. To measure such precision inaccuracies, a novel metric is introduced for comparing Lagrangian versus Eulerian representations of a fluid flow's properties. The presented metric enables direct assessment of tracing errors in numerical simulations through direct integration of flow data along specific paths. A series of computational experiments have demonstrated that traditional tracing metrics do not accurately capture the true tracking inaccuracies. On the other hand, the presented metric has consistently provided accurate evaluations across a range of fluid dynamics simulations involving both passive and active flow conditions. The presented research therefore offers a trustworthy means of monitoring the accuracy of simulations performed using Lagrangian methods.

This study aims to examine the accuracy of robotic ultrasound in measuring the angles of spinal vertebrae using 3D imaging and compensation algorithms, compared to conventional X-ray imaging. Robotic ultrasound offers a safer alternative for monitoring scoliosis progression, especially in young patients. Research suggests the spinal curvature in scoliosis patients typically begins between 1-2 vertebrae and increases in size by 1 degree per month, making early detection crucial. To increase the detection rate, reliable monitoring methods are needed. A total of 60 spinal segments from 20 patients were analyzed in this study to compare the accuracy of robotic ultrasound with scoliosis-specific software against X-ray imaging, focusing on lumbar and thoracic regions. Results showed the mean absolute deviations of robotic ultrasound measurements were 1.7 degrees for lumbar and 2.3 degrees for thoracic regions, indicating relatively small errors. A high degree of correlation was found between robotic ultrasound and X-ray imaging, with most angles within 2 degrees of the reference values. Given its precision in vertebral angle measurements, robotic ultrasound may be a viable alternative for scoliosis diagnosis and monitoring, especially in children. Its safety benefits could lead to a more reliable long-term diagnosis.

To integrate duration and payment patterns, we developed a time-scaled system enabling flexible analysis of durations in various units, such as days, months, or years. Traditional methods typically standardize durations to a specific unit, like years, but our approach represents duration distributions in any unit with a scalar factor. This representation can be achieved through a time-warping technique and is illustrated with real-world data applied to credit risk analysis. We analyzed the duration of default for consumers in a portfolio of credit contracts in a Brazilian bank. Initially, we noticed that conventional scaling methods distorted the true default duration, resulting from unbalanced distribution shapes. In contrast, our new scaling approach accurately maintains the natural shape of duration distributions and accurately predicts transaction values, outperforming the existing state-of-the-art model. Furthermore, feature engineering-based results revealed that our time-scaled system enhanced the performance of logistic regression models on credit risk, achieving a 3.86% area under the receiver operating characteristic curve without the use of any machine learning algorithms, such as random forests or gradient boosting machines.

This research examines the ability of various leading NLP methods to detect hate speech. It specifically investigates whether these models can be easily misled into producing the opposite of the desired output. The investigation utilizes a German dataset to evaluate the performance of the models on hate speech that includes an additional category where models are given false information about the presence of hate speech in a post. The analysis reveals that certain types of hate speech detection models can be misled, and reveals what characteristics of the text that the models are mislearning to predict. The results suggest that semantic-based NLP techniques are the most effective at identifying hate speech in the provided dataset, and imply that a combination of semantic and syntactic-based methods may be the best overall approach. The research also highlights potential weaknesses in the leading NLP models that could be exploited by malicious users to corrupt their results.

We've developed a novel MIMO framework that combines multiple network architectures, including MRC, BeamNet, and DeepNet. Typically, MIMO operates on individual network components, but our work integrates a unified approach by means of a specially designed unmixing step. Firstly, the output from each network is generated independently and sent through the unmixing step, where its contribution is determined and subtracted. This proposed unminging step mitigates two key issues: it helps eliminate unwanted effects within individual networks and and brings their outputs closer for coherent signal combination. Our findings indicate that our MIMO approach yields optimal performance with the MRC, surpasses BeamNet in sparse scenarios, and even outperforms DeepNet in cases with moderate Delay-Spread where other methods fall short. Our MIMO output enhancement is also notable when compared to the individually enhanced DeepNet outputs.

Historical document analysis necessitates the identification of suitable datasets, despite the numerous digital collections available, due to their considerable volume, ill-defined metadata, and unsuitable selection, mainly because of a lack of context. A proposed data mining approach aims to aid humanities scholars in pinpointing relevant datasets for specific research tasks, like identifying historical artifacts from a particular era or location. To accomplish this, we design an ontology to encapsulate the categorization of metadata, and an ontology-driven system is developed to identify suitable datasets based on an annotation scheme that captures task-specific requirements. Furthermore, we analyze the efficacy of the proposed method in both automated and semi-automated environments and discuss its limitations based on an experiment using institutional document collections.

This paper presents an innovative, two-pronged solution to enhance the accuracy of industrial robots' trajectory tracking, which involves combining two techniques: adaptive feedforward and adaptive feedback control. Through feedforward control, the robot rapidly captures the target trajectory, and subsequently uses feedback control to make subtle adjustments. Additionally, the paper discusses how to effectively capture the desired trajectory by adapting the robot's model. A simulation specific to a Panda P3AT robot demonstrates the proposed approach, showcasing its robustness and capacity to handle external disturbances. Compared to other control methods, the proposed solution results in a significant 42% reduction in the maximum error and a 78% reduction in the integrated error when tracking a square wave trajectory, as well as an 83% reduction in the integrated error when tracking a sawtooth wave trajectory.

Myocardial infarction survivors often go on to experience additional heart-related issues, known as post-MI heart disease, which can vary greatly in terms of expression and spread across an individual's heart muscle over time. Currently, there are limited quantitative studies exploring how long-term heart disease progresses in people after a myocardial infarction, as well as how individual characteristics such as gender and ethnicity impact heart disease development in these individuals. In this research, we aim to detail the distinct ways in which heart disease tends to spread and progress over time in individuals who have previously experienced a myocardial infarction, as well as examine how various factors like automated external defibrillator placement and medication use contribute to heart disease progression in these individuals. Furthermore, we seek to establish a predictive model allowing for individualized estimates of post-MI heart disease risk across different locations and time points in the future. In order to accomplish these goals, we looked at detailed magnetic resonance imaging images of heart muscles obtained from a large study involving over 1,000 individuals who had previously experienced a myocardial infarction, gathered information on patients' socio-demographic characteristics, physical activity, as well as data on post-MI treatment strategies like secondary prevention therapy and cardiac rehabilitation programs. By using a specialized statistical technique to model how heart disease progresses over time in these individuals, we were able to accurately detail the distinct ways in which heart disease tends to spread across an individual's heart muscle over time, as well as accurately assess

A recent research paper proposed an updated version of Becke's scheme for the electronic continuum, which can be found at arXiv:2106.04625. The revised ADS has faster convergence and lower numerical errors than the original ADS when applied to molecular interactions, especially when using finite methods to account for dispersion forces. The updated ADS also reduces errors associated with the singular Coulombic attraction in such finite methods. It converges much faster than the original ADS for interactions involving electronic states, at a rate comparable to the faster-converging DFT continuum methods. The revised ADS is compatible with a variety of charge models including oneface, multipole, and higher-order charge models. It is capable of generating transferable atom-centered basis sets for describing interactions between electronic states, which include a compact scheme applicable to interactions between closed-shell and open-shell electronic states. The updated ADS has been successfully implemented in Q-Chem, an ab initio simulation program, which now supports describing interactions between electronic states in molecules and complexes.

The Metric Dimension problem, a well-known NP-hard graph parameterized problem, has been investigated under various parameters. We reveal a significant distinction in its complexity parameterized by different graph measures, which is further contrasted by the same complexity under the parameterization of colored vertices in an $k$-colorable graph. Specifically, we demonstrate that the $w_k$ parameter leads to a fixed-parameter algorithm when combined with the $w$ parameter, but the use of the $k$ parameter alone results in a more complicated problem. Furthermore, we established the fixed-parameter tractability of the Disjoint Paths problem parameterized by the number of paths ($k$) and simplified the complexity under the parameterization of the number of terminals ($w_k$), which was achieved in collaboration with Kirkpatrick et al. who independently discovered a simpler algorithm using the $w$ parameter alone.

The upper, lower, and convex space structures in directed spaces diverge from those in partially ordered spaces with the Scott topology in several key aspects. Firstly, the lattice operations in the former outperform those in the latter. Secondly, the closed algebras in the former exist across various fields but are absent in the latter. Thirdly, the basic frame-like structure in the former surpasses that in the latter. We have found that decision algorithms previously developed for the Scott topology can now be similarly applied to directed spaces within this framework. Notably, the decision algorithms' behavior on spaces with the upper topology exactly mirrors that of partial orders with the Scott topology when dealing with (convex) frame-like structures containing two elements.

In scorching hot climates near the ground, a process called lower-tropospheric radiative heating creates a unique atmosphere where warm air rises, yet precipitation remains low. This leads to limited water supply in clouds, resulting in thin, iridescent patches of cloud cover. This research aims to explore the effects of large-scale geographical features on cloud formation within hothouse climates on solar-powered planets like KELT-9b and the Earth's Sahara Desert using computer models. These models simulate atmospheric behavior and discover that mountains and valleys can drastically reduce or enhance cloud cover, depending on the location and strength of the ground's underlying features. Generally, valleys act as traps for air and water, increasing moisture and cloud formation, whereas mountains and plates can force air upward, decreasing water content and cloud cover. These findings suggest that scaling these atmospheric phenomena to other planets like KELT-9b is feasible, providing potential clues for detecting exoplanets with similar scorching hot atmospheres. Moreover, understanding the complex interplay between ground topology, atmospheric geometry, and cloud formation can aid in creating detailed simulations of Earth's and other planetary atmospheres.

Recent findings suggest that higher-spin extensions of non-Abelian gauge theory, involving spin greater than one, can be described by an action closely related to that of Hofman-Sopukiwski duality.  This action, incorporating Faddeev-Popov terms within the context of soft limits, adheres to higher-spin duality when using the spin-one connection as the gauge field.  By examining the equations of motion and implementing Hofman-Sopukiwski duality, it has been proven that higher-spin Yang-Mills theory minimally couples to a spin-one connection, maintaining higher-spin duality.  This action, already shown to be the free field limit of higher-spin electromagnetism, can now be seen as derived from a higher-spin Maxwell theory via the substitution of spin-one connection for gauge field, thus providing further understanding of higher-spin electromagnetism and its interaction with matter.

Deep learning networks have demonstrated impressive resilience despite substantial noise in their labels, but labeling quality remains a significant concern for these models. Typically, a certain level of label noise is inherent in datasets, with some classes even lacking reliable examples. Furthermore, existing methods often fail to account for scenarios where some data points completely lack relevant labels. The proposed Bayesian statistics-based labeling refurbishment mechanism (BLRM) addresses these challenges by first establishing a Bayesian interpretation of the network's learning process. Building on this foundation, BLRM introduces an advanced labeling correction approach that incorporates the likelihood of observing dataset observations given model parameters. The results demonstrate that BLRM can effectively eliminate severe label noise and even discover latent class structures within "stochastic" datasets. During the testing phase, BLRM further refines the labels using a Bayesian inference process, leading to improved robustness in the face of noise. The research showcases BLRM's capability to upgrade deep neural networks and their predictions in noisy environments, while also achieving superior performance compared to other state-of-the-art approaches.

A routine approach is presented to prove that for any n-dimensional cube with uniformly spaced vertices, a non-ordinate regular simplex with positively weighted vertices exists within it, as long as the number of interpolation nodes exceeded the product of 2 and the (n-1)th Fibonacci number divided by 2.

We analyze a class of random walks with correlations by introducing a matrix that captures the probability of transitioning to any state within a specified time frame, and then derive the characteristic polynomial of this transition matrix using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, resulting in a closed-form expression. Subsequently, we apply the obtained expression to determine the eigenvalues of the transition matrix, and then utilize these eigenvalues to calculate the rate of convergence of certain statistics, such as the law of motion and a function representing the concentration of particles at a particular location and at a particular time point. Additionally, we derive an upper limit on the mixing time of this random walk.

The vast amount of computational resources available today make it cost-effective to employ high-performance hardware, leading to the widespread adoption of clock-driven optimization techniques in terminating proof assistants like Isabelle/HOL. Nevertheless, relying solely on clock-driven strategies can be problematic as it causes the proof search to run indefinitely, necessitating manual interruption in the worst-case scenario. Clock-driven strategies have been deemed unacceptable in past studies, resulting in the development of hardware-based clock minimization methods, which we now propose to adapt for use in proof assistants. Our study focuses on Isabelle/HOL as our proof assistant and Terminology as our benchmark, demonstrating a significant simplification in termination proofs by minimizing the use of a clock through a novel, automated approach. This new method employs clock minimization based on the principles of runtime analysis, specifically by identifying maximal runtime bounds for each function and utilizing this information to terminate proof search when these bounds are exceeded. The effects of clock minimization on Isabelle/HOL's performance have been examined, and the outcomes suggest that this method could efficiently accelerate Isabelle/HOL's execution.

In modeling wall-bound turbulence, a common issue arises from the absence of a established and accepted model. A proposed synthetic eddy method treats the wall by applying a special form of eddy packet that adheres to the wall, named the hairpin packet. This packet has previously been linked to near-wall turbulence scaling. This work develops a model for turbulent transport based on the idea that this packet moves along the wall, with associated effects. A formula for calculating the turbulent energy transfer based on this packet has been devised and tested, showing promise when compared to experimental results and direct numerical simulations data in a fully developed, turbulent boundary flow.

A gauged version of the baby Skyrme model is investigated with a specific $SU(2)$ gauge group and it reveals the existence of three distinct gauged solitons - vortex, skyrmion, and black hole solitons, each with a varying self-interaction level. By applying a two-sphere world manifold, the Dirac equation for zero modes is solved to determine the quantized gauge flux linked to the solitons. The research further examines the energy and configuration relations among the gauged solitons linked to the non-linear skinmer term, gauged parameter, and monopole charge.

We analyze a lattice simulation of a Weyl semimetal model originally proposed in P. Spru kang, et al., Sci. Adv. 2 (2016), DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.1600003. Initially, this model exhibited a unconventional texture of Lorentz-broken geometric phase at the charge neutral point, alongside other intriguing phenomena. However, the crystal symmetry present in the system contradicts the absence of time-reversal symmetry alleged in the model. Furthermore, this symmetry is not strictly enforced in the model either. Consequently, a spiral geodesic that naturally arises from the crystal symmetry, rather than the time-reversal symmetry, is the actual origin of the texture of the geometric phase observed in the traditional Weyl semimetal simulation. Meanwhile, another distinct geometric phase derived from the combination of time-reversal and crystal symmetry is suppressed in the simulation. As a result, it fails to transition into the proposed peculiar states with unusual anomaly-like transport characteristics that were declared in the original research paper. To avoid confusion with the earlier work, we advocate the abandonment of the nomenclature "LOM" and instead suggest "Lorentz-broken phase of crystal symmetry" or "geometric phase of crystal symmetry" to accurately describe these phenomena. Our design offers a compact optical nanoantenna, combining a U-shaped wire and a driving plate, allowing spectral positions of resonances to be tuned independently. Research on this structure demonstrates enhanced light interaction at nanoscale levels, offering a new approach for achieving strong light-matter interactions in compact optical systems. The properties and behavior of our designed nanoantenna were thoroughly investigated using finite-different-time-domain numerical analysis. In contrast to previous studies on dual-nanoantenna systems, our setup features a compact antenna design, facilitating a substantial enhancement of the radiated light's amplitude for a given driving strength. The amount of light radiated was found to increase in direct proportion to the driving strength, unlike conventional resonance patterns. The optical response of our nanoantenna was also evaluated using both driven and coupled modes. The results revealed a nanoantenna system with two resonances not influenced by the capacitively coupled interaction, preserving the characteristics and number of resonances despite coupling. The Controlling the Light Emitted Radiation Width using a Nearby Metal Surface Nanoantenna Experiment (CLEAR) is a promising platform for investigating quantum optics, emulating behaviors similar to those found in double-nanoantenna systems, at a scale that is significantly more compact.

Amorphous materials have long been overlooked as lacking the structural order found in crystalline solids, with its mechanical properties thus excluding itself from studies of resistance capabilities.  Yet, with the presence of fluctuations in arrangement due to lack of order, it is now recognized that these materials can provide valuable knowledge in understanding deformation processes.  A study has demonstrated that utilizing these fluctuations can significantly boost a material's capacity to withstand damage under extreme conditions, comparable to a shuffle board player utilizing all available sides of the stick to push around objects.  This concept was successfully applied to a class of simple theoretical materials and was verified through simulation testing, leading to improved resistance in resulting materials.  It is anticipated that this concept will allow for the creation of strong, resilient materials in future.

The calculation of tight-binding parameters for silicene decorated with Mn atoms on a (2x2) honeycomb structure has been carried out. Studies were conducted into the magnetic and electronic properties of Mn-decorated silicene with varying degrees of spin polarization. Since Mn atoms occupy different sublattices in a (2x2) structure, the arrangement of Mn on either sublattice affects the onsite interaction parameter of the resulting system. Additionally, the effect of Mn atom substitution with Mn impurities on the electronic properties of silicene has been examined. Calculations of the Fermi energy's resonance widths for silicene decorated with Mn atoms on a (2x2) honeycomb structure have been performed.

The centre of the Milky Way harbours a supermassive black hole, and a supernova remnant named Sgr A East, located just 130 parsecs from the galaxy's centre, emits a faint radiation signal in the far infrared spectrum, but these emissions are often obscured by the galactic disk's strong radiation noise. Using the Herschel space observatory's data from fixed points in space, and a unique mathematical model that adapts to local variations in noise, researchers were able to uncover two far infrared peaks corresponding to the galactic bulb's radiation signal, and were able to distinguish between the galactic bulb's signal and that of a nearby nearby gas cloud. By combining data from various frequencies, researchers were able to create complete maps of the galactic bulb's emissions, and were able to determine the dimensions, and emission patterns, of a gas cloud surrounding a central black hole, and representing its radiation pattern as a three-dimensional model of a specific kind.

This paper investigates the KNN and SVM algorithms' resilience to overfitting when dealing with the class imbalance issue, and compares their performance to state-of-the-art neural networks on various practical datasets. Our findings indicate that KNN and SVM suffer significantly less from overfitting than the evaluated deep neural network architectures, which includes ResNet, DenseNet, and Inception. Notably, KNN exhibits minimal sensitivity to class imbalance, while SVM shows some degree of sensitivity but still manages to maintain high accuracy at the KNN level. Of further interest, KNN and SVM tend to converge to each other in terms of performance on highly imbalanced datasets, and when paired together, they achieve results comparable to the state-of-the-art neural networks. These conclusions are based on the use of KNN's traditional and SVM's soft margin variants. An open-source implementation of the study can be accessed on the UDA-MADLIB GitHub repository.

This study receives support from the National Science Foundation, award number 2120196. It seeks to assess the impact of the coronavirus pandemic on local news outlets and the ability of federal stimulus packages to boost coverage of certain topics. We will achieve this goal by analyzing data from the Open News Data initiative, which collects information on the content, volume, and financial performance of news organizations. Additionally, we will utilize surveys to gather information on the operational status and resources of news outlets. Our findings will be presented in a user-friendly format to inform policymakers and the public.

A FMM-based implementation in N-Body simulations is highly beneficial for astrophysical projects like galaxy cluster simulations, where numerous particles are involved. This paper integrates the publicly accessible FMM library for Python, adaptating it to meet the needs of Faustino2, a C++ framework originally designed for N-Body and Particle-in-Cell astrophysical simulations. The resulting code utilizes Python modules for ease in setting up and running tasks, while leveraging the speed and efficiency of C++/C code. Specifically, this integration offers O(N) complexity at near O(1) cost per particle using O(N^2) preprocessing steps, with a distance criterion controlling accuracy and performance. The accuracy of this code was assessed in terms of time and energy conservation. In comparison to STK, a C++ library for Time-step Limited O(N) algorithms, results indicate similar performance with potential gains in future development. Furthermore, this code provides a'sandbox' for experimenting with various algorithms and accelerators, providing a flexible environment for research into integrators, the multigrid approach, and potential extensions through hardware accelerators like the FPGA.

A specific type of electron-proton scattering, known as $e$p → eO)p, has been studied at the Jefferson Lab's CLAS collider with an accompanying twist where one or more dynamical neutrons within the proton are temporarily replaced by an electron. This complex scattering process is particularly valuable for analyzing a double spin asymmetry as the relative orientations of beam polarization, target polarization, and the direction of the incoming electron's momentum are linked. This measured asymmetry, which was found to be around 8.3 Gaussian standard deviations away from zero, was ultimately linked to the presence of a particular quark contribution. In simpler terms, this finding represents one of the initial observations of a double spin interaction within a particular quark of the proton and is believed to offer fresh insights into the underlying structure of protons. This measurement also helped to refine our current knowledge of the individual properties of the strange vector meson, specifically the ρ(770) and ϕ(1020), by examining their decay patterns and orientation alignments.

Deep reinforcement learning methods have limitations when controlling high-dimensional systems, partly due to their own complexity. The challenge of mapping expert knowledge to these systems' parameter spaces is further exacerbated. While behavioral cloning can learn control policies, its performance may not translate to similar environments. However, its learned function approximator can still offer insights if it were tailored to recognize expert actions. We propose augmented policy cloning as a pre-processing technique that acknowledges the inherent noise in expert data and focuses on identifying actionable patterns. By utilizing an augmented neural network, we encode additional context, such as state and action context, to enhance the learning process. The augmented approach is now capable of leveraging the expert's experience and adapting it to the student policy, something traditional behavioral cloning cannot do. We utilize inverse reinforcement learning to create a belief network, which captures the essential information behind noisy expert actions. Augmented policy cloning effectively tunes high-dimension control policies, even when grounded in uncertain expert knowledge. Moreover, it proves effective in multiple transfer scenarios, including when policies are applied to similar but unobserved environments.

In a study, the production of a Higgs boson accompanied by a heavy neutrino was examined, along with the possibility of observing this process using data collected by the ATLAS and CMS experiments during Run II at the LHC. Specifically, the research focused on Higgs production via weak interaction and the decay of a top quark, accompanied by a heavy neutrino, which decays into a resonant scalar or pseudoscalar particle. This then decays into a pair of tau leptons or hadrons. For two types of Higgs bosons - the standard model's Higgs and its seventh dimension's counterpart - the study analyzed the associated production cross-sections, ranging from 125 GeV to 100 GeV, in relation to various mass values for heavy resonances, ranging from 500 GeV to 3000 GeV. It further investigated the potential for detecting these processes through two major search methods: direct detection of the decay products of the resonant particles against known standard model backgrounds, particularly focusing on a pair of hadronic tau leptons, and indirect search for missing energy, especially against the background of top quark production with significant unobserved energy. Ultimately, the study found that, with sufficient data, both experiments should be capable of detecting these processes with a significance of at least 2 standard deviations if the Higgs boson mass equals 125 GeV, with mass values for heavy resonances above 800 GeV and production rates exceeding 10

The resonant spin maser has demonstrated superior sensitivity and precise spectral linearity compared to conventional pulsed EPR and NMR, with operational limitations imposed by the sidebands from microwave frequency modulation. Our research focuses on enhancing the maser's response by integrating digital signal processing techniques for increased sensitivity and improved line resolution. This is accomplished by applying maximum likelihood estimation and non-uniform fast Fourier transformation algorithms to simulate the response of the resonant spin system when interacting with the microwave field. Computational tests using Collected Data from experimental devices have shown the efficacy of these methods in developing more sideband-optimized frequency-domain spectra. This innovation sets the stage for the development of highly sensitive spin-triplet sensors capable of detecting various triangles within the time domain. Consequently, the integration of digital signal processing is anticipated to significantly broaden the applicability of the resonant spin maser in numerous scientific and technological fields.

We provide an overview of the primary findings related to the hypergeometric groups generated by the K3 surface extremal periodic orbits derived from Heerema's classification, also examining one orbit previously unreported. Furthermore, we establish relationships between these hypergeometric groups and the GL$_2(\mathbb{Z})$ generated by Tg modes as described in the research of Borovoi, also analyzing their connection to K3 surface automorphisms, their implications in the context of Tg modes, invariant sublattices, root systems, and the K3 surface's period map.

We suggest a radio telescope strategy to identify the process of $\chi_1^0 \to \chi_2^0 \gamma$ decay, where $\chi_2^0$ is a dark neutralino confined to a hidden sector, disconnected from our observable world. As a result, $\chi_1^0$ particles decay into $\chi_2^0$ particles and enormous amounts of energy, in the form of gamma rays, which may be detectable through the radio emission generated from the process of Cherenkov radiation on the dark neutralinos' path. This idea aims to explore the dark sector using very long baseline interferometry with radio telescopes. Using a simplified model of the dark sector, we saw how the signal we're aiming for may be stronger than what is projected to be seen at the future eLISA gravitational wave detector. Additionally, we noticed how this method could independently confirm the mass and composition of the $\chi_1^0$ particle, free from the limitations of LHC experiments. Finally, we noted that even minimal production levels of $\chi_1^0$ at the LHC could still result in noticeable signals, even with the presence of a significant amount of background noise.

The genus of a graph, G, is the minimum number of non-intersecting surfaces required to embed G without overlapping edges. We've established criteria to determine if a graph's genus is at its minimum in two specific scenarios: when the graph is connected and when the sum of its simplest closed surfaces equals the graph's number of vertices. We've also developed a method to calculate the genus of specific transitive graphs and identified the minimum genus for certain types of cyclic and symmetric graphs. This work aims to advance our understanding of genus by providing a more detailed analysis of non-planar graphs.

This study explores stochastic optimization techniques for solving multi-agent learning problems on networks, with a focus on reducing communication costs. By leveraging local, private information, nodes aim to minimize a shared objective function in a decentralized manner. We'll examine how averaging methods fit into this framework and outline existing reductions in communication costs. Two primary strategies will be discussed: reducing the number of communication rounds and lowering the cost per round. Additionally, we'll delve into the potential trade-offs, along with how techniques like data sharing and topological exploration can be employed.

Our goal is to develop a machine learning model that can learn language patterns 
from various languages with shared origins, like French, Spanish, and Portuguese, 
and improve its performance on each language individually, using only labeled data.
We found that a multi-task approach with transfer learning is effective in training 
better models for each language when compared to training each model separately.
Also, combining data from all three languages results in better performance than 
training each model alone or together in pairs. 
Despite having similar structures, our model did not exhibit expected similarities 
when learning these Romance languages concurrently.
We investigated several strategies to enhance the model's ability to capture 
similarities between the languages, including using a shared embedding space and 
adding a task that focuses on shared tasks.
These attempts showed limited success in reducing differences in the model's architecture 
or its performance when testing separately.
More surprisingly, our model showed a higher tendency to make mistakes on clearly 
similar tasks in the Portuguese dataset when comparing its performance when testing 
alone versus together with the other languages.
It seems the model's ability to learn and generalize is more determined by its design 
than its potential to learn and capture patterns from related languages in a group.

In the search for Dark Matter, using Gas Time Projection Chambers with ionization detectors can be an effective approach, especially when analyzing samples of rare natural occurrences that have a built-in reference for the interaction energy. Present research in this field typically relies on a single dimension - recoil electron saturation yield - to differentiate between electron and nuclear recoil interactions. We have developed new observables that utilize multiple properties of the interaction to differentiate between these two types of recoil. These new observables were tested on a simulation of the MOON experiment, using observables extracted from the primary event and those inherited from the daughter gamma rays. They showed significant promise in enhancing Dark Matter detection capabilities in Gas Time Projection Chambers. Specifically, they offered improved discrimination between electron and nuclear recoil interactions at lower interaction energies, especially in situations where the energy ranges of interest are below 100 keV. These new observables also provided more accurate estimation of the Dark Matter cross-section when analyzing a sample of rare zinc events. Finally, they facilitated a more reliable evaluation of the analysis's performance through associated uncertainties.

The development of intelligent transportation systems necessitates a precise evaluation of driver behavior. However, assessing driver behavior with minimal expertise is challenging because what constitutes optimal driving practices varies based on external circumstances such as weather and time. Furthermore, prior studies have shown that expert feedback is necessary for developing accurate models of driver behavior. Expert knowledge can be incorporated into machine learning algorithms through methods like constraint and constraint learning. Future advancements in assessing and improving driver behavior could utilize advancements in reinforcement learning, which enables the model to incorporate expert knowledge and adapt to new situations. Nevertheless, current models are limited in their ability to explain their decision-making processes, making reading the mind of experts a prerequisite for implementation. To address this limitation, researchers propose creating symbolic models that can replicate the behaviors of these models, thereby providing insight into their decision-making processes and enabling the detection of potential errors in expert input. This research examines the use of algorithms that can create these symbolic models, focusing on the specific application of explaining the behavior of driver risk models. Researchers successfully developed a system that can convert black-box driver risk models into symbolic models, demonstrating its capabilities with an analysis of driver risk factors. This research demonstrates that its approach outperforms traditional methods by significantly reducing the number of features needed to explain the model, from thousands to sixty-four, thereby saving computation time and enabling the model to be reimplanted onto other devices and devices with limited capabilities.

Despite notable progress in scene text recognition, a significant issue remains due to the presence of Out-Of-Vocabulary words in existing training datasets. To address this problem, our proposed approach utilizes a self-supervised strategy to capture the visual semantics for any word, thereby enabling direct word-level ground truth generation when word semantics are recognized. In practical terms, our approach can be implemented using an unsupervised language model, effective even with limited training data. We have created a new OOV dataset to evaluate the effectiveness of various text recognition models in a zero-shot setting, where the models are not given any information about the test words. Compared to the state-of-the-art approaches, our proposed method achieves improvements of 6.9%, 11.1%, and 14.4% in character error rate (FER@3) on the ICDAR 2013, VRD, and GTR-7 datasets respectively.

The similarity of two fields, each defined within its own range, can be observed in both theoretical and real-world scenarios [1-6].  For instance, certain properties of a field remain consistent when another field of a different nature is applied [7-8].  The comparisons typically made in such contexts are either very broad, like [9-11], or very specific, as in [12-13].  In this context, we aim to define a precise framework to assess the similarity of fields, both broadly and precisely, and to extend the concept to higher dimensions.  Our proposed method is illustrated in three specific instances: a comparison of an elliptic $2d$ field against two types of $2d$ and $3d$ fields.

We conducted an experiment combining magnetic levitation and visualizations
of a liquid gain of momentum by utilizing the magnetic levitation technique
to decrease the disturbances originating from the supporting system while
simultaneously increasing the momentum transfer between the fluid and the
levitated object, we tested the hydrodynamic damped flow around a cylindrical
object placed near the bottom surface of a viscous liquid within a narrow
channel, the setup consisted of a cylindrical object suspended above a plate
filled with a fluid, the object and plate were magnetized, and supported by a
thin film of levitated fluid, and observed using particle imaging, the results
showed distinct layers within the fluid, the shadow of the object revealed its
orientation, and tracked a streamer flowing past the object, the data included
images, force measurements, and the trajectory of the streamer, the outcomes
revealed a complex interplay of object and fluid dynamics, the results indicated
a reduction in object turbulence and fluid momentum due to the distorting
effect of the thin film, the data showed consistent force acting on the object
and consistent flow trajectories near the object, the results successfully
minimized support-induced disturbances and enhanced the object's momentum transfer.

Our results show that non-holomorphic Sp(n,Z) double cover Maass forms L-functions with specific properties share crucial characteristics and similarities with Dirichlet L-functions, whereas L-functions of SL2(Z) cusp forms and SL2(Z) Maass forms behave differently. Additionally, newly developed restrictions on SLL(s,chi) and L(s,M) critical zeros count towards the 2k-1th and 2k-th zero in consecutive sequences of Hecke eigenvalues, revealing more intricate patterns of L-function zeros beyond the critical strip. These discoveries also lead to precise estimations of Hecke operator eigenvalues at SLn(Z) level.

We use the Landauer-Büttiker model to study transport characteristics in a wide class of junctions composed of graphs, focusing on graphs with normal conductor and graphene nodes that are disordered. Although the graphs with normal conductor and graphene nodes have distinct electronic structures, we find that their transport characteristics share a striking resemblance. Our findings reveal that the low-degree nodes of these graphs do not exhibit a perfect normal conductor response, but rather approach a perfect normal conductor response asymptotically as the coordination number increases. This tendency is consistently observed in various transport properties, regardless of whether we use a tight-binding model or a standard conductance model. Notably, we observed a remarkable correlation between the spectral and transmission properties of these graphs, even in junctions with dissipative interfaces. These findings could help clarify the unexpected normal conductor-like response observed in the transport properties of graphene.

This study seeks to expand upon the weakly non-linear operator theory originally developed for Carnahan-Strang preconditioner in 2019. The proof of a general iterative convergence formula is demonstrated for non-linear operators that satisfy a monotone condition, specifically in the context of $\nabla$-regular Banach lattices and certain Banach spaces. The findings are then applied to a nonlinear resolution of the Helmholtz equation, yielding a novel Helmholtz preconditioner. The paper provides a detailed analysis of the preconditioner's performance and presents accompanying numerical results.

Our research builds upon Boyle's existing work, where he showed that every large graph containing no independent subgraphs of size $d+1$ must also contain a pancyclic subgraph of size at least $(d^2+2d-3)$ vertices. This result allows us to restate Boyle's original result as follows: for the family of r-regular graphs, the independence number of a graph in this family is at most $(d+1)$, which also means it has a corresponding pancyclic subgraph of size at least $(d^2+2d-3)$ vertices. In order to obtain this result, we employ Ramsey theory, the Blshchuk-Zdor criterion, long Ramsey theory, the Erdos-Sos construction, the Erdos-Ko-Rado theorem, Cartwright-Wilson's theorem, and the theory of cocycles. This research also reveals a corresponding pancyclic subgraph of size at least $(d^2+2d-3)$ vertices within the family of quasi-$r$-partite graphs. In addition, we determine the maximum possible size of a cocycle of size $d$ within the family of $r$-partite graphs.

Research into extremely hot and dense matter, where conditions differ from normal matter, has been conducted by heavy-ion collisions. In a dense medium with a complex composition, particles exhibit altered behavior compared to a uniform background, resulting in changes in momentum and the presence of anomalous dispersion. By analyzing the collective behavior of particles in this background, researchers have derived a theoretical model quantifying how particles interact and move together. This model has been applied to understand the movement and production of various hadrons generated in central Au+Pu collisions at 11.5 AGeV. The study focuses on altering the initial conditions in a specific region, simulating diverse responses among identical quark systems, and examining changes in pressure and the movement of particles, such as their gradient and velocity. The findings reveal that, even with uniform pressure, the initial setup can affect the direction of particles and their velocity based on pressure gradients. These outcomes have been visually represented to illustrate anomalous patterns in particle movement, along with correlations between particle production, initial setup, and specific particle types.

To enhance scalability and efficiency in solving complex PDEs on diverse platforms, including GPUs, a novel asynchronous algorithm called ASASK is proposed. This method incorporates elements from the existing SASK approach, which introduces asynchrony at the equation level, leading to significant performance gains according to empirical studies. Further, ASASK achieves a 30% average improvement in solving linear systems in various real-world applications when compared to SASK, while demonstrating comparable error levels. Additionally, ASASK significantly reduces memory access patterns in data-intensive SASK workflows, resulting in substantial speedup benefits that are expected to reach nearly 100% in less data-intensive scenarios.

Using the Lanczos technique on a time-independent Schr\"odinger equation in the basis of the basis set constructed from the basis of the ground state of a single water molecule, we've analyzed the influence of static electric fields on the water dimer's resonance. By employing the coupled-channel method to account for all interactions between the two molecules, we've calculated the resonance parameters for the primary resonances. Our results show that the resonance characteristics match those found in literature for a single water molecule, but differ in a meaningful way. Additionally, we've determined that the primary resonances in water dimer are significantly less pronounced than those in water dimer cation. A brief overview of our approach can be found in accompanying documentation.

This research introduces a novel optimization technique grounded in transport dynamics for resolving the Schrödinger problem. This method is based on an Ottonello et al. paper that applies the Sinkhorn algorithm to the Boltzmann-Gibbs entropy model. Our study tackles the practical aspects of this approach. Specifically, we demonstrate that when there's no Schrödinger solution, the Sinkhorn algorithm converges towards a solution that includes a non-negative transport cost function. Furthermore, we establish a link between the Ottonello model and the classical Bregman divergences, thereby illustrating its relationship with the Boltzmann-Gibbs entropy's monotonicity properties. The paper also examines the possibilities of computing the Sinkhorn solution and proposes a heuristic solution-based on perturbing the Ottonello model with a parameter epsilon. This technique finds application in an accurate Otto solution for the Boltzmann-Gibbs entropy model.

A precise measurement, based on 36.1 fb^-1 of data collected using the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider, reports on the cross-section of top-quark pair production in proton-proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy level. The measurement, leveraging t¯T channel definitions and top-quark mass reconstructions, fair to the CT10, NNLO QCD and BMN predictions. The inclusion of additional systematic uncertainties yielded two different measurements, derived from two distinct top-quark mass estimation methods. The "Poisoned" approach, taking into consideration only data obtained from t¯T events where both top-quarks decayed into electrons or muons, resulted in a measured cross-section of approximately 0.78 pb with a corresponding uncertainty of about 0.27 pb. Conversely, the "Unpoisoned" approach, incorporating additional systematic uncertainties stemming from simulation events involving electrons or muons, yielded a measured cross-section of roughly 0.73 pb with an associated uncertainty of approximately 0.18 pb. Both measurements appear to be in line with the BMN and NNLO QCD theoretical models.

Our research examines the development of entanglement between a central entity and multiple surrounding ones in a disordered system of interacting spins that weakly couple to the central entity. We discovered that the amount of entanglement between the central entity and any individual surrounding spin reaches a maximum according to the central exchange model, whereas our continuous model indicates gradual increases without peaks. Furthermore, the total entanglement measured among all surrounding spins reaches a peak earlier than the individual maximum entanglement in each case. We found that the total entanglement is a more reliable indicator of the overall quality of entanglement among all spins within the disordered system. These findings have the potential to guide the creation of robust many-body entanglement within future experiments using superconducting quanta.
We establish criteria for a modified Bessel function, first introduced by Waterman in 1985, to exhibit Janowski convexity and starlikeness properties in the unit disk.

The COVID-19 pandemic marked a distinctive period in recent history, characterized by an uncommon suddenness in spread and gravity. As a global phenomenon, it inevitably brought human societies to a temporary halt, thereby exposing the intricate nature of urban encounters and community connections. In this unique circumstances-driven research study, we seek to answer how cities influenced by distinct pandemic phases fared in terms of urban diversity, community cohesion, and innovative potential. To this end, we employed a multidiscited approach that combined 1) statistical analysis of long-term trends in urban services and community services and 2) in-depth interviews with local stakeholders and residents across two American cities, namely Baltimore and San Francisco. Notably, our research found that Baltimore, which experienced a more prolonged and prolonged pandemic phase, demonstrated relatively lesser decline in urban diversity and increased resilience compared to San Francisco, which faced a more sudden and acute pandemic. Through our analysis, we sought to uncover mechanisms and strategies that contributed to urban strength in the face of adversity, with a focus on customizing local responses rather than universally applying lessons learned from past crises.

Developing accurate pressurization models for two-phase mixtures is critical in modeling water hammer events, and researchers have proposed multiple approaches to tackle this issue. Although some methods approximate boundary surfaces using empirical or correlation-based equations, a new model dubbed FSMSN simplifies these predictions by assuming phase density ratios can be represented as linear combinations of density ratios at phase boundaries. This work presents FSMSN, a first-order accurate computational fluid dynamics solver that leverages this approximation, and compares it to other methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency for different water hammer scenarios.

The interaction between light and chiral optical cavities is a key factor in achieving strong interactions between light and specific types of chiral particles. However, the inherent symmetry of traditional cavities means they can't differentiate between handedness, limiting their ability to enhance interactions with particles of a particular orientation. We've discovered a one-handed optical cavity that can enhance interactions specifically with handedness-matched chiral emitters. When a weak signal from one cavity is combined with a stronger signal from the opposite handedness, it results in an enhanced, linearly scalable optical response within the ensemble of emitters. We've shown both theoretical and simulated models confirm this phenomenon and discuss potential applications in improving the detection of homogeneous chiral molecules, such as those found in life sciences, as well as in specific types of sensing applications.

Two-dimensional anti de-Sitter spaces within the context of two-dimensional string theory can be viewed as a simplified version of quantum gravity that mimics the low-energy phenomenon known as semi-classical behavior. Building upon earlier findings by Fairlie and Zou, we have discovered an infinite sequence of higher spin symmetries present in these two-dimensional anti de-Sitter backgrounds, deriving an explicit form using the $sl(2, \mathbb R)$ algebra and identifying the corresponding higher rank charges. We propose that the infinite sequence of higher spin symmetries should be present in two-dimensional string theory and demonstrate how they can be incorporated as 2-dimensional conformal gravity variables within the context of free bosonic string theory. Furthermore, we have discovered that dressing the dressing field of live strings by specific worldsheet operators can be used to generate an infinite sequence of higher spin gauge fields, and we suggest that these dressing field dressings could be used as "pre-quantum observables" in a quantum deformation of two-dimensional gravity that deviates from the semi-classical limit of string theory.

Researchers seeking an engine capable of producing the Alcubierre warp drive have been exploring various options for generating the warp bubble, but a consensus on the stable configurations remains elusive. Our paper uses a model based on a spherical warp bubble to investigate the stability of the stress energy tensor in the warp drive regime. By analyzing the matter or energy required for stable solutions, we find that different components of the warp drive setup, such as classical or quantum matter, and different forms of energy, contribute to both stable and unstable configurations. We present a detailed analysis of the conditions necessary for a stable warp bubble, demonstrating both stable and unstable configurations within the same framework. Our research provides the first comprehensive analysis of a specific warp drive setup and helps address the lack of stable solutions in the Alcubierre spacetime.

The management of urban underground infrastructure systems, encompassing metro, sewer, gas, and water networks among others, poses a high level of complexity. This complexity stems from the interconnected, age-old, and partly hidden nature of these systems, making it difficult for decision-makers to handle decision problems effectively. The GUIDES framework aims to address this issue by providing a versatile model to support a wide range of management tasks, incorporating multi-faceted information and optimized solutions for near-optimal outcomes. This paper showcases the applications and benefits of the GUIDES framework in practical scenarios within the existing Berlin metro system.

To assess the heat generated by an electric current in a two-dimensional plasma arrangement, researchers measured the thermal energy released within a Penning trap holding approximately 83 kilogram electrons. This was achieved by analyzing the plasma's quasi-steady quadratic shift in response to varying ambient radiation power. Specifically, they measured a maximum temperature increase of 238 nanokelvin per second, which aligns with theoretical predictions based on Coulomb crystal electron configurations. This experiment served as a laboratory model to investigate ambient heat and electron collision effects on ultra-low-frequency electric currents.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive examination of the electromagnetic and non-electromagnetic aspects of Tip-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy, comprising local optical, infrared spectroscopy, and scanning tunneling microscopy. The primary contributors to the electromagnetic effect stem from plasmonic and photonic phenomena, exhibiting diverse spatial distribution, spectral characteristics, and time-dependent behavior. In contrast, non-electromagnetic effects, such as molecular syndication, electron transfer, and phonon coupling, primarily contribute to chemical bond formation, electron hopping, and molecular rigidity, respectively. Our review delves into the interdisciplinary origins of these processes, highlighting the significance of electromagnetic and non-electromagnetic interactions for ultimately understanding molecules at contact, near-contact, and non-local levels.

Our team's past research revealed the presence of Anti-Matter Excess (AME) in the CAPSULE experiment's photon measurements at the Super-Beta-II set-up.
